name: Russian Federation (G0011)

techniques.comment:
Mass unlawful detentions and abductions of civilians in the occupied territories: "armed groups continued to commit abductions, to subject people to physical and psychological torture and ill-treatment," and "people were abducted for ransom, for forced labor, and for exchange for fighters captured by the Ukrainian authorities"(Citation: Доклад Верховного комиссара ООН по правам человека о положении в области прав человека в Украине (A/HRC/27/75) 2014).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers abducted Chechens and concealed information about their fate, whereabouts or condition from their relatives.

Russian servicemen, fighters of OMON (police special forces) and of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) detained Chechens at checkpoints and led them away from their homes, sometimes at night(Citation: Условия содержания задержанных в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чеченской Республике. Обращение с задержанными 1995)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996). Russian soldiers checked passports against arrest lists, which they received from the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs, detained Chechens by them even with documents and passes, and then handed them over to the headquarters of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs in Ichkeria. Women and old people also ended up on these lists(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

Russian servicemen and police officers did not let detained Chechens inform their families about themselves, and their relatives considered them missing. The occupiers put the abducted in pits at military units and did not register the arrest (see: "Filtration Camp System")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996).

The Russian military transported detained Chechens from commandant's offices to filtration camps, and on the way people often disappeared without a trace. When relatives found out where a person was being held, the Russian guards immediately moved him elsewhere(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

To inquiries about missing people who appeared on the lists of the filtration camps, Russian agencies replied that these people had been released(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). The Chechen society "Victims of War" searched for Chechens whom the occupiers had detained in Grozny and at checkpoints from 11 December 1994 to May 1995, and did not find a single one of them on the Russian list of 252 released. At the addresses from the Russian lists, the women of the society found no people with such surnames(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

Relatives of the missing filed statements with the society "Victims of War". As of 8 August 1995, 1308 peaceful citizens of Ichkeria were listed as missing(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). By mid-October 1996, the society's list held 1432 missing Chechens(Citation: Russia/Chechnya: A Legacy of Abuse 1997). In the spring of 1997, Ichkeria handed Russia a list of 1563 missing(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

The Russian military tortured and killed some of the abducted, and relatives later found their bodies where Russian units had been stationed (see: "Killing of Prisoners and Detainees")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 9 January 1995, the occupiers detained Shamsa Magomadov in Grozny, and the guards of the filtration camp in Mozdok, a town in Russian-controlled North Ossetia, recorded that they had released him on 2 February(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). Shamsa Magomadov did not return home, and in the winter of 1995-1996 the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs promised his sister to exchange her brother for a captured Russian soldier (see: "Hostage-Taking")(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 21 May 1995, at checkpoint No. 13 near Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, the Russian military detained Ruslan Parshoev from that village, and the Russian major Morozov took him to his unit near Assinovskaya, a stanitsa in the west of Ichkeria. The next day, Lvov, the chief of staff of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs in Ichkeria, ordered the detainee sent to Khankala, the main base of the occupation troops on the eastern outskirts of Grozny, where he was taken by fighters of the "Rus" special forces unit, and Ruslan Parshoev went missing(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). In the summer of 1995, the occupiers abducted at a checkpoint on the road to Grozny Khamad Kurbanov, the representative of the president of Ichkeria in Russia, who had just been released after a month without charge in a Moscow prison(Citation: Russia: Amnesty calls on Russian authorities to release or charge Chechen detainees 1995). Russian guards held Khamad Kurbanov in a pit near Assinovskaya and in the filtration camp in Grozny until a commission under the international OSCE mission secured his release at the negotiations between Russia and Ichkeria(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). On 23 December 1995, the Russian military, working from lists, took Ruslan Soslambekov, chairman of the movement "People's Diplomacy for Peace and Unity", at a checkpoint at the entrance to Grozny, kept him for 28 days in the filtration camp on the outskirts of the city, then released him(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996).

In February 1996, the Russian military stopped at checkpoints 26 acquaintances of Madina Magomadova from the society "Victims of War", and all of them disappeared(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

At dawn on 1 August 1996, OMON fighters of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs in helicopters, jeeps and armored personnel carriers attacked the settlement of Dolinsky north-west of Grozny(Citation: CHECHEN REPUBLIC - RUSSIAN FEDERATION: "Disappearance" / Possible extrajudicial execution (UA 196/96, EUR 46/35/96) 1996). Movla Idrisov from Dolinsky told a Reuters correspondent on the day of the raid that the OMON men went into the first and second floors, led away all the men they found, and left one: a 65-year-old with one leg, on crutches(Citation: Dawn raiders seize Chechens 1996). The urgent action of Amnesty International of 6 August 1996 says that the OMON men led away 18 Chechens, among them Aslanbek Gassayev and Umakh Mogamedov: "The men were led with sacks over their heads to a waiting bus and driven away. They have not been seen since"(Citation: CHECHEN REPUBLIC - RUSSIAN FEDERATION: "Disappearance" / Possible extrajudicial execution (UA 196/96, EUR 46/35/96) 1996). In 1996, the UN Working Group on Enforced Disappearances requested from Russia information on the fate of two of them, and in 1997 Russia replied that their cases were being investigated by the Prosecutor General's Office, the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the FSB(Citation: Report of the Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances (E/CN.4/1997/34) 1996)(Citation: Report of the Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances (E/CN.4/1998/43) 1998).

On 24 August 1996, eight Russian soldiers led away from a yard in Grozny Aleksei Karmayev, a 67-year-old disabled man who had complained to the headquarters of the 276th Regiment of the Russian army about looting, after which the disabled man went missing(Citation: Russia/Chechnya: A Legacy of Abuse 1997)(Citation: Russia/Chechnya: Report to the 1996 OSCE Review Conference 1996).

By the end of October 1996, the prison department of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs replied to a list of more than 1300 missing, handed over after the ceasefire in June 1996, that forty people from the list had been held in custody and released, but all forty had been released before 1993, before the war. About the rest the department said nothing. On 22 January 1997, Izmailov, an officer of the Russian search group, said on air on the ORT television channel that the missing Chechens were most likely no longer alive, and did not specify whether the Russian military had killed them in battle or shot them on detention, or whether they had died in custody(Citation: Russia/Chechnya: A Legacy of Abuse 1997). In January 1998, the UN Working Group on Enforced Disappearances reported that Russia had not clarified the fate of a single missing person about whom it had been asked(Citation: Report of the Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances (E/CN.4/1998/43) 1998).

On 10 June 1996, the working groups of Russia and Ichkeria on the search for the missing agreed to stop detentions based on lists and other papers without legal force(Citation: Protocol of the Meeting of the Working Groups, Formed under the Negotiations Commissions, to Locate Missing Persons and to Free Forcibly Detained Persons 1996).

In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996). On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Russian servicemen and police officers extorted money, gold, cars and other valuables from Chechens.

At checkpoints, Russian police officers and soldiers took money from drivers for passage and took cars away from Chechens. Such posts stood in Grozny at every stop and on the road from Gudermes to Argun, towns east of Grozny(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

Russian guards of the filtration camps and of the pits at military units demanded money from detained Chechens for their release (see: "Hostage-Taking")(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996)(Citation: Условия содержания задержанных в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чеченской Республике. Обращение с задержанными 1995).

Russian troops surrounded villages and took money from Chechens in exchange for not bombing them and for letting the Chechens leave(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997)(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-083) 1996). Russian servicemen demanded weapons that the Chechens did not have and took money instead. Often, a month after the payment, a new Russian unit surrounded the village and demanded money again(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

On 7-8 April 1995, Russian soldiers who were storming Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, brought the men from Vygonnaya Street out of a basement and demanded gold and money from the women in exchange for not taking the men away. The occupiers took the men, stripped and bound with wire, to the pits near Assinovskaya, a neighboring stanitsa, and to the filtration camp in Mozdok, a town in Russian-controlled North Ossetia (see: "Filtration Camp System")(Citation: Трагедия села Самашки. Чечня. Апрель 1995. Дневник правозащитника 1995). In May, the headquarters of the joint grouping of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs in Ichkeria, in a "Memo", prohibited soldiers at the posts from taking belongings and food from Chechens passing through(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In the summer of 1995, the puppet government in Grozny began paying compensation from the Russian budget to Chechens whose homes the occupiers had destroyed(Citation: Кавказский ренессанс 2002)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Officials of the puppet government who distributed the payments usually kept 15 to 50% of each family's money for themselves. By the count of the Chechen journalist Musa Muradov, of the 60 thousand families of Grozny who had lost their housing, no more than one and a half thousand received money(Citation: Кавказский ренессанс 2002). In the autumn of 1995, Russian soldiers at the checkpoints near Achkhoy-Martan and Sernovodsk, villages in the west of Ichkeria, took from everyone who entered or left the village 100,000 rubles (23 dollars) at Achkhoy-Martan and 50,000 rubles at Sernovodsk(Citation: The situation of human rights in the Republic of Chechnya of the Russian Federation. Report of the Secretary-General (E/CN.4/1996/13) 1996).

Before the assault in March 1996, Chechens in Samashki sold cows to buy weapons, hand them over to the Russian servicemen and save their homes. Zinaida Baisayeva, who lived in the village, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Moscow on 22 April 1996: "Approximately 9-10 times we gave money so that they would not bomb us. But they shelled us anyway every night." On the night of 14 March 1996, the occupiers surrounded Samashki. Russian servicemen told the village head and the elders that they would give a "corridor" so that fighters of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria could leave the village at night, and that they would then check passports and leave. Zainap Baisayeva from this village told the Glasnost tribunal: "For this one-hour corridor they asked, as I was told, 58 million rubles. This money was collected from the residents of the village. My brother gave a million [rubles] — the last he had earned… All the money was handed over to the checkpoint, to whoever was in command there." For a second "corridor", for Chechen civilians to leave the village, the Russian servicemen demanded 10 thousand dollars. Chechens from Samashki told human rights defenders of Memorial that on 14 March the village head took weapons and 50 million rubles (10 thousand dollars) to Russian checkpoint No. 13. On the morning of 15 March, the occupiers gave the Chechens two hours to leave the village (see: "Sham Corridor") and began the assault(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

In the spring of 1996, the occupiers and the puppet government in Grozny forced villages to sign "Protocols on Peace and Accord" and to surrender weapons (see: "Collective Punishment")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Chechens in Gekhi, a village southwest of Grozny, paid Russian servicemen about a hundred million rubles when signing the "Protocol on Peace and Accord". In Mesker-Yurt, a village southeast of Grozny, the occupiers received a hundred thousand rubles from each house(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). On 7 April 1996, Russian servicemen ordered Saidash Shamakhurov from Gikalovo, a village south of Grozny, to drive in his own car to Khankala, the main base of the occupation troops on the eastern outskirts of Grozny. On 27 April, the occupiers exchanged him for a captured Russian soldier (see: "Hostage-Taking"), and three days later returned his car to him, taking 2,000 dollars and one more prisoner for it(Citation: Russia/Chechnya: A Legacy of Abuse 1997). In April 1996, the occupiers surrounded Shali, a town southeast of Grozny, and Russian soldiers at the post did not let Chechens out of the town, demanded money from them and fired into the ground in front of them. On 26 April, more than a thousand Chechen women and children left Shali on foot(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-083) 1996).

The 1995 report of the observer mission of Russian human rights organizations says that Russian guards extorted money where they held detained Chechens before sending them to filtration camps, because no one controlled these places and they had no official status(Citation: Условия содержания задержанных в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чеченской Республике. Обращение с задержанными 1995).

Despite the "Memo", Russian servicemen and police officers kept extorting payments at checkpoints until the end of the war in 1996, and Chechens complained about them to human rights defenders(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

The exploitation of the Odesa tragedy to build a state propaganda myth and invert the roles: the actual picture, per the UN, is clashes "between supporters of unity and supporters of the federalization of Ukraine, as a result of which 48 people died," while the investigation remains incomplete and "no one has yet been held to account"(Citation: Доклад Верховного комиссара ООН по правам человека о положении в области прав человека в Украине (A/HRC/27/75) 2014). The tragedy was used as moral justification for further aggression - by the same device as the "crucified boy" fake, for which "there is no evidence to support Pyshniak's claim"(Citation: Fake: Crucifixion in Slovyansk 2014).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Russia presented its attacks as a forced response and shifted the blame for the war onto Ichkeria.

Russian President Yeltsin, Chernomyrdin, chairman of the government, Defense Minister Grachev and the commanders of the occupation troops declared the offensives of the Russian army a response to attacks and provocations by the army of Ichkeria, and blamed the leadership of Ichkeria for the breakdown of negotiations(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). The commanders said this to journalists of Russian news agencies, radio and television(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Caught in the Crossfire: Civilians in Gudermes and Pervomayskoye 1996).

On the night of 29 November 1994, Russian President Yeltsin declared that the fighting in Ichkeria could not be stopped, and threatened to use all the forces of the state if the army of Ichkeria and the puppet opposition did not lay down their arms within 48 hours(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-94-229) 1994)(Citation: Борис Ельцин дал два дня на размышление 1994). Russia itself had armed the puppet opposition and led it into battle, and on 29 November the Security Council of Russia decided to start the war(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 18 February 1995, during the "ceasefire", Russian artillerymen shelled the positions of the army of Ichkeria near Shali, Argun and Gudermes, towns to the east of Grozny, and the defenders did not return fire (see: "Sham Ceasefire")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 19 February, the Russian government declared that the army of Ichkeria had attacked Russian units on the southern outskirts of Grozny and wrecked the negotiations(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-95-034) 1995).

On 7 April 1995, the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) stormed Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria. On 7 and 8 April, the occupiers killed 103 peaceful Chechens in the village (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). On the evening of 7 April, Russian television channels, citing the military, reported that fighters of the army of Ichkeria had shot the village elders. That day, Russian soldiers had fired on the cars in which the elders were travelling, and all eight people survived (see: "Lies about Its Own Actions")(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). On 1 May 1995, Sergei Kovalyov, a deputy of the Russian parliament, said at a hearing in the US Congress that this report had served as a pretext for a punitive action against the village(Citation: Hearing on Chechnya (CSCE 104-1-6) 1995). In July 1995, six of the ten deputies of the Russian parliament's commission that investigated the causes of the war wrote in their conclusion that the command of the occupation troops had decided to storm Samashki "after yet another killing of three servicemen (border guards)"(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995)(Citation: Госдума о чеченском кризисе 1995)(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-95-141) 1995). The border guards had been killed in January 1995, three months before the storming, in the neighboring stanitsa of Assinovskaya(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995).

After unknown persons made an assassination attempt in Grozny on 6 October 1995 on Romanov, the commander of the occupation troops, Russian President Yeltsin on 9 October and Defense Minister Grachev on 10 October blamed the attempt on supporters of Dzhokhar Dudayev, the president of Ichkeria. Russia suspended negotiations with Ichkeria and ordered the troops to resume the offensive(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-95-196) 1995). On 14 December, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Gudermes, the second-largest town of the republic, and the occupiers stormed it until 20 December and killed at least 267 townspeople (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 26 December, Shkirko, the commander of the occupation troops, stated that whoever opens fire first is to blame for the deaths, and that the fighters of the army of Ichkeria attack first(Citation: Caught in the Crossfire: Civilians in Gudermes and Pervomayskoye 1996).

In January 1996, the Russian government wrote to the UN Secretary-General that Russia had from the very beginning wanted to settle the matter by negotiations, and that supporters of Dzhokhar Dudayev, the president of Ichkeria, were wrecking the peace process with provocations(Citation: The situation of human rights in the Republic of Chechnya of the Russian Federation. Report of the Secretary-General (E/CN.4/1996/13) 1996). In late January, Chernomyrdin, chairman of the Russian government, in a letter to deputies of the Russian parliament, blamed the leadership of Ichkeria for the breakdown of negotiations and promised to launch propaganda before new strikes on the republic. The head of the government warned that casualties were inevitable, including among peaceful Chechens(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 7 May 1996, the crews of five Russian helicopters fired rockets at Urus-Martan, a town south-west of Grozny where there had been no fighting for a year and a half, and killed five Chechens at the market (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: RFE/RL Newsline, 9 May 1996 1996). Fatima Ashgerieva, who was travelling by bus to Urus-Martan that day, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Prague in May 1996: "We did not hear a single shot from the direction of Urus-Martan, only shots from the helicopters"(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). On 10 May, Russian pilots again killed one Chechen in Urus-Martan and seriously wounded eight, among them four children. On 12 May, the crews of Russian helicopters killed 20-year-old Khasmagomed Arsemikov and wounded eight women(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

On 12 May 1996, Tikhomirov, the commander of the occupation troops, justified the strike on Urus-Martan on the Vesti program of the RTR television channel: "There was at the same time an attempt to provoke actions by the federal [Russian] troops… And at the same time fire at the helicopters. Which, of course, provoked retaliatory actions by the federal troops"(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 13 May, officials of the Russian-controlled Urus-Martan district said on the Vremya program of the ORT television channel that there were no armed units in the town and that no one had fired at the Russian helicopters(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-094) 1996). On 13, 14 and 17 May, police of the occupation administration and the Russian military searched houses in Urus-Martan but did not find a single fighter of the army of Ichkeria(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 9 July 1996, a month after Russia and Ichkeria agreed on a ceasefire in Nazran, a town in Russian-controlled Ingushetia, the occupiers began a new offensive (see: "Sham Ceasefire")(Citation: Протокол заседания Комиссий по переговорам о прекращении огня, военных действий и мерах по урегулированию вооруженного конфликта на территории Чеченской Республики 1996). On 17 July, while Russian pilots were bombing the surroundings of Shatoy and Vedeno, villages in the mountains in the south of Ichkeria, Chernomyrdin, chairman of the Russian government, stated that Ichkeria had been the first to resort to provocation, contrary to the agreements signed in Moscow and Nazran(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt, a town in Russian-controlled Dagestan (see: "Sham Treaties")(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996). Three years later, on 21 September 1999, Russian pilots began bombing Grozny, and on 29 September the Russian army invaded the republic again(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Russia officially called the new war a "counter-terrorist operation"(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

The legal formalization of the territory's severance: the treaty on "accession" was signed on March 18, 2014, and the law ratifying it was "Adopted by the State Duma on March 20, 2014, approved by the Federation Council on March 21, 2014"(Citation: Федеральный закон № 36-ФЗ о ратификации договора с Республикой Крым 2014).

The imposition of corrupt gas-supply schemes through intermediary companies: Moscow "used a series of intermediary trading companies (Itera from 1998, Eural Trans Gas from 2003, Rosukrenergo (RUE) from 2005) to transport, and sometimes to supply, the gas to Ukraine," a practice that "was long criticized in European government circles and by corporate governance bodies (where there was concern about their opacity)"(Citation: The Russo-Ukrainian gas dispute of January 2009 2009). RUE's co-owner Dmytro Firtash told the US ambassador in December 2008 outright that "He acknowledged ties to Russian organized crime figure Seymon Mogilevich, stating he needed Mogilevich's approval to get into business in the first place"(Citation: Cable 08KYIV2414: Firtash makes his case to the USG 2008).

The use of economic blackmail and promises of a loan together with a gas discount to coerce V. Yanukovych into derailing the signing of the Association Agreement with the EU: on December 17, 2013, a reduction of the gas price "to 268.5 dollars per thousand cubic meters" (instead of 410) was announced, along with the fact that "Ukraine, under the bilateral agreements, will receive 15 billion dollars from the Russian National Welfare Fund, selling Moscow its government securities for that amount." Putin stressed: "We consider this a temporary solution, bearing in mind that long-term, long-lasting agreements must and will be reached"(Citation: Виктор Янукович и Владимир Путин достигли компромисса в Москве 2013).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Russia decided which journalists could work in Ichkeria, confiscated their footage and persecuted them for reporting on the war.

On 1 December 1994, ten days before the open invasion, Chernomyrdin, chairman of the Russian government, by directive No. 1886-r created the Temporary Information Center(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-94-232) 1994)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 9 December, by resolution No. 1360, the Russian government instructed the center to issue journalists accreditation, the permit to work in Ichkeria, and to withdraw it immediately for information the center deemed false. The government gave the Russian Interior Ministry (MVD) and the FSK (predecessor of today's FSB) the right to expel from Ichkeria any outsiders they deemed dangerous(Citation: Постановление Правительства Российской Федерации № 1360 Об обеспечении государственной безопасности и территориальной целостности Российской Федерации, законности, прав и свобод граждан, разоружения незаконных вооруженных формирований на территории Чеченской Республики 1994).

On 29 December 1994, the Russian MVD announced that the Temporary Information Center's accreditation gave no right to travel where the Russian Internal Troops (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) were stationed(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

At the end of January 1995, the Russian government created the Mobile Information Center in Mozdok, a town in Russian-controlled North Ossetia where the occupiers' headquarters stood. Only this center's accreditation gave journalists the right to be in the "combat zone", and there only under the supervision of servicemen or officials. The occupiers usually counted all of Ichkeria as this zone(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

The Russian military expelled journalists without accreditation from the republic, and detained journalists with accreditation and confiscated their tapes and equipment, explaining that accreditation from the Ministry of Defense or the MVD was also needed(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 15 December 1994, Soskovets, deputy chairman of the Russian government, announced that the government could strip the NTV television channel of its broadcasting license for its reports on the victims of the war in Ichkeria. After public protest, the government dropped this threat(Citation: Attacks on the Press in 1995: Central Europe and the Republics of the Former Soviet Union 1996).

At the end of May 1995, officers of the Russian FSB arrested NTV journalists near the stanitsa of Assinovskaya in the west of Ichkeria for filming Russian troop positions, although the commander of the Russian division had allowed it. The FSB held the journalists for six hours in a filtration camp and released them (see: "Filtration Camp System")(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). On 3 June 1995, the Russian military arrested three foreign journalists on the border between Ichkeria and Russian-controlled Dagestan and reprimanded them for not having the proper accreditation. Four days later, on 7 June, the occupiers let the journalists go to Moscow but confiscated their tapes and film(Citation: Attacks on the Press in 1995: Central Europe and the Republics of the Former Soviet Union 1996).

On 25 June 1995, Yelena Masyuk, a journalist of the Russian television channel NTV, recorded an interview with Shamil Basayev, a commander of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria, in the Nozhai-Yurt district in the southeast of the republic(Citation: Attacks on the Press in 1995: Central Europe and the Republics of the Former Soviet Union 1996). In April 1996, the journalist told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Moscow: "To get accreditation to work in Chechnya, you had to get to the military airfield in Mozdok, where the accreditations were issued — but to drive onto the airfield, you already had to have that accreditation." About the road to Shamil Basayev she told the tribunal: "To get to the Chechen village where, by my guess, Basayev was at the time, I had to walk 12 kilometers on foot around the Russian checkpoints"(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). On 13 July 1995, the Prosecutor General's Office of Russia opened a criminal case against Yelena Masyuk for not telling the investigators where she had taken the interview. At the end of August, the prosecutor's office closed the case without charges and asked the Russian government's press agency to make sure such interviews did not happen again(Citation: Attacks on the Press in 1995: Central Europe and the Republics of the Former Soviet Union 1996).

From 6 to 9 March 1996, while the Armed Forces of Ichkeria were attacking the occupiers in Grozny, Russian officials forbade television crews in the city to film(Citation: Attacks on the Press in 1996: Russia 1997). On 8 August 1996, a Russian soldier at a checkpoint near Grozny told four journalists of foreign media to turn back and threatened to destroy their equipment, and when they turned around, the occupiers fired a grenade launcher at their car and missed. Two hours later, Russian pilots fired on the journalists from helicopters at another entrance to the city but wounded no one(Citation: Attacks on the Press in 1996: Russia 1997).

In its report for 1996, the international organization Committee to Protect Journalists wrote that throughout the war Russian troops refused to recognize journalists' accreditation, spoiled their film, destroyed their equipment and fired on their cars from checkpoints and combat helicopters(Citation: Attacks on the Press in 1996: Russia 1997).

In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996). On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers shelled and bombed entire villages and towns of Ichkeria for refusing to submit.

As a rule, the command of the occupation troops demanded that the Chechens in the villages hand over their weapons, not fire at Russian soldiers, or make the Armed Forces of Ichkeria leave the village(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). In other villages Russian commanders demanded the handover of captured Russian servicemen or passage for their vehicles through the village(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997)(Citation: Прощения нам не будет 1996). Commanders of the occupation troops, citing their intelligence data, demanded that the Chechens in a village hand over an arbitrary number of assault rifles in exchange for safety(Citation: Russia: Partisan War in Chechnya on the Eve of the World War II Commemoration 1995).

If a village did not meet the demands, Russian troops surrounded it. The occupiers did not let Chechens out of the village and did not let food and medicine through to them (see: "Medical and Humanitarian Blockade"). Russian artillery shelled the surrounded village, and aircraft bombed it (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks"). The Russian military opened fire before the deadline they themselves had set, or after the village had handed over its weapons(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Russia: Partisan War in Chechnya on the Eve of the World War II Commemoration 1995).

After fighters of the army of Ichkeria took Russian special forces soldiers prisoner on 8 January 1995, Russian pilots in helicopters threatened to bomb Komsomolskoye, Alkhazurovo and Roshni-Chu, villages to the southwest of Grozny, and then struck the outskirts of Roshni-Chu, although the special forces soldiers were not in the village(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). In January the crews of Russian helicopters scattered over Bamut, a village to the southwest of Grozny, leaflets of the command of the occupation troops threatening to respond with "powerful missile and bomb strikes" if fire was opened from the village at Russian troops(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). In January the occupiers scattered over Shali, a town to the southeast of Grozny, leaflets threatening to open "return fire" "on the whole village" for "a single shot [toward the occupiers] from Shali"(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995).

From 26 February to 3 March 1995 the Russian military at the post near Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, threatened the elders with a strike on the village if they did not persuade their fellow villagers to "settle the matter peacefully"(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). On 8 March the elders undertook to get the army of Ichkeria out of the village and hand over heavy weapons, and the Russian general Kosolapov signed an agreement with them under which Russian troops would not enter Samashki and would not use force against Chechen civilians (see: "False Guarantees of Safety"). The elders fulfilled their obligation, but from 13 March the Russian military at the posts let no one out of Samashki for 25 days and did not let food and medicine through (see: "Transport Blockade")(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). On 6 April Romanov, the deputy commander of the occupation troops, demanded that by seven in the morning of 7 April the village hand over 264 assault rifles, two machine guns and one infantry fighting vehicle and let the Internal Troops of the Russian MVD (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) into the village, but the elders replied that there were not that many weapons in the village(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). On 7 April a Russian general who refused to give his name gave the elders until 4 p.m., but the occupiers began shelling the village with mortars earlier. Yuzbek Shovkhalov, an elder of Samashki who took part in the talks with the command of the occupation troops, told a Memorial observer on 9 April 1995 what happened when Russian troops stormed the village: "'Give us the militants [this is what the Russians called the Armed Forces of Ichkeria].' I say: 'There are no militants here'… Armored personnel carriers... They fire from heavy machine guns. Right in the village. At the house where people live... Either they burn the house down, or the house perishes, anything at all..."(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). On 7 and 8 April the Russian military killed 103 Chechen civilians in Samashki, whom human rights defenders recorded by name (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 3 March 1995 the command of the occupation troops demanded that the Chechens in Argun, Gudermes and Shali, towns to the east and southeast of Grozny, persuade the Armed Forces of Ichkeria to leave in order to save people's lives(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). On 23 March the occupiers captured Argun, and on 30-31 March, when the defenders were forced to leave, Gudermes and Shali (see: "Military Intervention")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 8 April Labunets, the commander of the occupation troops in the south of Ichkeria, threatened in writing to shell Zakan-Yurt, a village to the east of Samashki, with artillery if the Chechens in the village did not hand over their weapons and surrender the fighters of the army of Ichkeria, and on 11 April soldiers of the Russian MVD searched every yard and found no weapons(Citation: Трагедия села Самашки. Чечня. Апрель 1995. Дневник правозащитника 1995)(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). In April 1995 the Chechens in Bachi-Yurt, Koshkeldy and Alleroy, villages in the east of Ichkeria, under threat of bombing bought assault rifles and handed them over to the occupiers, but the Russian military shelled these villages anyway (see: "Total Destruction of Infrastructure")(Citation: Russia: Partisan War in Chechnya on the Eve of the World War II Commemoration 1995)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). The Internal Troops of the Russian MVD and the Russian police kept Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria where more than 10,000 people and more than 3,000 refugees lived, encircled for more than five months, from 30 September 1995 until the storming in March 1996(Citation: Прощения нам не будет 1996)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Artemov, the commander of the occupation troops in the southwest of Ichkeria, threatened the village in writing with artillery and air strikes if the village did not disarm about a hundred fighters of the army of Ichkeria and let Russian vehicles through Sernovodsk(Citation: Прощения нам не будет 1996).

On 11 February 1996 the command of the occupation troops demanded that the Chechens in Novogroznensky, a settlement in the east of Ichkeria, hand over their weapons and expel the defenders, and when the defenders did not leave, the occupiers killed at least 50 Chechen civilians in the settlement by shelling and storming (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). In March 1996 the Russian military demanded that Katyr-Yurt, a village to the southwest of Grozny, hand over assault rifles and ten captured Russian soldiers who were not in the village, and on 28 March a Russian pilot dropped bombs on the village and killed nine people from the Khazhgiriyev family (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In the spring of 1996 the command of the occupation troops and the puppet government in Grozny forced villages to sign a "Protocol on Peace and Accord". Under this document a village undertook to surrender the defenders, hand over weapons and let the Russian military in, and for a single fighter of the army of Ichkeria found in the village the occupiers threatened to shoot Chechens and destroy the village(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). On 31 March 1996 Russian President Yeltsin, by Decree No. 435, made the signing of such protocols part of his program for Ichkeria(Citation: Указ Президента Российской Федерации от 31 марта 1996 г. № 435 «О программе урегулирования кризиса в Чеченской Республике» 1996), and Russian aircraft bombed villages that refused to sign the protocol(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 17 April 1996 the Chechens in Chiri-Yurt, a village to the south of Grozny, released captured Russian servicemen under an ultimatum from General Shamanov, but as the occupiers' vehicles were leaving the village, Russian tank crews with a single shot razed to the ground the house of the family of Abdulla Dakhayev, the representative of the authorities of Ichkeria in Chiri-Yurt(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 19 April the occupiers surrounded Shali, and on 25 April demanded that the town surrender the defenders, hand over weapons and release captured Russian soldiers. On the same day Russian pilots bombed the town (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-083) 1996)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). At the end of April the elders of Komsomolskoye signed a peace agreement with the occupiers, but from 30 April to 1 May Russian pilots bombed the village and wounded four Chechen civilians(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-087) 1996). On 6 May Russian troops captured Shali without a fight; there turned out to be no defenders or prisoners there(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On that day the occupiers surrounded Komsomolskoye and threatened to destroy it if the fighters of the army of Ichkeria did not hand over their weapons by nightfall, but at about three in the afternoon, before the deadline, Russian artillery opened fire and killed several Chechen civilians(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

On 8 July 1996 Tikhomirov, the commander of the occupation troops, at a press conference in Khankala, the main base of the occupation troops on the eastern outskirts of Grozny, threatened Ichkeria with retaliatory measures if Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, the acting president of Ichkeria, did not return all Russian prisoners on 9 July(Citation: Ультиматум — оружие миротворцев 1996). From 9 to 15 July Russian troops surrounded and shelled Gekhi, a village to the southwest of Grozny where a unit of the army of Ichkeria was stationed, and Makhkety, a mountain village in the southeast of the republic. In Gekhi the occupiers killed 19 Chechen civilians, in Makhkety 25 (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-139) 1996)(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999)(Citation: Путь к миру вымощен «адекватными мерами» 1996). From 10 July the occupation command introduced a curfew in Ichkeria and banned driving into and out of Grozny by car(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999).

The Russian military destroyed the houses of relatives of the leaders of Ichkeria and the commanders of its army(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). On 15 July 1996 the crews of seven Russian helicopters struck Starye Atagi, a village to the south of Grozny, with missiles and destroyed the house of the mother of Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, the acting president of Ichkeria, but the mother and the neighbors survived(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999)(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-139) 1996). In the summer of 1996 the Russian military blew up the house of the father of Shamil Basayev, one of the commanders of the army of Ichkeria, in the mountain village of Vedeno(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 19 August 1996 Pulikovsky, the acting commander of the occupation troops, demanded that the army of Ichkeria leave Grozny and gave the citizens of Ichkeria 48 hours to leave the city, where, according to some data, at least 50-70 thousand people remained, and according to others, 300 thousand(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999)(Citation: Human Rights Watch World Report 1997: The Russian Federation 1997). The general threatened after that deadline to strike the city with aircraft, artillery and multiple rocket launchers, which cannot fire with precision, and on the night of 20 August, without waiting for the deadline to expire, the occupiers resumed the shelling and bombing of Grozny(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999).

The human rights defenders of Memorial write that the command of the occupation troops made its demands of a whole village and, in case of refusal, threatened reprisals against everyone who lived in it(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). A Human Rights Watch report of May 1995 says that demands to hand over weapons sometimes serve the Russian military as a pretext for attacking a village or for detaining Chechens(Citation: Russia: Partisan War in Chechnya on the Eve of the World War II Commemoration 1995). It is unknown how many such crimes the occupation troops committed from December 1994 to August 1996.

On 21 August 1996 General Lebed, the secretary of the Russian Security Council, canceled General Pulikovsky's threat to strike Grozny and called it a bad joke to journalists(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999)(Citation: Оказывается, это была шутка 1996).

In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996). On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

An attempt to strike a deal with the US leader over Kyiv's head in order to block Ukraine's Euro-Atlantic integration under the threat of its dismemberment: Ukraine's accession to NATO would create "a field of conflict for you and us, long-term confrontation," while Moscow, relying on anti-NATO forces, "would be working on stripping NATO of the possibility of enlarging. Russia would be creating problems there all the time"(Citation: Memorandum of Conversation: Meeting with President of Russia (Sochi) 2008). As retold by Kommersant's source from the summit itself: "You understand, George, that Ukraine is not even a state! What is Ukraine? Part of its territory is Eastern Europe, and part - a considerable part - was gifted by us!" - with a transparent hint "that Russia could begin the severance of Crimea and Eastern Ukraine"(Citation: Блок НАТО разошелся на блокпакеты 2008).

Total indoctrination of Russian society with the ideas of the philosopher I. Ilyin (so-called "white fascism") and the transformation of the "Russian World" concept into a state ideology (rashism) that justifies the metropole's cultural superiority and existential right to violence against its neighbors(Citation: Рашизм: Звір з безодні 2023).

The use of a hacker group linked to the security services to compromise Ukrainian artillerymen's software: "the filename 'Попр-Д30.apk' was linked to a legitimate application which was initially developed domestically within Ukraine by an officer of the 55th Artillery Brigade named Yaroslav Sherstuk," and "in-depth reverse engineering revealed the APK contained an Android variant of X-Agent" - an implant whose exclusive operator is FANCY BEAR(Citation: Danger Close: Fancy Bear Tracking of Ukrainian Field Artillery Units 2016). The same toolkit was used in cyberattacks on the Ukrainian power grid in the winters of 2015 and 2016(Citation: 2015 Ukraine Electric Power Attack 2023)(Citation: 2016 Ukraine Electric Power Attack 2023).

Масштабные операции спецслужб РФ по кибершпионажу, перехвату данных (в том числе через взлом публичных сетей Wi-Fi) и скрытому развертыванию деструктивного ПО против украинских организаций и граждан(Citation: APT28 Nearest Neighbor Campaign 2025)(Citation: Campaign C0026 2023).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Throughout the war, Russia called the army and the authorities of Ichkeria "bandits", "bandit formations" and "terrorists", and Chechens "militants".

On 2 November 1993, Russian president Yeltsin, by decree No. 1833, approved a military doctrine under which the army could be used against "illegal armed formations"(Citation: Указ Президента Российской Федерации от 2 ноября 1993 г. № 1833 «Об Основных положениях военной доктрины Российской Федерации» 1993)(Citation: Постановление Конституционного Суда Российской Федерации № 10-П по делу о проверке конституционности указов Президента и постановления Правительства о Чеченской Республике 1995). With these words Russian officials designated the Armed Forces of Ichkeria(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 27 December 1994, Russian president Yeltsin, in a televised address to the citizens of Russia, called some of the defenders of Ichkeria professional "terrorists" and mercenaries from other states. The president set Russian soldiers and police officers the task of disarming the "bandit formations". Yeltsin warned Russians that their relatives could fall victim to the "rampant banditry" in Ichkeria(Citation: Обращение Президента РФ Б. Н. Ельцина к гражданам в связи с ситуацией в Чечне (телеэфир 27 декабря 1994 года) 1994). Commanders of the occupation forces called the people in Grozny and in the villages that the Russian army was pounding "bandit formations" and "militants"(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

A soldier of the Russian border troops who fought in Ichkeria told the newspaper Rossiyskiye Vesti about retraining in Stavropol, a city in the south of Russia. There the soldiers were told to set booby traps without thinking about who would be blown up by them: a child would grow up to be a "mujahid", and a woman would give birth to a new "militant"(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 7 April 1995, the Internal Troops of Russia's Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) began the assault on Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). On 8 April, a Russian soldier was driving women and children out of a cellar on Vygonnaya Street. Mariet T., a Chechen woman from that street, told observers of Memorial that the occupier shouted at them: "These aren't women, they're bitches, whores, they kill ours too, and we're supposed to spare theirs?!" Then the Russian military herded some of the women into a room and others into a cellar and shot at them (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians"). Ruslan N. from Samashki recalled how MVD soldiers detained him that day: "They took my passport and right there, in front of me, tore it up… 'You'll go down as a militant. You've got a militant's mug'". At a military unit north of the village, the servicemen beat him unconscious. Ruslan N. survived(Citation: Трагедия села Самашки. Чечня. Апрель 1995. Дневник правозащитника 1995).

Russian officials and military men, from the prime minister to the soldier conducting a search, called the authorities of Ichkeria "bandits"(Citation: Этот день победы... 1995)(Citation: OMRI Daily Digest, 20 January 1995 1995), its army "bandit formations"(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010) and "terrorists"(Citation: План Ельцина по Чечне 1996)(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-063) 1996), and Chechen civilians "bandits"(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996) and "militants"(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. On 11 and 12 July 1996, unknown persons blew up two trolleybuses in Moscow(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). According to Amnesty International, at the site of the second explosion Moscow mayor Luzhkov told a Russian police general that all Chechens should be expelled from the city. The general replied that if he were allowed to, he would introduce terror on the streets. Alexander Litvinenko, a former FSB officer, and the historian Yuri Felshtinsky write that those who blew up the trolleybuses "were not caught and… it was not determined whether they were Chechens or not"(Citation: ФСБ взрывает Россию 2002). In the two days after the explosions, the Moscow police, which verified documents "overwhelmingly against dark-skinned people", detained 5,770 people for violating residence registration rules(Citation: Human Rights Watch World Report 1997: The Russian Federation 1997). In a 1999 report, Amnesty International wrote that for several years Luzhkov's statements served the police as an implied instruction to persecute and intimidate Chechens solely because they were Chechens(Citation: Russian Federation: For the Motherland. Reported grave breaches of international humanitarian law. Persecution of ethnic Chechens in Moscow (EUR 46/46/99) 1999).

At a hearing in the US Congress, the Russian journalist Yevgenia Albats said that those whom Russia called "bandits" were ordinary citizens who had stood up for their land, their houses and their families(Citation: Hearing on Chechnya (CSCE 104-1-6) 1995). Human rights defenders of Memorial write that until June 1995, and again from late January 1996, Russia waged the war without calling it a war or the enemy an enemy(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

The official denial of the Ukrainian nation's right to independent statehood: the article by the head of the Russian state declares outright that "Ukraine's genuine sovereignty is possible precisely in partnership with Russia," while "the wall that has arisen in recent years between Russia and Ukraine" is declared a split of "between parts of what is essentially one historical and spiritual space"(Citation: Статья Владимира Путина «Об историческом единстве русских и украинцев» 2021).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Russia did not recognize Ichkeria as an independent state, nor its elected president and government as a party to the war and to negotiations.

On 9 December 1994, two days before the open invasion, Chernomyrdin, chairman of the Russian government, by Resolution No. 1360 ordered the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Ministry of Defense to disarm the "illegal armed formations" (as Russia called the Armed Forces of Ichkeria)(Citation: Постановление Правительства Российской Федерации № 1360 Об обеспечении государственной безопасности и территориальной целостности Российской Федерации, законности, прав и свобод граждан, разоружения незаконных вооруженных формирований на территории Чеченской Республики 1994). On 17 December, Russian President Yeltsin, by Decree No. 2200, created a Russian administration for Ichkeria. On 20 December, the Russian government, by Resolution No. 1411, obliged all enterprises, organizations and institutions of the republic to carry out the decisions of this administration (see: "Installation of a New System of Governance")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

Throughout the war, the president, ministers and generals of Russia refused to negotiate with the leadership of Ichkeria or demanded that it first surrender its weapons and disband its army(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 1 February 1995, Ilyushenko, acting Prosecutor General of Russia, charged Dzhokhar Dudayev, the elected president of Ichkeria, with high treason, calls for terrorism, violation of national and racial equality and violation of the law on referendums(Citation: OMRI Daily Digest, 2 February 1995 1995). The Prosecutor General's Office of Russia issued a warrant for the arrest of the Chechen president and put him on the all-Russian wanted list(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 30 July 1995, Russia signed an agreement with Ichkeria on the cessation of hostilities. The Russian delegation added to its first line that Ichkeria was not recognized by the legislation of Russia(Citation: Чечня (Нохчичьо) - взгляд изнутри 1995)(Citation: Agreement on the peaceful regulation of the situation in the Chechen Republic (on a set of military issues) 1995).

On 12 December 1994, the day after the open invasion, the Russian delegation at the negotiations in Vladikavkaz, the capital of North Ossetia, demanded that the representatives of Ichkeria recognize the republic as part of Russia(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 17 December 1994, Dzhokhar Dudayev, the president of Ichkeria, informed Yeltsin by telegram that he had ordered a ceasefire against the Russian troops and proposed to begin negotiations without preconditions, which he would lead himself(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-94-243) 1994). On 18 December, Yeltsin by telegram ordered the president of Ichkeria to appear that same day in Mozdok, a town in Russian-controlled North Ossetia, at the headquarters of the occupation troops and to sign a document on the surrender of weapons and a ceasefire(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-94-243) 1994)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). The press service of the Russian president told the Russian news agency ITAR-TASS that further telegrams from the Chechen president would not be answered(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-94-244) 1994). On 23 December, Dzhokhar Dudayev conveyed through Sergei Kovalyov, the Russian human rights commissioner, to Russian Foreign Minister Kozyrev that he was ready to cease fire immediately and to negotiate on everything, including the disarmament of the army of Ichkeria, but received no answer from Moscow(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 27 December, Yeltsin, in a televised address to the citizens of Russia, declared: "the regime in Grozny [as the Russian president called the government of Ichkeria] is illegal", and of negotiations he said: "The subject of negotiations is a ceasefire and the surrender of weapons"(Citation: Обращение Президента РФ Б. Н. Ельцина к гражданам в связи с ситуацией в Чечне (телеэфир 27 декабря 1994 года) 1994)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 31 December, the Russian army began the storming of Grozny, the capital of Ichkeria (see: "Military Intervention")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 18 January 1995, Russian President Yeltsin said on Russian television that he would not talk to Dzhokhar Dudayev(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). From February to June 1995, Russian Defense Minister Grachev and Kulikov, the commander of the occupation troops, replied to the proposals of a ceasefire from Aslan Maskhadov, the chief of the Main Staff of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria, that they would talk only about the surrender of weapons and the disbanding of the army of Ichkeria(Citation: Russia: Three Months of War in Chechnya 1995)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: OMRI Daily Digest, 19 May 1995 1995). On 19 May 1995, Yeltsin rejected the law by which, on 12 April, Russian deputies had instructed the Russian government to begin direct negotiations with the leadership of Ichkeria immediately and without preconditions(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: OMRI Daily Digest, 22 May 1995 1995). On 5 July 1995, two weeks after negotiations with Ichkeria began in Grozny, Chernomyrdin, chairman of the Russian government, and the Russian negotiators declared that they would not discuss its status(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 10 January 1996, Chernomyrdin, chairman of the Russian government, said: "Chechnya is Russia"(Citation: У нас там не оказалось подводной лодки: Кизляр - Первомайское, январь 1996 1996). On 11 January, the Russian government, in a letter to the UN Secretary-General, named the government of Ichkeria as the cause of the war, declaring it illegal and Ichkeria itself part of Russia(Citation: The situation of human rights in the Republic of Chechnya of the Russian Federation. Report of the Secretary-General (E/CN.4/1996/13) 1996). On 7 April, Mikhailov, Russian minister for nationalities, said that the parties to the negotiations should be the commanders of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria. On 17 April, Russian Justice Minister Kovalyov declared that direct negotiations with Dzhokhar Dudayev, "a subject of criminal proceedings", were impossible, and invited him to come to a Russian court. On 21 April, the Russian military killed the president of Ichkeria (see: "Neutralization of the Opposition"). On 25 April, Justice Minister Kovalyov announced that negotiations with the commanders of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria would be conducted by the puppet government in Grozny(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 27 May 1996, Russian President Yeltsin received in the Kremlin, for negotiations on a ceasefire, a delegation of Ichkeria headed by Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, acting president of Ichkeria. The Russian organizers of the meeting assigned the representatives of Ichkeria seats at the side of the table, while Yeltsin sat at its head. Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev demanded to sit opposite the Russian president, as at negotiations between two states, and to Yeltsin's "Sit down" he replied across the negotiating table: "I will not sit down to that tone". The Russian president moved to the middle of the table(Citation: Итоги: переговоры Ельцина и Яндарбиева в Кремле 1996). The Russian delegation did not write the names of the parties into the ceasefire agreement, and Chernomyrdin, chairman of the Russian government, and Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev signed it with their surnames and no titles. Mikhailov, Russian minister for nationalities, explained this to journalists at a press conference at the Russian news agency Interfax: "If we had written 'Ichkeria', that would practically mean recognizing the existence of a republic that does not exist..."(Citation: Итоги: переговоры Ельцина и Яндарбиева в Кремле 1996). On 28 May, the Russian organizers of the meeting did not let the delegation of Ichkeria meet with Moscow journalists, and in the evening the delegation flew to Russian-controlled Ingushetia(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 25 July 1996, General Pulikovsky, acting commander of the occupation troops, told journalists that with the commanders of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria he would discuss only the place and time of the surrender of weapons(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-145) 1996). On 28 July, Pulikovsky replied on air on the Russian television channel RTR to Aslan Maskhadov's proposal to discuss ending the war that he did not know where to look for the leadership of Ichkeria(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-146) 1996)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

Human rights defenders of Memorial write that the president and government of Russia called the war their internal affair(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 31 August 1996, General Lebed, secretary of the Security Council of Russia, and Aslan Maskhadov, the chief of the Main Staff of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria, signed in Khasavyurt, a town in Russian-controlled Dagestan, the agreements on the withdrawal of the occupation troops (see: "Sham Treaties"). Russia and Ichkeria postponed the decision on the independence of Ichkeria for five years, until 31 December 2001(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). The word "Ichkeria" does not appear in the agreements: the republic is called the Chechen Republic(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996). In September 1999, the Russian army invaded Ichkeria for the second time since 1994(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers left Chechens without drinking water.

Russian pilots and artillerymen more than once destroyed substations and the water supply system in Grozny, the capital of Ichkeria, leaving the townspeople without water(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996)(Citation: Russian Federation/Northen Caucasus: Drinking water scarce in Grozny 1996).

Russian servicemen fired from armored personnel carriers and helicopters at Chechens who were going for water (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")(Citation: Russia: Three Months of War in Chechnya 1995)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

On 31 January 1995, the occupiers shelled Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, from tanks and helicopters, leaving the Chechens in the village without water (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). In February 1995, Russian artillery shelled and aircraft bombed Argun, a town east of Grozny. Chechens in Argun hid in basements and went out for water only between seven and nine in the morning, while the crews of Russian helicopters fired at passers-by in the streets(Citation: Russia: Three Months of War in Chechnya 1995).

During the assault on Grozny in February 1995, Russian servicemen in the Katayama settlement within the city limits shot 28-year-old Dzhenchuraeva with the cannon of an armored personnel carrier as she was carrying water. Her brother tried to carry the body home and survived, although the occupiers wounded him in the shoulder. Lipkan Bazaeva, a teacher from Grozny and the wife of the murdered woman's cousin, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Prague in May 1996: "She went for water, believing that a woman would not be killed"(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

On 7 April 1995, the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) and OMON troops (police special forces) stormed Samashki. On 8 April, Russian soldiers searched houses in the village and set fire to most of them (see: "Total Destruction of Infrastructure"). On 10 April, a Chechen woman named Karnukaeva of Rabochaya Street told the mission about soldiers in the neighbors' yard, where she had hidden on 8 April: "They say to the old woman: 'Is this your drinking water?' Чечня. Апрель 1995. Дневник правозащитника 1995).

Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996). On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).
