Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

Russian servicemen brought bodies in a "Ural" truck to the Karpinsky cemetery in the west of Grozny from the checkpoints and from the filtration camps to which the occupiers took detained Chechens. Gravediggers laid them in fresh pits, three to five in each(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996). At the start of the war, the Russian army took some of the bodies to Rostov, a city in the south of Russia, to the refrigerator railcars of its 124th medical laboratory, and did not give them back to the families of the dead(Citation: Безымянные солдаты 1997)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

On 17 December 1994, Russian soldiers in armored personnel carriers shot up a column of cars with refugees from Grozny near the border with Russian-controlled Ingushetia and killed ten people. The occupiers took the bodies away, and the Russian police in Ingushetia found only one of them(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 31 December 1994, the occupiers detained two young Chechens in the basement of a hospital in Grozny, where they were hiding from the shelling. The parents of one of them later collected his body from a morgue in Moscow and buried him at home, while the relatives of the other had still not found him by 2015(Citation: «Хуже всего - не знать»: День пропавших без вести 2015). From December 1994 to May 1995, the occupiers detained 27 Chechens in Grozny and took them to the filtration camp in Mozdok, a town in Russian-controlled North Ossetia, and by April 1996 their bodies were brought back from there. Those whom the Russian escort shot or threw out of the vehicles on the way to Mozdok were buried unidentified by villagers, and relatives later found them by descriptions of the bodies and clothes(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

On 28 January 1995, soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) led two brothers, aged 18 and 21, under escort through their unit on Mayakovsky Street in Grozny, shot them and secretly buried them in the yard of a house on the grounds of the unit. On 2 April, when the unit had left, their father Khusein Khamidov found the grave from a neighbor's account, took the bodies out of the ground in the presence of a forensic doctor and buried his sons by his house(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997)(Citation: Hunt for War Dead Mired in Mistrust 1995). At the end of March 1995, criminal investigators from Moscow began opening the pits with bodies at the cemetery near the cannery in the Zavodskoy district of Grozny. Forensic doctors of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs recorded the cause of death as shooting, death by fire or knife wounds, and some of the bodies had no head(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

On 7 April 1995, the occupation troops stormed Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria. On 7 and 8 April, Russian servicemen went from house to house and killed Chechen civilians (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians"). The 1995 report of the Observer Mission of Russian human rights organizations says: "Numerous accounts by witnesses have been recorded of the deliberate burning by Russian servicemen of the bodies of dead residents." The Mission named 13 people whose bodies the occupiers had burned. On the evening of 7 April, Russian soldiers killed Ali Sugaipov, Emin Nadyrov, Khamzat Kharkharoyev and his son Akhmed, and on the morning of 8 April fellow villagers found their burned bodies in one yard(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). Russian tank crews wounded 62-year-old Dogu Tsatishayev, and soldiers shot him dead at point-blank range with an automatic rifle in house 93 on Sharipov Street, poured gasoline over the body and set it on fire(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). On 20 April, Tamara Mutiyeva from Samashki told observers of the Russian human rights organization "Memorial" that Russian servicemen had killed and burned her half-sister. Andrei Blinushov, one of the observers, recorded in his diary: "To this day the sister and mother of the murdered girl are collecting pieces of her bones in the ruins of the house"(Citation: Трагедия села Самашки. Чечня. Апрель 1995. Дневник правозащитника 1995).

On 9 May 1995, soldiers of the 503rd regiment of the Russian army unlawfully detained at a checkpoint Ayub Domayev, Aslambek Suleimanov and Shamkhan Tashukhadzhiyev from Shali, a town southeast of Grozny, and killed all three (see: "Killing of Prisoners and Detainees"). Vladimir Yemelyanenko, a correspondent of the Moscow weekly Moskovskiye Novosti, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Moscow on 21 February 1996 that the military did not let the relatives onto the grounds of the regiment and in answer to their questions "said that no such people had passed through here"(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996). On 3 June, the 503rd regiment left its camp in a field near Shali, and a conscript soldier who had fled the regiment showed the families where the soldiers had buried the three Chechens. Near the camp of the reconnaissance company, at a depth of two meters, the relatives found the bodies of Ayub Domayev and Aslambek Suleimanov. In another place in the field they dug up the car in which the three Chechens had been traveling, crushed by tank tracks. On 6 June, the body of Shamkhan Tashukhadzhiyev was found at the cemetery on the outskirts of Shali(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996).

In September 1995, Chechen women from Grozny found by the fresh pits at the Karpinsky cemetery five green military shell boxes containing bones and ashes, and handed them over to the OSCE mission. According to the expert examination, one of the boxes contained the remains of people aged 20-23, burned, doused with sulfuric acid and broken into small pieces(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996). In early October 1995, the Czech journalist Petra Procházková filmed at the Orthodox cemetery in Grozny pits with several dozen bodies, to which the occupiers brought new bodies at night in their vehicles, and reported this to the OSCE(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

At the end of February 1996, Russian servicemen killed the detained Sharip Batayev, a Chechen from Arshty, a village in Russian-controlled Ingushetia, and buried the body at a depth of 20 centimeters on a hillside below the trenches of the reconnaissance troops of the 693rd regiment of the Russian 58th Army. On 20 March, investigators from Ingushetia dug up the body, and on the same day it was buried according to Muslim custom(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). From 3 to 9 March 1996, Russian troops stormed Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria, and burned the mosque there, to which on 4 March villagers had brought the bodies of Chechens killed by the occupiers in order to bury them later(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-044) 1996). On 11 March, women from Sernovodsk, whom the occupiers had let home for a few hours, found seven burned bodies by the burned-down mosque(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). During the assault on Sernovodsk, the crews of Russian helicopters wounded an elderly Chechen with rockets at the resort near the village where refugees lived, and the wounded man died on the threshold of his room. The occupiers searched the resort, and after that only burned remains were found where the body had been(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). On 20 March 1996, Russian soldiers who had landed from a helicopter near a dairy farm by Nagornoye, a village next to Grozny, shot detained unarmed Chechens there: two according to Human Rights Watch, five according to the Chechen women's committee. The killers cut off the ears of the dead and slit their stomachs with a knife(Citation: Russia/Chechnya: A Legacy of Abuse 1997)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). On 12 May 1996, Russian troops captured Kharsenoy, a mountain village in the south of Ichkeria, and shot seven young Chechens from the village. Fellow villagers buried one of them, while the bodies of the other six the occupiers never gave back to the relatives(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). On 15 July 1996, in the northwestern suburb of Grozny, soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs from two armored personnel carriers shot unarmed people in passenger cars. The occupiers set fire to the cars with the bodies, and cut off the ears of some of the dead(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-139) 1996)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

The 1997 report of Human Rights Watch says that from March 1995 to January 1997 the "Victims of War" society headed by Khusein Khamidov helped recover 926 bodies from mass graves in Ichkeria. Forensic doctors in Rostov established the names of 426 of them, and about 80 more mass graves had not been opened by January 1997(Citation: Russia/Chechnya: A Legacy of Abuse 1997).

In June 1996, the prosecutor's office of the administration installed by Russia in Grozny handed over to Russian prosecutors 342 cases on crimes of the occupiers, among them on cut-off ears and on bodies thrown from helicopters. Russian prosecutors returned more than half of the cases for further investigation, and closed or did not consider the rest (see: "Impunity of Perpetrators")(Citation: Russia/Chechnya: A Legacy of Abuse 1997). On 3 October 1996, a month after the peace agreements in Khasavyurt, Chernomyrdin, the chairman of the Russian government, and Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, the acting president of Ichkeria, signed a statement in Moscow. Under it, Russia undertook to open access to burial sites for examination and excavation at Ichkeria's first request(Citation: Заявление от 3 октября 1996 года, подписанное руководителями делегаций на переговорах в Москве 1996). By mid-October 1996, Russian officials, contrary to the statement, were not letting the "Victims of War" society open the graves: they said they had no bodies, or demanded bribes(Citation: Russia/Chechnya: A Legacy of Abuse 1997).

In December 1997, several dozen bodies of Chechens, wrapped in blankets, still lay in the refrigerator railcars of the 124th laboratory of the Russian army in Rostov. A delegation of Ichkeria came to Rostov and asked for them back, but the laboratory staff did not return a single body(Citation: Безымянные солдаты 1997). In 2019, Alexander Cherkasov of "Memorial" reported that several years earlier about a hundred unidentified remains from the time of the war had been taken out of the refrigerators of the 124th laboratory: some were sent to the Chechen Republic, others were buried under numbers in cemeteries in Moscow(Citation: Александр Черкасов, председатель Совета ПЦ «Мемориал»: «Нам пришлось подменить собой государство» 2019).

In 2014, Russian servicemen found in the Oktyabrsky district of Grozny a mass grave from the first war with the remains of more than 160 people and took them to Rostov for examination. According to the experts, apart from two Russian servicemen, those lying there were most likely civilian men, women and children. On 31 December 2016, the remains of 109 people from this grave were brought from Rostov to Grozny. Relatives identified two of them by genetic profiles and took them, while the other 107 were buried in two temporary mass graves at the cemetery near the village of Pobedinskoye outside Grozny, and the relatives received no lists of the dead(Citation: В Грозный привезли останки 109 мирных жителей, погибших в первую чеченскую войну 2017)(Citation: Жители Чечни возмутились переносом процедуры опознания останков из братской могилы 2017).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers destroyed the museums, research institutes and ancient monuments of the Chechens.

During the storming of Grozny, Russian artillerymen shelled, and pilots bombed, the center of the city, where the museums and research institutes of Ichkeria stood(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). Russian pilots fired rockets at ancient towers and settlements in the mountains in the south of Ichkeria(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). The occupiers occupied the ruins of museums and looted what had survived (see: "Theft of Cultural Property")(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). Russian troops burned almost the entire Central State Archive of the Chechen Republic and the republican libraries in Grozny (see: "Burning of Books and Archives")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Soldiers of the occupation troops destroyed mosques and leveled ancient burial mounds (see: "Destruction of Shrines and Necropolises")(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

In January 1995, Russian troops destroyed the Chechen National Museum in Grozny. The museum held about 320 thousand exhibits, among them archaeological finds of the ancient and medieval Caucasus, traditional Chechen clothing and old manuscripts(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). The museum's director Isa Adayev told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Prague in May 1996: "From 1 to 4 January 1995, the museum building was shelled quite deliberately from several directions". When the director got to the museum on 7 January, "it was no longer a museum — nothing was left of it — only ruins". On 18 January, Russian special forces seized the ruins(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). Khotin, deputy director of the museum center of the Russian Ministry of Culture, who inspected the ruins of the museum in late March 1995, told the public tribunal of the Glasnost Foundation in Moscow in February 1996: "The nature of the destruction shows that barrage fire was used there. Next to the museum there is a small park of about 50 fairly old trees. Well, all those trees are cut in half. All of them!"(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996).

In early 1995, the occupiers destroyed in Grozny the Research Institute of the Humanities of the Chechen Republic, founded in 1907(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). In 1995, Russian pilots fired rockets at and bombed Kogo-Maista, an old settlement in the mountains in the south of Ichkeria, far from the fighting. In the strikes, the occupiers destroyed six towers that had stood for thirteen centuries, killed the Chechen boy Deni Murtazov and wounded a woman of his family so badly that she became disabled(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

The human rights defenders of "Memorial" write that Russian troops destroyed or irreparably damaged in Grozny the university, the pedagogical and petroleum institutes, and the geological museum. In "Memorial's" assessment, Russian troops did not take the rescue of cultural property into account and inflicted irreparable damage on the culture of the Chechen people(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996). On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

The deliberate injection of false historical narratives into the international arena: Ukraine, according to the Russian leader, "is not a nation built in a natural manner" and "an artificial country created back in Soviet times," and its territories were supposedly gifts - "In the 1920s and 1930s Ukraine obtained territory from Russia -- that's the eastern part of the country. In 1956, the Crimean peninsula was transferred to Ukraine"(Citation: Memorandum of Conversation: Meeting with President of Russia (Sochi) 2008). From this the thesis of its possible disintegration was derived: "the country could just split apart"(Citation: Memorandum of Conversation: Meeting with President of Russia (Sochi) 2008).

The official denial of Russian troops' participation during the operation – and Putin's later admission (call-in show, 17 April 2014) that the denial was a lie: "behind the backs of Crimea's self-defense forces, our servicemen, of course, stood"(Citation: Прямая линия с Владимиром Путиным 2014). In the same broadcast an interlocutor congratulated him on having "honestly said that the 'little green men' are our peaceful military"(Citation: Прямая линия с Владимиром Путиным 2014).

A massive campaign of fabricating fakes to dehumanize Ukrainians: on state television it was claimed that "Ukrainian armed forces herded city residents to the central square and publicly executed a small boy and his mother," yet "there is no evidence to support Pyshniak's claim," and the residents of Sloviansk who were interviewed did not confirm the story(Citation: Fake: Crucifixion in Slovyansk 2014). The same method produced the fabricated "death of a 10-year-old girl" in the Petrovskyi district of Donetsk (March 2015): BBC correspondents on the ground established that no such girl had ever existed(Citation: Би Би Си разоблачили ложь российских СМИ о якобы погибшей 10-летней девочке 2015). In parallel ran an operation to conceal responsibility for the destruction of flight MH17: the Russian Ministry of Defense "made a series of self-contradictory claims blaming Ukraine, rather than Russia or Russian-led separatists, for the Boeing 777's shoot down," while a deputy defense minister publicly repeated "a fabricated claim that originated on Twitter of how a Spanish air traffic controller named Carlos saw two Ukrainian fighter jets near MH17"(Citation: The Kremlin's Shifting, Self-Contradicting Narratives on MH17 2018).

Total information control and a ban on calling the invasion a war - officially it was declared a "special military operation" whose stated aims were "demilitarization and denazification"(Citation: Report of the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine (A/HRC/52/62) 2023). The informational cover for energy terror rested on the "response" narrative: "There is a lot of noise now about our strikes on the energy infrastructure of the neighboring country. Yes, we are doing this. But who started it?"(Citation: Путин назвал удары по энергообъектам Украины ответом на действия Киева 2022).

Direct energy blackmail and the cut-off of gas supplies at the height of winter: on January 1, 2006 - "at 10.00am Moscow time on January 1, 2006, Gazprom cut off gas supplies to Ukraine"(Citation: The Russian-Ukrainian gas crisis of January 2006 2006); on January 1, 2009 - "Russian exports to Ukraine were cut off on 1 January," after which exports to the EU were "drastically reduced on 6 January and cut completely from 7 January," and in the worst-affected Balkan countries a humanitarian emergency ensued, with "parts of the populations unable to heat their homes"(Citation: The Russo-Ukrainian gas dispute of January 2009 2009).

Deliberate restoration of old Soviet or imperial names to captured cities and streets (in particular, the renaming of Bakhmut to Artemovsk) in order to erase Ukrainian national memory and visually integrate them into the space of the Russian Federation.

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Russia expelled human rights defenders from Ichkeria and squeezed out of the republic the international missions that were recording the crimes of the occupiers.

On 9 December 1994, two days before the open invasion, Russian prime minister Chernomyrdin, by resolution No. 1360, ordered officers of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and of the FSK (the predecessor of today's FSB) to expel from Ichkeria visitors whom they deemed a threat to security(Citation: Постановление Правительства Российской Федерации № 1360 Об обеспечении государственной безопасности и территориальной целостности Российской Федерации, законности, прав и свобод граждан, разоружения незаконных вооруженных формирований на территории Чеченской Республики 1994). Under this resolution, the occupiers expelled human rights defenders from the republic more than once(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

The Russian military at checkpoints did not let human rights defenders, deputies of the Russian parliament or the Red Cross into the villages they were storming. When deputies and human rights defenders came to inspect the filtration camps, officers of the occupation forces did not let them talk to the detained Chechens(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

Russian politicians and commanders demanded many times the recall of Tim Guldimann, head of the mission of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), which had been working in Grozny since 24 April 1995(Citation: Supporting the Doves against the Hawks: Experiences of the OSCE Assistance Group to Chechnya 1998)(Citation: Russia/Chechnya: Report to the 1996 OSCE Review Conference 1996).

On 27 January 1995, the Russian Ministry of Defense did not allow Sergei Kovalyov, then Russia's human rights commissioner, to travel with an OSCE delegation to the filtration camp in Mozdok, a town in Russian-controlled North Ossetia. The members of the delegation saw Chechens there with marks of beatings (see: "Torture and Abuse")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Human Rights Watch World Report 1996: The Russian Federation 1996)(Citation: OSCE Group Reports Bilateral Rights Abuses 1995). On 26 March 1995, men of the Russian police special forces detained near Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, participants of the anti-war "Peace March" from Russian civic and religious organizations, took them to Nazran, a town in Russian-controlled Ingushetia, to Assinovskaya, a stanitsa in the west of Ichkeria, and some to Moscow. On 11 April, the Russian military at the checkpoint did not let the marchers into Samashki(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995)(Citation: Трагедия села Самашки. Чечня. Апрель 1995. Дневник правозащитника 1995).

On 7 and 8 April 1995, the Internal Troops of Russia's Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) stormed Samashki and killed 103 Chechen civilians (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). From 8 April, the Russian military at the checkpoint near the village did not let into Samashki the observers of the human rights mission of Sergei Kovalyov, Russia's former human rights commissioner(Citation: Трагедия села Самашки. Чечня. Апрель 1995. Дневник правозащитника 1995)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 11 April, Boris Titenko and Anatoly Shabad, deputies of the Russian parliament, spent an hour persuading the commanders of the post to let them through. Andrei Blinushov, an observer of Memorial, recorded the answer in his diary: "entry into Samashki requires the written permission of the commander of the grouping of MVD troops, Colonel General Kulikov"(Citation: Трагедия села Самашки. Чечня. Апрель 1995. Дневник правозащитника 1995). On 12 April, the Russian military let the observers with the deputies into the village. On 13 April, Kulikov, commander of the occupation forces in Ichkeria, forbade letting into Samashki anyone not registered as a resident of the village, including human rights defenders(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

The occupiers took the Chechen men detained in Samashki to the filtration camp in Mozdok (see: "Filtration Camp System"). On 19 April 1995, Andrei Blinushov and Yuly Rybakov, a deputy of the Russian parliament, came there for an inspection. The report of the human rights defenders' mission says: "all the main documentation was unexpectedly removed from the point [the filtration camp] and the individual questioning of the detainees was cut short". General Yegorov, who in April had replaced Kulikov at the head of the occupation forces, announced to both of them that the inspection was over(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995).

On 19-20 April 1995, Lebedev and Kharchenko, colonels of the occupation forces, denied that there were pits near Assinovskaya where people were being put, and did not let Valery Borshchev, a deputy of the Russian parliament, Sergei Kovalyov, head of the human rights mission, or Memorial staff see the Chechens detained there (see: "Filtration Camp System")(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995)(Citation: Трагедия села Самашки. Чечня. Апрель 1995. Дневник правозащитника 1995)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 26 May 1995, the occupiers, under resolution No. 1360, forcibly took two observers of the human rights mission, Alexander Lavut and Boris Smushkevich, from near Assinovskaya to Mozdok. In June, both observers were working in Grozny again(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 2 June, Kulikov, by this time again in command of the occupation forces, ordered Médecins Sans Frontières to withdraw its teams from Shatoy and Makhkety, villages in the south of Ichkeria, by six in the evening, and announced that for two months no charitable organization could appear in the south of the republic. The same day, both teams left these villages(Citation: War Crimes and Politics of Terror in Chechnya 1994-2004. MSF Speaks Out 2014)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 7 October 1995, unknown persons fired rockets at the building of the OSCE mission in Grozny, and the mayor of the city appointed by Russia demanded that the mission leave. The puppet government overturned the mayor's decision, but on 12 October the OSCE, because of the threat to its staff, temporarily reduced the mission from six people to two(Citation: OSCE voices concern on increasing tension in Chechnya (press release, Vienna, 11 October 1995) 1995)(Citation: OSCE Faces Problems In Chechnya 1996)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). In late October 1995, the occupiers at a checkpoint did not let two members of a British Christian community that opposes wars into Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria. The members of the community drove into the village across a field(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

From 3 to 9 March 1996, while the occupiers were storming Sernovodsk, Russian soldiers at the checkpoints did not let Alexander Guryanov, an observer of Memorial, come closer than 400 meters to the village(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). On 8 March, the Russian military at the checkpoint at the entrance to Sernovodsk fired on two deputies of the Russian parliament, and the commander of the checkpoint threatened to shoot them next time(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). On 10 March, the Russian military commandant of Sernovodsk forbade letting journalists, human rights defenders, foreigners and the Red Cross into the village, and the occupiers threatened to fire on the vehicles of the Red Cross and other humanitarian organizations if they were not moved away from the village(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). From 4 to 9 April, the occupiers did not let a delegation of the British Christian community into Sernovodsk and Samashki, although on 5 April Russian president Yeltsin had announced that international observers could travel freely around the republic(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

On 9 June 1996, the puppet government declared that Tim Guldimann had exceeded his authority when he held direct negotiations with the delegation of Ichkeria, and called the presence of the OSCE mission in the republic undesirable(Citation: RFE/RL Newsline, 10 June 1996 1996)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 24 June, Tikhomirov, commander of the occupation forces, accused the head of the mission at a press conference of taking the side of Ichkeria and of being capable of wrecking the ceasefire negotiations(Citation: Will Lebed Discipline Tikhomirov? 1996). In early August 1996, when the Armed Forces of Ichkeria attacked the occupiers in Grozny, Russian pilots hit the mission building with two rockets from helicopters. Four of its staff hid in the cellar for eight days and were unharmed(Citation: Supporting the Doves against the Hawks: Experiences of the OSCE Assistance Group to Chechnya 1998).

A Human Rights Watch report of January 1997 says that Russian agencies repeatedly obstructed the International Committee of the Red Cross from visiting people detained on criminal charges in connection with the war, and demanded that the committee first obtain a judge's permission(Citation: Russia/Chechnya: A Legacy of Abuse 1997).

In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996). On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

Deliberate mass killings of people without regard to their ethnic origin, solely on the basis of their Ukrainian citizenship and affiliation with the Ukrainian state(Citation: Рашизм: Звір з безодні 2023).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers unlawfully detained Chechens and held them without charges in filtration camps and in pits at military units.

On 12 December 1994, the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs created filtration camps by directive No. 247. The ministry set them up in prison railcars in Mozdok, a town in Russian-controlled North Ossetia, in the prisons of Stavropol and Pyatigorsk, cities in the south of Russia, and in the building of a motor depot in Grozny(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Условия содержания задержанных в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чеченской Республике. Обращение с задержанными 1995).

Russian servicemen together with police officers detained Chechens at checkpoints and during "zachistki" ("sweeps", as Russians called house searches and detentions of Chechens). In its detention orders, the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs most often referred to the decree of the president of Russia of 2 November 1993 No. 1815 "On Measures to Prevent Vagrancy and Begging"(Citation: Указ Президента Российской Федерации от 2 ноября 1993 г. № 1815 «О мерах по предупреждению бродяжничества и попрошайничества» 1993). The decree concerned vagrants, while most of the detained Chechens had their documents on them(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

Before sending them to the camps, the occupiers held Chechens for several days in pits and prison vans at checkpoints and at their bases, in places with no official status(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). There were such pits in the 503rd and 506th regiments of the Russian army near Shali, a town southeast of Grozny(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). From February 1995, the occupiers brought Chechens to Assinovskaya, a stanitsa in the west of Ichkeria, and from there sent them to Mozdok(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In the camps, Russian guards beat and tortured detained Chechens during interrogations, including with electric current (see: "Torture and Abuse"). The guards did not treat the wounded(Citation: Условия содержания задержанных в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чеченской Республике. Обращение с задержанными 1995). The occupiers did not let detained Chechens tell their relatives where they were. For their families, the people went missing (see: "Abduction of People")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

The Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs released most of the detained Chechens from the camps as innocent. From each of them the ministry took a signature saying they had no complaints(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

According to a certificate by Zlydenko, deputy head of Russia's prison service, from 11 December 1994 to 22 July 1995, 1,325 people passed through the camps in Mozdok and Grozny. The Ministry of Internal Affairs handed a hundred of them over to investigators (see: "Manufacturing Criminals"). The ministry gave another 141 people up for exchange for captured Russian servicemen (see: "Hostage-Taking")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

During the storming of Grozny in early January 1995, the Russian troops of General Rokhlin detained men in the bomb shelters near the cannery, where they were hiding from the shelling, and took them to Mozdok(Citation: Условия содержания задержанных в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чеченской Республике. Обращение с задержанными 1995). On 3 January, the guards carried more than 60 of them in the back of a single truck and killed at least eight on the way (see: "Killing of Prisoners and Detainees")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 10 January, the Chechen Umar Kasayev died in the Pyatigorsk prison: the Ministry of Internal Affairs did not give him the medical care he needed(Citation: Условия содержания задержанных в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чеченской Республике. Обращение с задержанными 1995).

On 7 April 1995, the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) stormed Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria. Officers of the FSK (the predecessor of today's FSB) flew in to the Russian checkpoint near the village with lists of Chechens "subject to filtration"(Citation: Трагедия села Самашки. Чечня. Апрель 1995. Дневник правозащитника 1995)(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). On 8 April, soldiers of the Internal Troops and of police special units from Orenburg and Moscow searched the houses of Samashki. By 10 April, the occupiers had unlawfully detained and taken out of the village more than 200 Chechen men aged 15 to 70, and the escort shot three of them dead on the way (see: "Killing of Prisoners and Detainees")(Citation: Трагедия села Самашки. Чечня. Апрель 1995. Дневник правозащитника 1995)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Azman Ansarova from Samashki told the "Memorial" observers that when one of the detained men showed a soldier his passport, "he took the document and tore it to shreds. 'I don't need your documents,' he says. 'You are Chechens — we are going to kill you'… Then they took our sons and drove them away"(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). The occupiers sent some of the men by helicopter to Mozdok and held others in pits and prison vans near Assinovskaya. On 5 August 1995, Khasan Rasuyev from Samashki told "Memorial" how the guards loaded the detainees into the back of a truck: "And in stacks — into the back. In four layers, I think, one on top of another"(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). Near Assinovskaya, the Russian military released most of the men without certificates of detention, and from Mozdok, by 18 April, the Ministry of Internal Affairs had released 65 Chechens from Samashki as innocent and given 12 up for exchange(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995).

In April 1995, Russian servicemen took the brother of the Chechen woman Khaza Arsanukayeva from his home in Grozny at night, citing his residence registration in Kalmykia, a Russian-controlled republic by the Caspian Sea. The soldiers beat him at the headquarters of the occupation troops and took him to the filtration camp on the northeastern outskirts of the city, and a week later the guards released him: he could not walk(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996).

On 15 March 1996, at the checkpoint near Samashki, the occupiers picked out 91 Chechens from among those leaving the village before the assault and took them to the prisons of Pyatigorsk and Stavropol. Five weeks later, the Ministry of Internal Affairs released them without charges(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). In March 1996, soldiers of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs detained three Chechens at the checkpoint between Goity and Starye Atagi, villages south of Grozny, and on 7 April Russian servicemen took the Chechen Saidash Shamakhurov from Gikalovo, a village near Grozny. The Russians held all four in Khankala, the main base of the occupation troops on the eastern outskirts of Grozny, and exchanged them for their own captured soldiers (see: "Hostage-Taking")(Citation: Russia/Chechnya: A Legacy of Abuse 1997).

In its 1995 comments, the UN Human Rights Committee expressed concern at reports of torture, ill-treatment and arbitrary detention in filtration camps(Citation: Comments of the Human Rights Committee: Russian Federation (CCPR/C/79/Add.54) 1995). In early 1997, the human rights defenders of "Memorial" wrote that Russian agencies "are not making substantial efforts to search for Chechens who were detained and went missing"(Citation: Неизвестный солдат кавказской войны, 1994-1996: Потери российских войск: погибшие, пропавшие без вести, пленные 1997). "Memorial" published the accounts of detainees and lists of Chechens whom the Ministry of Internal Affairs held in the prisons of Pyatigorsk and Stavropol from January to February 1995(Citation: Условия содержания задержанных в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чеченской Республике. Обращение с задержанными 1995).

On 10 June 1996, in Nazran, a town in Russian-controlled Ingushetia, Russia undertook before Ichkeria to close the filtration camps and the other places where it unlawfully held Chechens(Citation: Protocol of the Meeting of the Working Groups, Formed under the Negotiations Commissions, to Locate Missing Persons and to Free Forcibly Detained Persons 1996). In June, the Ministry of Internal Affairs closed the last camps(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Russian courts convicted no one for creating the camps and for the unlawful detentions (see: "Impunity of Perpetrators")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996). On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

Coercing residents of the occupied territories into taking Russian passports: "the policy of mass conferral of Russian citizenship to residents of occupied areas of Kherson, Zaporizhzhia, Donetsk, and Luhansk regions exacerbated the coercive environment there," and "those who refused Russian passports were denied access to public services, notably social security, healthcare, and education, and risked unemployment" and "faced a heightened risk of arbitrary detention when crossing checkpoints"(Citation: Report on the human rights situation in Ukraine, 1 February to 31 July 2023 2023).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers took peaceful Chechens hostage and released them in exchange for captured and killed Russian servicemen, weapons or money.

Russian servicemen drew up lists of detained Chechens for exchange and put on them people who by their age could not have carried weapons(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). According to a certificate by the prison service of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs, from 11 December 1994 to 22 July 1995 the ministry handed over 141 prisoners of the filtration camps for exchange for captured Russian servicemen (see: "Filtration Camp System")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

Russian police officers and soldiers promised to release a detained Chechen if his relatives brought money, a Russian soldier out of captivity or the body of a dead one(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). The occupiers used the hostages' relatives to find out where the Armed Forces of Ichkeria were holding captured Russians: the relatives searched for captives to rescue their own, while the Russian FSB collected information from them and on 29 July 1995 drew up a certificate on the places where Russian soldiers were being held(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Неизвестный солдат кавказской войны, 1994-1996: Потери российских войск: погибшие, пропавшие без вести, пленные 1997).

On 9 January 1995, Russian servicemen detained Shamsu Magomadov in Grozny (see: "Abduction of People"). In the winter of 1995-1996, his sister Madina Magomadova sought her brother's exchange from Colonel Pilyugin of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs. She told "Memorial": "They told me: 'Yes, your brother is alive, we will exchange him — find a soldier [a captured Russian soldier]'. I found a soldier — I went through all those mountains, villages, there is a war on, under fire I searched for a soldier — I found one, brought a photograph. They tell me: 'The soldier is a deserter, he is not subject to exchange…' … 'Go find an officer'. … I found an officer, brought a photograph of the officer... They tell me: sorry, Comrade Magomadova, your brother has been taken away from here, and where he is supposed to be, he has not been brought yet. We cannot find him". The occupiers never released Shamsu Magomadov, and nothing is known of his fate(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

Russian servicemen and security services put up for exchange the captured relatives and guards of the president of Ichkeria. On 19 February 1995, the occupiers detained in Grozny Makharbi Dudayev, the president's younger brother, and on 6 April the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs put him up for exchange in Malye Atagi, a village south of Grozny, together with 16 prisoners of the filtration camps. The ministry exchanged the prisoners for a captured Russian major and released the president's brother separately(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: За спинами мирных жителей. Захват заложников и использование гражданского населения в качестве «живого щита» федеральными войсками России в ходе вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1996)(Citation: Трагедия села Самашки. Чечня. Апрель 1995. Дневник правозащитника 1995). On the night of 28 May 1996, Russian border guards detained the widow of the president of Ichkeria with her bodyguard at the airport of Nalchik, the capital of Russian-controlled Kabardino-Balkaria, and the Russian FSB released the widow but exchanged the bodyguard for a captured Russian priest(Citation: Миллион первый 2002)(Citation: Russia Detains Widow of Late Chechen Rebel Leader 1996).

Russian soldiers and filtration camp guards demanded ransom for detained Chechens. In late March 1995, the guards of the military unit near Assinovskaya, a stanitsa in the west of Ichkeria, asked detained Chechens who would pay more to get out(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). In April 1995, the guards of the filtration camp on the northeastern outskirts of Grozny received five million rubles for the release of a detained Chechen(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996). On 15 May 1995, Russian soldiers put a detained Chechen from Shali, a town southeast of Grozny, into a pit at their unit, offered to let him out for money and released him after 18 hours(Citation: Условия содержания задержанных в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чеченской Республике. Обращение с задержанными 1995). In December 1995, Russian servicemen detained five elderly Chechens at a checkpoint, and their relatives ransomed them from a filtration camp for ten million rubles(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996). On 17 April 1996, Russian soldiers detained a Chechen woman with her two brothers at the entrance to Grozny and demanded three million rubles for them, and in the evening released all three, and the brother gave them the money(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). On 18 April, Russian servicemen took six Chechens from their homes in Novye Aldy, a settlement on the southwestern outskirts of Grozny, and their relatives ransomed them from the filtration camp at the city motor depot(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

The Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs and the command of the occupation troops demanded captured Russian servicemen, their bodies and weapons for detained Chechens. In March 1996, officers of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs demanded that the female relatives of a Chechen, held since January in the filtration camp in Grozny, dig up and bring the bodies of three officers of a Russian police special unit, and in late March, having received the bodies, released him(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). In March 1996, soldiers of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs detained three Chechens at the checkpoint between Goity and Starye Atagi, villages south of Grozny, and on 28 March the occupiers exchanged them for five Russian soldiers(Citation: Russia/Chechnya: A Legacy of Abuse 1997). On 7 April 1996, Russian servicemen took Saidash Shamakhurov from Gikalovo, a village south of Grozny, to Khankala, the main base of the occupation troops on the eastern outskirts of Grozny, where investigators demanded that he record on tape his request to be exchanged for 15 captured Russian soldiers and 48 construction workers. On 27 April, the occupiers exchanged him for a Russian soldier(Citation: Russia/Chechnya: A Legacy of Abuse 1997). In May 1996, soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) detained in the center of Grozny 17 to 20 Chechens who were repairing heating pipes and demanded during interrogation that their relatives bring weapons or captured Russian servicemen for them. The next evening the guards let them go(Citation: Russia/Chechnya: A Legacy of Abuse 1997).

Russian soldiers took hostages during assaults and when encircled. On 7 April 1995, during the storming of Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, the occupiers took four Chechen men hostage, drove them into a pit in a garage and fired at them with assault rifles. One the occupiers killed on the spot, the wounded second one the next day; two survived (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 10-12 August 1996, soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs, encircled by the Armed Forces of Ichkeria, held about 500 patients, their relatives and medics hostage in City Hospital No. 9 in Grozny. On 12 August, the occupiers left the hospital, taking a hundred hostages as a human shield, and released them near the former driving school where Russian units were stationed, once the defenders had handed over four captured Russian soldiers (see: "Use of People as “Human Shields”")(Citation: За спинами мирных жителей. Захват заложников и использование гражданского населения в качестве «живого щита» федеральными войсками России в ходе вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1996)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 11 and 12 August 1996, when the Armed Forces of Ichkeria were liberating Grozny from the occupiers, soldiers of the 101st Brigade of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs took Chechen men from the blocks around the "15th Gorodok", their base on Lenin Street, and held them there as hostages. On 14 October 1996, Magomed Taramov told "Memorial" how on 12 August Russian servicemen took him from his home together with his son Alimkhan: "We are no 'boyeviki' [as Russians called the Armed Forces of Ichkeria], we took no part in the armed actions. They led us out into the street, and there by the wall stood another nine or so people... In all, about twenty-four of us were gathered". For the release of the hostages, the brigade's officers demanded that relatives bring wounded soldiers from the encircled Russian checkpoints and the bodies of the dead, or get the army of Ichkeria to let food through to those posts. Garib Asiyalov, whom the hostages' female relatives called to the talks at the "15th Gorodok", in October told "Memorial" the words of a Russian officer: "…I answer to Kulikov [the head of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs]. We will trade head for head — our wounded or dead one for your living one". According to him, for the wounded and dead soldiers whom the relatives brought by truck, the brigade released 32 hostages(Citation: За спинами мирных жителей. Захват заложников и использование гражданского населения в качестве «живого щита» федеральными войсками России в ходе вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1996). On 16 August, when relatives brought the bodies of eight Russian servicemen to the base, the occupiers released Magomed and Alimkhan Taramov(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 17 August 1996, soldiers of the 101st Brigade searched the blocks near the "15th Gorodok" and took Chechen men from there to the base as hostages. The brigade's officers promised to release them for the bodies of Russian soldiers buried near the bus station and the chemical plant, and on 19 August, when Russian soldiers brought 28 bodies out through the positions of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria, they released the hostages. The human rights defenders of "Memorial" published the names of twelve of them(Citation: За спинами мирных жителей. Захват заложников и использование гражданского населения в качестве «живого щита» федеральными войсками России в ходе вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1996) and write that at the "15th Gorodok" and in City Hospital No. 9 in Grozny the soldiers of the Internal Troops took hostages on the direct orders of the commanders of their units(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In his report of 26 March 1996, the UN Secretary-General cited reports by human rights organizations: Russian troops often detained any Chechen man, whether there was evidence against him or not, in order to exchange him for captured Russian soldiers(Citation: The situation of human rights in the Republic of Chechnya of the Russian Federation. Report of the Secretary-General (E/CN.4/1996/13) 1996). The human rights defenders of "Memorial" write that Russian agencies repeatedly used civilian prisoners of the filtration camps as hostages and in most cases offered Ichkeria in exchange Chechens who had not taken part in the fighting. In "Memorial's" conclusion, hostage-taking became a regular practice for the Russian military(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

Russian prosecutors put none of the occupiers who took hostages in Hospital No. 9 and at the "15th Gorodok" in Grozny on trial (see: "Impunity of Perpetrators")(Citation: Russia/Chechnya: A Legacy of Abuse 1997)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996). On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).
