In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Throughout the war, Moscow shielded its soldiers, police officers and commanders of the occupation troops from responsibility for crimes against Chechens.

In Ichkeria, Shkirko, commander of the Internal Troops of the Russian Interior Ministry (MVD; predecessors of today's Rosgvardia), went by the surname "Shirokov", and Lvov, chief of their staff, by "General Yagodin". Romanov and Labunets, deputy commanders of the occupation troops, were called "Antonov" and "Alekseyev"(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Трагедия села Самашки. Чечня. Апрель 1995. Дневник правозащитника 1995).

Military prosecutors closed cases about people whom Russian soldiers had shot dead in cars at checkpoints, citing Articles 23 and 27 of the Russian law on the Internal Troops of the MVD(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 17 December 1994, the Russian military shot up a column of refugees from Grozny near the stanitsa of Nesterovskaya in Russian-controlled Ingushetia. Russian prosecutors suspended the case without finding those responsible(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 3 January 1995, Russian pilots bombed Arshty, a village in Ingushetia inhabited mostly by Chechens (see: "Collective Punishment"), and in a second bombing, on 18 April, killed three women there. Russian prosecutors closed both cases, finding no crime(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 14 January 1995, Lobov, secretary of the Russian Security Council, said that a special commission should establish the truth about the bombings of Grozny. Russia created no such commission(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 24 January 1995, the two sons of Khusein Khamidov disappeared in Grozny. On 2 April, the father dug up a pit in the yard of a house on Mayakovsky Street, where a unit of the Internal Troops of the Russian MVD had previously been stationed, and found their bodies (see: "Killing of Prisoners and Detainees"). The prosecutor's office of the puppet government opened a case and gathered evidence. Russian military prosecutors suspended it without finding those responsible(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 24 April 1996, Khusein Khamidov, who had been searching for missing people in Ichkeria since January 1995, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Moscow: "There is not a single case that has been investigated and brought to court… when you hand them documents, hand them a statement about some crime that was committed, they say: 'You tell us who did it, soldiers of the Russian regular army, or of SOBR [the police special forces], or of the MVD'… But who knows who committed the crime — their uniform is one and the same. And on that basis they refuse us"(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

Russian courts gave Polivtsev, a captain of the 81st regiment of the Internal Troops of the Russian MVD, four years for the murder of four Chechens in Grozny on 25 January 1995(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 7-8 April 1995, the Russian Internal Troops stormed Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, and killed 103 Chechen civilians (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians"). On 12 April, a colonel of the Russian MVD at a post near the village introduced himself to human rights defenders as Oblomov, although the surname "Yelansky" was written on the strap of his assault rifle. On 19 April, the Russian prosecutor Dzhapov told Andrei Blinushov, an observer of the Russian human rights organization Memorial, that he did not know how to hold the fighters of the MVD special units to account. The observer wrote in his diary, from the prosecutor's words: "the MVD special units leaving Chechnya destroy all their documentation concerning their actions on the territory of this republic. These units often act in masks, without any insignia on their uniforms, and all the officers use two or three pseudonyms instead of their real surnames"(Citation: Трагедия села Самашки. Чечня. Апрель 1995. Дневник правозащитника 1995). On 27 April, Ilyushenko, acting prosecutor general of Russia, opened a case on the killings and arson in the village(Citation: Трагедия села Самашки. Чечня. Апрель 1995. Дневник правозащитника 1995). In mid-May, Russian military investigators questioned some of the victims and witnesses, but did not open the graves and never came to Samashki again. On 14 January 1997, the prosecutors closed the case. On 21 November 1997, Smirnov, deputy chief military prosecutor of Russia, named the reason to Memorial: "the servicemen acted in a state of extreme necessity and necessary defense"(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

The Russian serviceman Vershinin received three years from a court for shooting dead the boy Zelimkhan Dediyev on 17 April 1995 in the stanitsa of Petropavlovskaya northeast of Grozny(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 14 June 1995, the Prosecutor General's Office of Russia, by directive No. 15-6-95, ordered the prosecutor of the puppet government in Grozny to hand cases of crimes by Russian soldiers over to Russian military prosecutors only if the facts had been established beyond dispute. On 4 July 1996, that government's prosecutor wrote to Skuratov, prosecutor general of Russia, that Russian prosecutors had returned 112 cases to him without investigation, having found no indisputable proof of guilt in them. The letter says that unnamed commanders ordered that investigators not be let into military units and onto checkpoints(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). The soldiers Korovin, Shulin and Petrov received 14, six and three years for killing two Chechens on the night of 7 July 1995 in the settlement of Rodina near their unit(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-158) 1996)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). The Russian military did not let into their units the investigators of the puppet prosecutor's office who were investigating the murder of seven Chechens of the Chapanov family in the village of Prigorodnoye near Grozny on 7 July 1995. In January 1996, the puppet prosecutor's office suspended the case(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 17 December 1996, a court gave Permyakov, a fighter of the Russian police special forces, a suspended sentence of a year and a half for the "negligent killing" of Zaurbek Uzuyev, whom he had shot dead at a checkpoint on 8 September 1995 during a rally for the independence of Ichkeria(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Military prosecutors suspended the case on the bombing of Roshni-Chu, a village southwest of Grozny, in October 1995(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

Military prosecutors closed the case on the murder of Sharip Batayev, a Chechen from Arshty, whom scouts of the 693rd regiment of the Russian 58th Army shot dead at the end of February 1996. According to the prosecutors' version, the commander of the scouts was defending himself(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). In the spring of 1996, Russian prosecutors opened no criminal case on how the occupiers in March had burned Sernovodsk and destroyed Samashki, villages in the west of Ichkeria(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). On 30 June 1996, the military prosecutor Saprunov wrote to the prosecutor's office of the puppet government that the occupiers had beaten, on the way to Pyatigorsk, a town in southern Russia, half of the 91 Chechens from Samashki whom the Russian military had unlawfully detained on 15 March (see: "Torture and Abuse")(Citation: Russia/Chechnya: A Legacy of Abuse 1997)(Citation: Russia/Chechnya: Report to the 1996 OSCE Review Conference 1996). In March 1997, Russian prosecutors suspended the case without finding those responsible: those who made the detentions had been "wearing masks on their faces, so their identification is impossible"(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 10 December 1996, Sinitsyn, a prosecutor of the Chief Military Prosecutor's Office of Russia, replied to Memorial's request to investigate how soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian MVD had shielded themselves with civilians in Samashki in March 1996 and with the patients of Grozny City Hospital No. 9 in August 1996 (see: "Use of People as “Human Shields”"). Sinitsyn wrote that he had forwarded the human rights defenders' report to the prosecutors of the North Caucasus so that it could be attached to the press reports(Citation: Russia/Chechnya: A Legacy of Abuse 1997), and on 21 November 1997 Smirnov, deputy chief military prosecutor, replied that in Samashki people had been hiding behind armored vehicles from the shelling(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Military prosecutors suspended the cases on the bombings of Katyr-Yurt and Shalazhi, villages southwest of Grozny, in March and April 1996 (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Shevchenko, prosecutor of the occupation troops, without visiting the scene, stated that the soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian MVD who on 15 July 1996 had shot dead unarmed people in passenger cars on the outskirts of Grozny had used their weapons correctly(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-139) 1996)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). In mid-July 1996, Russian soldiers held without charges two Chechens from the Vedeno district in the southeast of Ichkeria in an army cell in Khankala, the main base of the occupation troops on the eastern outskirts of Grozny, and released them at the demand of military prosecutors. The prosecutor's office of the occupation troops recognized only this detention as unlawful, but opened no case, because the culprit, the commandant of Khankala, had died in the fighting in August 1996(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 8 August 1996, the Chief Military Prosecutor's Office of Russia replied to Yuli Rybakov, a deputy of the Russian parliament, that since 11 December 1994 prosecutors had opened 129 cases on crimes by the occupiers against civilians in Ichkeria. Of these, prosecutors had sent 21 cases to the courts, closed 21, left 26 unfinished and suspended 61 - 48 because they had not found those responsible, and 13 because they did not know where the accused were(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 29 September 1997, the Directorate of Military Courts of Russia replied to Memorial's inquiry that over the whole war the courts had convicted 18 soldiers and officers, seven of them for murder(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 26 July 1995, the UN Human Rights Committee expressed regret that no one had been held accountable for the ill-treatment of prisoners and detainees in Ichkeria(Citation: Comments of the Human Rights Committee: Russian Federation (CCPR/C/79/Add.54) 1995). The Human Rights Watch report of January 1997 says that Russia systematically violated human rights and just as systematically failed to hold those responsible to account(Citation: Russia/Chechnya: A Legacy of Abuse 1997). Human rights defenders of Memorial write that over the whole war Russia held not a single senior commander to account. According to their data, Russian courts convicted no one for the bombings of the villages and towns of Ichkeria, the filtration camps, torture, hostage-taking and human shields(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

According to Human Rights Watch, at the peace talks in August 1996 the Russian delegation objected to discussing responsibility for crimes(Citation: Russia/Chechnya: A Legacy of Abuse 1997). After the peace agreements in Khasavyurt on 31 August 1996 (see: "Sham Treaties")(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996), Russia moved the prosecutor's office of the occupation troops to Russian-controlled Dagestan. Human rights defenders of Memorial write that after this the prosecutors almost stopped investigating crimes by Russian servicemen and police officers(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 12 March 1997, deputies in Moscow, by resolution No. 1199-II, declared an amnesty for crimes connected with the war in Ichkeria(Citation: Постановление Государственной Думы от 12 марта 1997 г. № 1199-II ГД «Об объявлении амнистии в отношении лиц, совершивших общественно опасные деяния в связи с вооруженным конфликтом в Чеченской Республике» 1997). Under this amnesty, Russian prosecutors terminated unfinished cases on crimes by the occupiers(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Russian troops bombed and shelled the towns of Ichkeria without distinguishing residential houses from military targets(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

Russian aircraft dropped unguided bombs and cluster bombs filled with steel balls or needles on Ichkeria(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). The crews of Russian helicopters fired unguided rockets at towns and villages(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). The occupation troops shelled residential districts with tube artillery, mortars and the Grad and Uragan multiple rocket launchers, which cannot fire with precision(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). In Grozny, the capital of Ichkeria, the Russian military hit residential houses with people inside with depth charges, the kind used to sink submarines. Such a bomb pierces a dozen concrete floors and explodes inside the house(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

The occupiers shelled markets and hospitals(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Russian troops bombed villages before a storming, after capture and during "ceasefires" with Ichkeria (see: "Sham Ceasefire")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

Russian pilots bombed and artillerymen shelled the towns and villages of Ichkeria throughout the war, from September 1994 to August 1996. On 2 September 1994 Russian pilots struck three villages twenty kilometers from Grozny with rockets(Citation: Russia Confronts Chechnya: Roots of a Separatist Conflict 1998)(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-94-172) 1994). On 23 November pilots fired at a poultry farm in Shali and wounded seven Chechen civilians(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-94-227) 1994). On 25 November pilots struck the Grozny airport and the residential houses next to it and, according to different sources, killed three or six people(Citation: ФСБ взрывает Россию 2002)(Citation: Chechnya - Airport Attacked 1994). On 26 November, while Russian tank crews were storming Grozny, pilots fired at the city. According to the Chechenpress agency, the tank crews and pilots killed from 25 to 39 civilians(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-94-228) 1994)(Citation: Покушение на Джохара Дудаева 1994)(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-94-197) 1994). On 29 November pilots fired rockets at the airport and the center of Grozny and, according to the Department of State Security of Ichkeria, killed 14 people(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-94-230) 1994)(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-94-229) 1994). On 30 November Russian aircraft bombed Grozny twice and, according to an adviser to the president of Ichkeria, killed up to 80 people(Citation: ФСБ взрывает Россию 2002)(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-94-231) 1994). On 3 December 1994 a Russian pilot dropped a bomb on a five-story residential building in Argun, a town to the east of Grozny, but the bomb pierced the wall and did not explode(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996). On 12 December Russian pilots in helicopters and aircraft bombed the residential districts of Dolinsky, a settlement to the northwest of Grozny(Citation: Хроника первой российской войны в Чечне 2026)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 13 December pilots fired at four cars with refugees near the village of Novy Sharoy in the west of Ichkeria and killed three refugees(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996).

From 18 December 1994 Russian aircraft bombed Grozny, and from 19 December until the storming on 31 December they did so every day(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Deinekin, the commander of the Russian military aviation, said in an interview with the newspaper Moskovsky Komsomolets on 21 March 1995 that until 29 December, because of bad weather, the pilots could not use laser- or television-guided bombs and missiles over the city. Russian pilots dropped unguided bombs on the city through the clouds from a height of five to seven kilometers when, in the commander's words, "the ground could not be seen at all"(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). In January and February 1995 Russian troops shelled the residential districts of Grozny with tube artillery and multiple rocket launchers, and pilots bombed the city. Andrei Mironov, a Russian human rights defender who lived in Grozny for three months, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost foundation in Moscow in February 1996: "And then the shelling ends, you walk out of the house and see: corpses here, corpses there. Old people lying. Next to them a sled, on the sled a canister of water." About the needles with which the occupiers filled shells and bombs, the human rights defender told the tribunal: "All of Grozny was strewn with them. These elements are good only for hitting unprotected people"(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996). The human rights defenders of Memorial write that Russian pilots knowingly bombed Grozny without aiming and that such strikes inevitably killed many townspeople. By the estimate of the Observer Mission of Russian human rights organizations, from December 1994 to March 1995 the occupiers killed 25,000-29,000 civilians in the city (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On the night of 21 December 1994 Russian artillerymen hit a house in Novoartyomovo, a village near Grozny, with a shell and killed five children. Two more Chechen girls from this house died of their wounds in hospital(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 24 December, 19 unidentified bodies of townspeople killed by Russian pilots lay in the morgue of the Central Republican Hospital of Grozny(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). From 26 to 28 December 1994 Russian aircraft bombed about 40 villages(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 29 December the bodies of two children, two women and four more people, whom Russian artillerymen had killed while shelling the outskirts of Grozny, were brought to the morgue of the Central Republican Hospital(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 3 January 1995 Russian pilots fired at a bus stop near Starye Atagi, a village to the south of Grozny, and killed the driver of a truck standing nearby and several more people there(Citation: Russia: Three Months of War in Chechnya 1995). On that day Russian aircraft dropped cluster bombs on the bazaar, the hospital and the car market of Shali(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996). By the count of the human rights defender Andrei Mironov, with one bomb at the car market the pilots killed from 130 to 160 people(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996). On 31 January artillerymen shelled Samashki and killed four people on Chapayev Street. On 2 February artillerymen hit one yard on this street with a mortar and killed a woman and a 14-year-old girl in the morning, and three people at a funeral in the afternoon(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). On 11 or 12 March 1995 pilots bombed Mozdokskaya Street in Shali and destroyed 68 houses on it(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 22-23 March the crew of a Russian helicopter fired at a truck with refugees near the village of Mesker-Yurt near Shali and killed the driver and a passenger(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 26 March the crews of six Russian helicopters fired rockets at Samashki and seriously wounded four people(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). On 6 April artillerymen shelled Niki-Khita, a mountain village in the southeast of Ichkeria, with Grad rockets and missiles and killed two Chechen children(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions. Report by the Special Rapporteur, Bacre Waly Ndiaye (E/CN.4/1996/4) 1996). On 24 April 1995 pilots bombed Nozhai-Yurt, a village in the southeast of the republic where there were no fighters of the army of Ichkeria, and killed four Chechens(Citation: Extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions. Report by the Special Rapporteur, Bacre Waly Ndiaye (E/CN.4/1996/4) 1996)(Citation: Russia: Partisan War in Chechnya on the Eve of the World War II Commemoration 1995). According to the international organization Médecins Sans Frontières, in the 15 days before 27 May 1995, 74 people wounded by Russian pilots were brought to the hospital of Shatoy, a mountain village in the south of Ichkeria(Citation: War Crimes and Politics of Terror in Chechnya 1994-2004. MSF Speaks Out 2014). On 8 October 1995 Russian pilots bombed Roshni-Chu, a village to the southwest of Grozny, and, according to the villagers, killed 28 people - Chechen civilians and fighters of the army of Ichkeria(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-95-199) 1995)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). From 14 to 20 December 1995 Russian troops shelled and bombed the residential districts, hospitals and mosque of Gudermes, the second-largest town of Ichkeria(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Shkirko, the commander of the occupation troops, named 267 civilians killed in Gudermes(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Caught in the Crossfire: Civilians in Gudermes and Pervomayskoye 1996).

From 11 to 20 February 1996 Russian troops shelled Novogroznensky, a settlement in the east of Ichkeria, and, according to the Agence France-Presse agency, killed at least 50 Chechen civilians(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Jaromír Štětina, a correspondent of the Czech agency Epicentrum, asked Tikhomirov, the commander of the occupation army, at a press conference whether the general knew about the civilians in the settlement. The commander answered the journalist: "We cannot establish the difference between a militant [this is what the Russians called the fighters of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria] and a civilian resident"(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). Until the first days of March 1996 artillerymen destroyed the villages of Alleroy and Tsentoroy, to which the defenders of the settlement had been forced to retreat, and continued the shelling after the defenders had left them. The artillerymen killed Chechen civilians in these villages(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). From 3 to 9 March artillerymen shelled Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria, and killed at least 45 civilians(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). From 6 to 8 March, when the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated most of Grozny, Russian troops shelled the residential districts of the city, and after the defenders left, its southern districts for several more days. According to the Russian military prosecutor's office, 250 civilians died in Grozny on 6-11 March(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On the night of 14 March 1996 Russian troops surrounded Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria where about 12,000 people lived. On 15 March the Russian military gave the Chechens in the village two hours to leave before the storming, and about half of them did not manage to get out (see: "Sham Corridor"). At 10:16 Russian troops began shelling Samashki from armored personnel carriers, tanks, tube artillery and mortars, and from helicopters and aircraft, while the Chechens who remained in the village hid in cellars(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Viktor Kurochkin, a deputy of the Russian parliament, told the Glasnost tribunal in Moscow on 24 April 1996: "Eight or ten 'Uragans' [multiple rocket launchers] were working there — and that is the most terrible weapon for populated areas"(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). The human rights defender Andrei Mironov was in Sleptsovskaya, a stanitsa in Russian-controlled Ingushetia, on 17 March, and told the tribunal on 20 April: "I counted the explosions. At first it was one explosion per second, then more. The village was shelled for about six days. Of those, roughly five days — one explosion per second or slightly more often (1-2 explosions per second), that is, no fewer than 70 thousand shells a day"(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). By 19 March, when Russian troops opened a way out of the encirclement, the occupiers had destroyed almost all the houses in Samashki(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Sources differ on the number of Chechen civilians the occupiers killed in the village during the storming: 35 according to the villagers' list(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010) or about 600 according to a doctor who treated people in Samashki(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

On 28 March 1996 a Russian pilot dropped two bombs on Katyr-Yurt, a village to the southwest of Grozny, and killed nine people from the Khazhgiriyev family, among them two pregnant women and four children(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). On 3 and 4 April 1996 pilots bombed Shalazhi, a village to the southwest of Grozny, and killed three Chechens(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). On 25 April 1996 pilots bombed Shali, surrounded by Russian troops, where about 50 thousand civilians remained(Citation: CHECHEN REPUBLIC - RUSSIAN FEDERATION: Civilians under Russian bombardment - continued fear for safety of civilians in Shali (EUR 46/24/96) 1996). The pilots killed Chechen civilians and wounded, according to the head of the Shali district speaking to the Interfax agency, 29 people(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On that day Russian aircraft bombed Chishki, a mountain village to the south of Grozny, and killed one Chechen woman(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 7 May the crews of five Russian helicopters struck Urus-Martan, a town to the southwest of Grozny, and killed five Chechens at the market(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: RFE/RL Newsline, 9 May 1996 1996). On 10 and 12 May helicopter crews fired at the town again and killed one person each time(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

In July 1996 Russian troops shelled and bombed Gekhi, a village to the southwest of Grozny, and, according to the newspaper Izvestia, killed 19 Chechen civilians(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-139) 1996). Artillerymen shelled Makhkety, a mountain village of the Vedeno district in the southeast of Ichkeria, with Grad and Uragan rockets and by 15 July had killed 25 Chechen civilians there(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999)(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-139) 1996). On 15 July the crews of seven Russian helicopters destroyed six houses in Starye Atagi with missiles (see: "Collective Punishment")(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999)(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-137) 1996). In July 1996, while shelling Dargo, Belgatoy, Vedeno and other villages of the Vedeno district, Russian troops killed at least 30 Chechens(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). From 20 July until the first days of August 1996 Russian pilots continuously bombed the villages of five districts in the south of the republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In August 1996, when the army of Ichkeria attacked the occupiers in Grozny, Russian pilots bombed the city although low clouds prevented them from aiming(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). According to journalists' estimates, from 6 to 22 August 1996 the occupiers killed about 2,000 civilian townspeople in Grozny. Human rights defenders of Memorial write that no one kept an exact count(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 7 August pilots destroyed the surgical department of City Hospital No. 4 and killed seven medical workers(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 14 August the crew of a Russian helicopter five kilometers from Grozny fired at cars with civilians and killed at least four people, among them two children(Citation: RUSSIAN FEDERATION - CHECHEN REPUBLIC: Civilians trapped in Grozny (EXTRA 127/96, EUR 46/36/96) 1996). On that day Russian pilots bombed Komsomolskoye, a village to the northeast of Grozny, and killed nine Chechens(Citation: RUSSIAN FEDERATION - CHECHEN REPUBLIC: Civilians under bombardment in Komsomolskoye (EUR 46/37/96) 1996). On 17 August 1996 soldiers of the 101st Brigade of the Internal Troops of the Russian MVD (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) fired with assault rifles, the machine guns of armored vehicles and mortars at the residential houses near the "15th Gorodok", their base in Grozny, and killed four people(Citation: За спинами мирных жителей. Захват заложников и использование гражданского населения в качестве «живого щита» федеральными войсками России в ходе вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1996). From 19 to 21 August Russian artillerymen shelled Chernorechye, the southern district of the city(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010), Griboyedov Street(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010) and Minutka Square(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999) in Grozny, and on 20 August fired 60 Grad rockets at the city(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). In Chernorechye on 19 August artillerymen killed an elderly woman(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 21 August pilots dropped incendiary bombs from a great height on the five-story buildings on Saikhanov and Ulyanov Streets, where there were no fighters of the army of Ichkeria(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). The buildings burned out from the inside, while the people who were hiding in the cellars survived(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

The human rights defenders of Memorial write that firing without distinguishing targets was one of the main features of the actions of the Russian military throughout the war and that civilians suffered most from the bombing and shelling(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 25 January 1996 the UN Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial executions wrote in a report to the UN Commission on Human Rights that the Russian military had killed thousands of citizens of Ichkeria, including when they deliberately and indiscriminately shelled residential districts with heavy weapons and bombed them(Citation: Extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions. Report by the Special Rapporteur, Bacre Waly Ndiaye (E/CN.4/1996/4) 1996). It is unknown how many such crimes the occupation troops committed from September 1994 to August 1996.

In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996). On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers bombed Chechen television, jammed journalists' satellite links and kept them away from the sites of their strikes.

Commanders of the occupation forces ordered that journalists not be let into the sites of assaults and bombings. The Russian military and police at checkpoints did not let journalists, including those with accreditation from the Russian government, into the villages and towns that Russian troops were striking (see: "Censorship")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). Human rights defenders of the American Committee to Protect Journalists write that Russian troops in Ichkeria jammed journalists' satellite transmissions, exposed their film and destroyed their equipment(Citation: Attacks on the Press in 1996: Russia 1997).

On 29 November 1994, Russia announced that at 2 p.m. it would cut off all communications with Ichkeria(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-94-229) 1994). From 21 to 24 December, Russian pilots struck the television center in Grozny. Deinekin, commander of Russian military aviation, named the aim of these strikes: "to stop the rabid anti-Russian propaganda"(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 3 January 1995, Russian pilots bombed Shali, a town southeast of Grozny. Human rights defenders of Human Rights Watch write that the pilots were apparently trying to hit a radio communication tower, but killed several townspeople at the market and in the hospital (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")(Citation: Russia: Three Months of War in Chechnya 1995). On 7 and 8 April, the Internal Troops of Russia's Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) stormed Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, and killed 103 Chechen civilians there (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). On 11 April, the occupiers at the post near the village did not let journalists in and admitted them only on 13 April(Citation: Трагедия села Самашки. Чечня. Апрель 1995. Дневник правозащитника 1995)(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). On 8 October, Russian pilots bombed Roshni-Chu, a village southwest of Grozny (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks"). The occupiers blocked all the roads to the village, and men of the police special forces from the Russian city of Irkutsk at the post did not let journalists in, citing an order(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-95-198) 1995). From 11 December, before the "elections" of the head of the puppet government on 14-17 December, Russian soldiers at checkpoints did not let journalists without special passes into Grozny (see: "Sham Expression of Popular Will")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). From 14 to 20 December, after the Armed Forces of Ichkeria had liberated Gudermes, the second-largest city of the republic, the occupiers shelled and bombed the city, and until 25 December did not let the press in (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")(Citation: Caught in the Crossfire: Civilians in Gudermes and Pervomayskoye 1996).

In January 1996, the command of the occupation forces closed Grozny and the east of Ichkeria to the press(Citation: Caught in the Crossfire: Civilians in Gudermes and Pervomayskoye 1996). From February until the first days of March, the occupiers shelled with artillery the encircled settlement of Novogroznensky in the east of Ichkeria and the villages of Alleroy, Tsentoroy, Bachi-Yurt and Suvorov-Yurt (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks"). The Russian military did not let journalists in there(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). From 3 to 9 March, Russian troops shelled Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria, with artillery and fired on it from helicopters (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). From 6 to 9 March, while the Armed Forces of Ichkeria were attacking the occupiers in Grozny, Russian officials did not let journalists into the city(Citation: Attacks on the Press in 1996: Russia 1997). On 10 March, the Russian military commandant of Sernovodsk forbade letting journalists, human rights defenders and any foreigners into the village (see: "Expulsion of Foreign Missions")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 15 March 1996, the Internal Troops of Russia's Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Russian 58th Army began the assault on Samashki (see: "Military Intervention")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Sources differ on the number of Chechen civilians the occupiers killed in the village during the assault: 35 according to the villagers' list(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010) or about 600 according to a doctor who treated people there (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). On 17 and 18 March, the occupiers did not let independent journalists from Moscow through to the village. Maria Eismont, a correspondent of the Moscow newspaper Segodnya, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Moscow on 22 April that on 26 and 27 March the Russian military stopped her on the roads to Samashki, and that she got into the village five days later. In Sernovodsk, Russian soldiers who had taken part in the assault turned the journalists back with the words: "There's no need to go there, there's nothing for you to do there, all the more so since there is nothing at all left to look at." Alexander Trushin, a correspondent of the Moscow newspaper Obshchaya Gazeta, told the Glasnost tribunal on 21 April that in early April the chief of the Russian checkpoint near the village phoned a general and did not let the journalists through: "I asked the captain: 'Did you report why we are going, for what purpose?' He answered: 'Yes, the general knows, and nevertheless the order is not to let you through'"(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). Human rights defenders of Memorial write that reports of this assault did not reach television and radio(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 21 April 1996, the occupiers killed Dzhokhar Dudayev, the president of Ichkeria, during his conversation on a satellite phone with a mediator in the peace talks; according to the version that human rights defenders of Memorial consider likely, the Russian military located the signal of this phone (see: "Neutralization of the Opposition")(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-080) 1996)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 8 August 1996, while the Armed Forces of Ichkeria were liberating Grozny, Russian soldiers did not let four journalists of foreign media into the city through either of its two entrances(Citation: Attacks on the Press in 1996: Russia 1997).

Human rights defenders of Memorial write that in the second year of the war Russian troops cut off from the press the areas they deemed undesirable far more tightly and successfully than in the first year(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996). On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. On the seized land of Ichkeria, the occupiers installed their own organs of governance in place of the elected leadership of the republic.

On 30 November 1994, eleven days before the open invasion, Russian President Yeltsin, by secret Decree No. 2137, ordered the creation of a special administration for Ichkeria under the command of the Russian military. At the head of this administration stood the "leadership group" of Russian Defense Minister Grachev. Grachev received the right to direct the work of all Russian agencies, troops and special services in Ichkeria and to remove their officials(Citation: Постановление Конституционного Суда Российской Федерации № 10-П по делу о проверке конституционности указов Президента и постановления Правительства о Чеченской Республике 1995)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In the seized towns and villages, the command of the occupation troops set up military commandant's offices with broad powers over Chechens(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 17 December 1994, Russian President Yeltsin, by Decree No. 2200, ordered the Russian government to create within five days in Ichkeria an occupation civil administration made up of local branches of Russian ministries and agencies(Citation: Указ Президента Российской Федерации № 2200 О восстановлении федеральных территориальных органов исполнительной власти на территории Чеченской Республики 1994). At the head of the administration Yeltsin placed his plenipotentiary representative in Ichkeria, Minister for Nationalities Yegorov. On 20 December, the Russian government, by Resolution No. 1411, obliged all enterprises, organizations and institutions of Ichkeria to carry out Yegorov's decisions until the Constitution and laws of Russia were in full operation in the republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

The prosecutor's office and police of the puppet government were part of the Russian prosecutor's office and Ministry of Internal Affairs (see: "Puppet Government")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In January 1995, Russia replaced Yegorov at the head of the occupation administration with Semyonov, one of the leaders of Chechen-Ingushetia under Soviet rule. Semyonov's deputies were three appointees from the puppet opposition(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 29 December 1995, Russian President Yeltsin, by Decree No. 1430, gave Russian Interior Minister Kulikov charge in Ichkeria of maintaining order, fighting crime and disarming the army of the republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 19 February 1996, the Russian president, by Decree No. 214, repealed Decree No. 2200, by which he had created the occupation administration(Citation: Указ Президента Российской Федерации № 2200 О восстановлении федеральных территориальных органов исполнительной власти на территории Чеченской Республики 1994). In March 1996, Semyonov, head of the administration, left his post(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 5 June 1996, the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs created in Grozny, the capital of Ichkeria, a Coordination Center headed by Golubets, first deputy interior minister of Russia(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 29 March 1995, István Gyarmati, personal representative of the Chairman of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), reported to the OSCE Permanent Council in Vienna on his trip to Ichkeria. The OSCE press release on the report says: "The report expressed worry that the newly established local authorities in the Chechen Republic are viewed by many Chechens as alien to them and that Chechen politicians who support the federal [Russian] authorities are not supported by the population"(Citation: OSCE to deploy Assistance Group for Chechnya (press release, Vienna, 29 March 1995) 1995).

On 23 November 1996, Russian President Yeltsin, by Decree No. 1590, ordered the withdrawal from the Chechen Republic of the 101st Brigade of the Internal Troops (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) and the 205th Brigade of the Russian army, and allowed the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs to guard people and important facilities only in agreement with the leadership of the Chechen Republic(Citation: Указ Президента Российской Федерации от 23 ноября 1996 г. № 1590 «О мерах по обеспечению дальнейшего мирного урегулирования в Чеченской Республике» 1996)(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999).

In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996). On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 27 January 1997, the citizens of Ichkeria elected a parliament and a president - Aslan Maskhadov(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).
