In 1995, in its orders for the detention of Chechens, the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs most often referred to decree No. 1815 of Russian president Yeltsin of 2 November 1993 "On Measures to Prevent Vagrancy and Begging"(Citation: Указ Президента Российской Федерации от 2 ноября 1993 г. № 1815 «О мерах по предупреждению бродяжничества и попрошайничества» 1993). Most of the detained Chechens had their documents on them, and some of them the ministry took from their own homes(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). The first thing the occupiers did was tear up their identity papers in front of their eyes(Citation: Death in Chechnya 1995).

Russian investigators demanded that the detainees confess to helping the army of Ichkeria and told them, blindfolded, to sign papers they could not see(Citation: Death in Chechnya 1995). The occupiers extracted confessions by torture, including with electric current, in pits and prison vans at checkpoints and military units (see: "Torture and Abuse")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

The Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs released most of the detained Chechens without charges. According to a certificate by Zlydenko, deputy head of Russia's prison service, from 11 December 1994 to 22 July 1995, 1,325 people passed through the filtration camps for detainees in Mozdok, a town in Russian-controlled North Ossetia, and in Grozny. The ministry handed a hundred of them over to investigators (see: "Filtration Camp System")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

According to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, from 28 January 1995 to July 1996 the ministry charged 51 people of those who had passed through the camp in Grozny, released 1,024 and exchanged 109 for captured Russian servicemen(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 1 February 1995, Ilyushenko, acting prosecutor general of Russia, charged Dzhokhar Dudayev, the elected president of Ichkeria, with high treason and incitement to terrorism on the basis of a telephone conversation which the prosecutors said they had intercepted(Citation: OMRI Daily Digest, 2 February 1995 1995). The Prosecutor General's Office put the president of Ichkeria on a wanted list, and on 21 April 1996 the Russian military killed him near Gekhi-Chu, a village southwest of Grozny (see: "Neutralization of the Opposition")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Миллион первый 2002). On 6 April 1995, the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs took 16 Chechens out of the filtration camps and forced each of them to sign a paper that called him a fighter of the army of Ichkeria, although, by their own account, none of them had fought. In Malye Atagi, a village south of Grozny, the ministry handed them over to the army of Ichkeria in exchange for a captured Russian major (see: "Hostage-Taking")(Citation: Трагедия села Самашки. Чечня. Апрель 1995. Дневник правозащитника 1995).

On 15 March 1996, Russian soldiers at the checkpoint near Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, detained 91 Chechens who were leaving the village before the assault. Russian investigators interrogated the detainees in the prisons of Pyatigorsk and Stavropol, cities in the south of Russia. One of them, Murat Ganiev, told Human Rights Watch on 14 October 1996: "I told them I wasn't a fighter. … They said that if I said I was a fighter they would release the other forty-six. The only thing they gave us to sign was our release papers"(Citation: Russia/Chechnya: A Legacy of Abuse 1997). Five weeks after the detention, on 19 April 1996, the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs released all the Chechens from Samashki without charges(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In a report of January 1997, Human Rights Watch wrote that the Russian government had not disclosed how many Chechens from the filtration camps it was holding in prison on charges of taking part in the fighting, or under which articles they had been tried(Citation: Russia/Chechnya: A Legacy of Abuse 1997).

By January 1997, when the last Russian troops had left Ichkeria, deputies of the Russian parliament had drafted an amnesty only for Russian servicemen. This draft did not allow the release of Chechens who were held in custody for taking part, or allegedly taking part, in the fighting(Citation: Russia/Chechnya: A Legacy of Abuse 1997). On 12 March 1997, the deputies in Moscow, by resolution No. 1199-II, declared an amnesty for crimes connected with the war, but did not extend it to those charged and convicted under 17 articles of the Criminal Code, including for banditry and murder. The deputies allowed cases under these articles to be closed only against those whom Russia handed over in exchange for its own servicemen and citizens held in Ichkeria(Citation: Постановление Государственной Думы от 12 марта 1997 г. № 1199-II ГД «Об объявлении амнистии в отношении лиц, совершивших общественно опасные деяния в связи с вооруженным конфликтом в Чеченской Республике» 1997).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers killed unarmed Chechens on the roads, in houses and in cellars.

In the captured villages and towns Russian soldiers together with police officers went from house to house during "zachistkas" ("sweeps", as the Russians called the house searches and detentions of Chechens). The occupiers threw grenades into cellars where families were hiding from the shelling. Russian soldiers set houses on fire together with the people inside. Against the walls of houses the occupiers shot unarmed Chechens, among them women and old people(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Russian snipers fired at those who came out of houses and cellars. Under sniper fire Chechen families could not collect the bodies of their relatives from the streets and bury them for several days(Citation: Caught in the Crossfire: Civilians in Gudermes and Pervomayskoye 1996)(Citation: Russian Federation: Human rights violations in the Chechen Republic (EUR 46/20/96) 1996).

On 17 December 1994 the Russian military fired from armored personnel carriers at a column of refugees from Grozny at the border with Russian-controlled Ingushetia and killed ten people on the spot(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 22 December 1994 a Russian pilot bombed the cars that had gathered at a crossroads in Grozny, and then fired two more rockets at those who ran to help the wounded. In all, the occupiers killed up to twenty people at the crossroads(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996).

In early January 1995 special forces of the 67th Brigade of Russian military intelligence blocked a mountain road along which Chechen civilians were leaving Grozny to escape the shelling. The intelligence troops called in attack aircraft, and Russian pilots bombed the refugees' cars that had gathered at the roadblock(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). In Shali, a town to the southeast of Grozny, on 3 January 1995 Russian pilots dropped cluster bombs on the car market and bombed a second time those who ran to help the wounded (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996). Russian servicemen who were searching yards in the settlement of Butenko on the outskirts of Grozny shot four people with assault rifles on 29 January and 3 February 1995, among them three members of the Gagayev family(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). OMON officers, SOBR fighters (police special forces) and soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian MVD (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) searched houses in Petropavlovskaya, a stanitsa to the northeast of Grozny, on 3 February and killed five Chechens(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

In early March 1995 the Armed Forces of Ichkeria, at the insistence of the villagers, were forced to leave Samashki, a village in the west of the Chechen Republic. On 7 April, after shelling, about 250 soldiers of the Sofrino Brigade of the Internal Troops of the Russian MVD, OMON officers and SOBR fighters from Moscow, the Moscow region and Orenburg stormed the village. The occupiers captured Samashki after a short fight with a small group of armed Chechens from the village(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). In the evening Russian soldiers drove four men who were hiding in a storeroom into a car-repair pit in a garage and shot them with assault rifles. The occupiers killed 71-year-old Musait Isayev and wounded Nasruddin Bazuyev and Salavdi Umakhanov, while Abdurakhman Chindigayev survived. Salavdi Umakhanov told Oleg Orlov of Memorial on 4 August 1995: "Musa [Musait Isayev] says: 'Guys, don't shoot. The cattle have to be fed... Don't shoot'… In an instant they gave him a burst of automatic fire from there." The next day the Russian military killed the wounded Nasruddin Bazuyev and his daughter Raisa Masayeva(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 8 April, when no one in the village was resisting any longer, soldiers, OMON officers and SOBR fighters searched the houses. Sadulla Yusupov, an elderly Chechen from Samashki, told Oleg Orlov of Memorial on 13 April: "At ten in the morning soldiers came running here… They were screaming in inhuman voices, swearing, cursing, shouting: 'Come out, you bitches!' and they went up to every house and fired." A Russian soldier fired an assault rifle into the earthen cellar where he had hidden, and a second occupier threw a grenade in and wounded him. When he climbed out, Sadulla Yusupov saw the bodies of six neighbors on the street, among them two old men and a woman(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). The Russian military shot Lechi Arsayev dead from twenty meters, without trying to detain him, as he was hanging a white flag on the fence of his house. On Sharipov Street Russian soldiers set fire to a house where Chechens were hiding. The occupiers immediately shot Abi Akhmetova, who came out of the fire with her hands raised. The report of the Observer Mission of Russian human rights organizations says that Yuki Gaitukayeva, Madu Rasuyev and Kesirt Rasuyeva could not get out of the burning house and apparently burned alive(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). The mission published a list by name of 103 people whom the occupiers killed in Samashki on 7 and 8 April(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). The human rights defenders of Memorial write that at least half of them the Russian military killed deliberately(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 23 April 1995 drunken Russian servicemen opened fire near a shop in the center of Gudermes, the second-largest town of Ichkeria, and soldiers of other Russian units took it for an attack and fired in the town for three and a half hours. By the count of the prosecutor's office that Russia had installed in Grozny, the occupiers killed ten unarmed people that day and wounded eight(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 7 July 1995, during the talks between Russia and Ichkeria, the Russian military killed seven Chechens of the Chapanov family, among them children and old people, in Prigorodnoye, a village near Grozny(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). From 15 December 1995 the crews of Russian helicopters fired at Chechens who were leaving Gudermes to escape the shelling. On the road to the east of the town the pilots killed or wounded about fifteen people(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Caught in the Crossfire: Civilians in Gudermes and Pervomayskoye 1996). On 19-20 December 1995, having again captured Gudermes, which the Armed Forces of Ichkeria had liberated five days earlier, Russian soldiers went around the houses and threw grenades into cellars where old, sick and wounded people were hiding. Shkirko, the commander of the occupation troops, named 267 civilians killed in Gudermes (see: "Lies about Its Own Actions")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 3 March 1996 Russian soldiers who broke into Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria, fired from an armored personnel carrier at three men in a car, killing them and wounding a fourth(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 17 March, during the second storming of Samashki, Russian soldiers led about 40 Chechens, among them 10-15 children, out of a cellar in a yard on Kalinin Street and stood them against a wall. After going out of the gate, the occupiers threw three grenades into the yard and wounded 17 people, two women among them dying of their wounds(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). On 19 March Russian soldiers led the Chechens hiding in the cellars of one of the yards of Samashki out and lined them up against a wall. With a burst of automatic fire the occupiers killed Zakhud Zhadiyeva, a Chechen woman who did not understand the order "stand against the wall" in Russian(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). On 25 April 1996 soldiers from a Russian checkpoint fired at buses in which women and children were being taken out of the surrounded Shali. The occupiers wounded nine people, one woman among them dying of her wounds(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: CHECHEN REPUBLIC - RUSSIAN FEDERATION: Civilians under Russian bombardment - continued fear for safety of civilians in Shali (EUR 46/24/96) 1996). On the night of 15 July 1996 in the northwestern suburb of Grozny, soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian MVD fired from two armored personnel carriers at unarmed people in cars and killed 12 or 13 people. The occupiers set the cars on fire and cut off the ears of some of the bodies (see: "Desecration of the Dead")(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-139) 1996)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 1 August OMON officers of the Russian MVD attacked the settlement of Dolinsky to the northwest of Grozny and shot dead two young men who were sleeping in a car near the houses (see: "Abduction of People")(Citation: CHECHEN REPUBLIC - RUSSIAN FEDERATION: "Disappearance" / Possible extrajudicial execution (UA 196/96, EUR 46/35/96) 1996). On 10 August Russian soldiers who were capturing the area of Abakanskaya Street in Grozny fired flamethrowers into the cellars of houses without checking whether there were people inside. In the cellar of house No. 40 the occupiers burned 12 Chechens from two families, among them two children aged three and four and an 85-year-old woman(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 19 August 1996 the command of the occupation troops demanded that everyone who remained in Grozny leave the city within 48 hours (see: "Collective Punishment"). The next day near the village of Goity to the south of Grozny the crew of a Russian helicopter fired at refugees who were leaving the capital in buses and cars, and killed from ten to twelve people(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Human Rights Watch World Report 1997: The Russian Federation 1997).

Memorial concluded that Russian troops deliberately attacked civilians throughout the war and killed the most of them by bombing and shelling(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Tim Guldimann, the head of the mission of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe in Grozny, wrote that in March 1996 his staff, in a report to the organization's leadership, called Russia's actions a war against the civilian population without military necessity(Citation: Supporting the Doves against the Hawks: Experiences of the OSCE Assistance Group to Chechnya 1998).

The human rights defenders of Memorial write that Russia kept no count of the unarmed Chechens it killed(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). The Observer Mission questioned 265 refugee families from Grozny and, based on their accounts, estimated that from December 1994 to March 1995 the occupiers killed 25,000-29,000 people in the city(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). In March 1996 the UN Secretary-General, in a report to the UN Commission on Human Rights, cited the calculation of Russian human rights organizations: from 25 November 1994 to 15 April 1995, 26,550 civilians died in Ichkeria from Russia's war, among them 2,300 children under 15 and 5,050 women(Citation: The situation of human rights in the Republic of Chechnya of the Russian Federation. Report of the Secretary-General (E/CN.4/1996/13) 1996). In its annual report for 1996 Human Rights Watch estimated the number of civilians killed in Ichkeria since December 1994 at 18,500 to 80,000(Citation: Human Rights Watch World Report 1997: The Russian Federation 1997).

Over the whole war Russian military courts convicted seven servicemen for the killing of civilians (see: "Impunity of Perpetrators")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996). On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers did not let doctors and humanitarian aid reach the Chechens, and did not let the wounded out to the doctors.

Russian servicemen at the checkpoints around villages and towns surrounded before an assault did not let in doctors, UN and Red Cross staff, vehicles with food or buses for refugees. The occupiers did not let the Chechens they had wounded out to the doctors(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Russian soldiers fired on ambulances and vehicles of humanitarian organizations(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Chechnya Case Study. Interim Report 1996).

On 17 December 1994, Russian servicemen shot up a column of cars with refugees from Grozny near the border of Russian-controlled Ingushetia (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians"). The occupiers fired on ambulance doctors who were driving to the wounded from the Ingush side, and did not let them approach the site of the shooting until half past four in the morning(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In January 1995, Russian officials directed humanitarian aid to the northern districts of Ichkeria. To the south of Ichkeria and to Russian-controlled Dagestan, where Chechens had fled, Russian agencies sent no aid(Citation: The situation of human rights in the Republic of Chechnya of the Russian Federation. Report of the Secretary-General (E/CN.4/1996/13) 1996). On 6 January, in Troitskaya, a stanitsa in Ingushetia, a soldier of a patrol of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs shot dead Ruslan, an unarmed driver from a column that a refugee woman from Grozny was leading there for the elderly (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")(Citation: Russia. War in Chechnya. New Report From the Field 1995). In early April 1995, Russian officials held up for a day at a checkpoint just across the border of Ichkeria a Red Cross convoy with medical supplies for Grozny, citing the fact that the drivers did not have the required documents(Citation: Grozny Falls 1995).

On 7 April 1995, the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) stormed Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria. On 8 and 9 April, the special forces of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs at checkpoint No. 13 did not let into the village doctors of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), of Médecins Sans Frontières and of the Russian Red Cross(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995)(Citation: Трагедия села Самашки. Чечня. Апрель 1995. Дневник правозащитника 1995). Valery Borshchov, a deputy of the Russian parliament who was traveling to the village with the doctors on 8 April, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Moscow in February 1996: "As the major, the commander of the 13th post, explained…, they, the military, are guided not by the Geneva Conventions [international treaties on the protection of the wounded and of civilians in war], but by the orders of the local commander, Colonel General Kulikov"(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996). On 9 April, Dzeki Musayeva, born in 1920, died of a hypertensive attack without medical help(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). On 10 April, Russian servicemen allowed the wounded to be taken out, but did not let ambulances into the village, and Chechens from Samashki drove 15 wounded fellow villagers to the post on a bus, a truck and a tractor with a trailer. Russian servicemen from positions on the Sunzha ridge, a range of hills near the village, fired on the trailer and wounded Taus Ibishev a second time; he died a few days later in a hospital in Ingushetia. Ambulance doctors took the rest of the wounded from the post to hospitals in Ingushetia. After this, the occupiers let ICRC vehicles into the village, and on 13 April doctors of the Russian Red Cross. The report of the Observer Mission of Russian human rights organizations says that at least 13 wounded Chechens from Samashki died because they did not receive medical help in time. The Mission published a list by name of those killed in the village, including those who died of their wounds without medical help(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 30 September 1995, Russian Internal Troops and police surrounded Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria near the border with Ingushetia, and did not let UN staff with humanitarian aid reach the 3,000 refugees at the village resort, among them 2,100 children (see: "Transport Blockade")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: World Vision Team Re-Enters Sernovodsk. Trip shows shocking conditions in Sernovodsk and in Grozni hospital 1995). From 26 October, the soldiers did not let vehicles with food into Sernovodsk, and from November they let a truck with food in twice a week(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). To the appeal of the representative of the UN Secretary-General of 7 November 1995 about the shortage of food among the refugees of Sernovodsk, the Russian government replied almost four months later, on 29 February 1996(Citation: The situation of human rights in the Republic of Chechnya of the Russian Federation. Report of the Secretary-General (E/CN.4/1996/13) 1996). In December 1995, Russian servicemen fired on a Red Cross vehicle that was driving to Vedeno, a district center in the southeast of Ichkeria. The Red Cross staff could not come to terms with the occupiers and turned back(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-95-241) 1995).

On 14 December 1995, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Gudermes, the second-largest city of Ichkeria, east of Grozny, and on 19-20 December Russian troops captured it after five days of shelling and bombing (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). The Russian government did not allow humanitarian organizations to evacuate Chechen civilians from the city, and the townspeople walked on foot to Russian-controlled Dagestan. On the way, refugees froze to death, among them at least four children(Citation: Caught in the Crossfire: Civilians in Gudermes and Pervomayskoye 1996). In Osman-Yurt, a village in Dagestan, five-year-old Zali Zelimkhanova, who was walking with her family from Gudermes, died. On 21 January 1996, her mother Melkhash Zelimkhanova told human rights defenders of the international organization Human Rights Watch and of "Memorial" there: "When we were in the basement [in Gudermes] it was very cold, and by the time we got here my daughter, Zali, got sick and died a sudden death"(Citation: Caught in the Crossfire: Civilians in Gudermes and Pervomayskoye 1996). After the capture of Gudermes, Russian servicemen for several days did not let ICRC staff into the city, while the elderly, women and children froze without food or water in the basements of destroyed houses. On 26 December, the ICRC began distributing aid in Gudermes(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-95-249) 1995).

In December 1995 and January 1996, soldiers at Russian checkpoints hardly ever let through the vehicles of the Belgian section of Médecins Sans Frontières, and the doctors could not get medicines to Gudermes(Citation: Caught in the Crossfire: Civilians in Gudermes and Pervomayskoye 1996). On the eve of New Year 1996, Russian servicemen and officers of the Ministry of Internal Affairs at the posts around Sernovodsk beat the crews of vehicles that were bringing New Year presents to the children(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

In 1996, Russian servicemen at the checkpoints checked humanitarian organizations for passes for travel around Ichkeria. Russian agencies issued a pass for two weeks, often a few days before it expired, or did not issue one at all(Citation: Chechnya Case Study. Interim Report 1996). By 3 January, the occupiers had closed the roads around Grozny and to Gudermes to ICRC vehicles. The commanders of the occupation troops in Grozny and the military leadership in Moscow did not reply until the end of January to the ICRC's requests to name someone to negotiate with(Citation: Caught in the Crossfire: Civilians in Gudermes and Pervomayskoye 1996). On 5 March 1996, during the assault on Sernovodsk by the Russian units of Artemov, the commander of the occupation troops in the southwest of Ichkeria, the occupiers agreed with the ICRC to cease fire and let its staff through to the wounded and sick, but on 6 March the soldiers at the post did not let the ICRC vehicles through, saying that they had received no orders(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). The Chechens wounded by the occupiers reached doctors only on 9 March, when Russian troops captured Sernovodsk(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010), and the ICRC got into the village three weeks after the start of the assault on 3 March(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). During the assault on Samashki, on 16 March 1996 the occupiers did not let through 17 buses of the International Organization for Migration, which had agreed with the Russian military to evacuate those who remained in the village, and did not let the wounded out through Novy Sharoy, a village to the south, although the Chechens offered 100 million rubles and a car for this(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). On 19 March, when the occupiers opened the way out of Samashki, a doctor of the village hospital took the wounded to the hospital in Achkhoy-Martan, a district center in the west of Ichkeria(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In the spring of 1996, Russian troops surrounded the mountain villages of the Vedeno, Shatoy and Nozhay-Yurt districts in the south and southeast of Ichkeria. The soldiers did not let doctors or humanitarian organizations in(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 10 July 1996, Russian troops surrounded Makhkety, a mountain village in the southeast of Ichkeria, and blocked the only road out of it, while soldiers at the Russian checkpoints around Shali, a town southeast of Grozny, did not let vehicles with the wounded through. Seriously wounded Chechens were carried out of Makhkety along mountain paths; four of them died of their wounds in the hospital in Shali(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

The human rights defenders of Human Rights Watch wrote in their review for 1995 that Russian troops again and again blocked or delayed humanitarian aid to civilians in Ichkeria, especially at the start of the war, and at least once fired on a Médecins Sans Frontières vehicle with a clearly visible emblem of the organization(Citation: Human Rights Watch World Report 1996: The Russian Federation 1996). On 26 March 1996, the UN Secretary-General wrote in a report to the Commission on Human Rights that, according to Human Rights Watch, Russian agencies created bureaucratic obstacles for aid organizations, hindered the distribution of aid and did not allow the sick and wounded to be evacuated from Grozny. Sergei Kovalyov, Russia's human rights commissioner, informed the UN that Russia was obstructing the delivery of humanitarian aid to the war zone, including medicines to save the wounded(Citation: The situation of human rights in the Republic of Chechnya of the Russian Federation. Report of the Secretary-General (E/CN.4/1996/13) 1996).

In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996). On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

The use of regular troops without insignia to establish control over the peninsula. A year later V. Putin admitted it on his call-in show of 17 April 2014: "behind the backs of Crimea's self-defense forces, our servicemen, of course, stood. They acted very correctly, but… decisively and professionally"(Citation: Прямая линия с Владимиром Путиным 2014). Ukrainian garrisons on the peninsula were blockaded and disarmed, as Putin himself admitted: "and the way the Ukrainian units were disarmed - all of this was done so swiftly that it seemed it had been prepared for an incredibly long time"(Citation: Прямая линия с Владимиром Путиным 2014).

The overt crossing of the state border by regular Russian troops in the summer and autumn of 2014 to save the separatists from defeat: the "DNR" commander admitted that the decisive role was played by Russian servicemen who came "on leave" - "it was mostly 'vacationers' who advanced on Mariupol. When they left, both the front line and the opportunities became precarious"(Citation: Стрелков: Спусковой крючок войны нажал я 2014). The offensive resulted in heavy losses for the Ukrainian army near Ilovaisk and Debaltseve. The presence of regular troops continued into 2015: the GRU men captured near Shchastia were "soldiers of the 3rd Separate Guards Special Purpose Brigade of the Main Directorate of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces, who arrived on the territory of Ukraine on March 26 and were quartered in Luhansk"(Citation: «Короче, разведка — россияне». Как искали, судили и защищали капитана Ерофеева и сержанта Александрова 2016).

The invasion by the regular Russian army and massive missile and air strikes on Ukrainian cities: "On 24 February 2022, the President of the Russian Federation, Vladimir Putin, announced his decision to conduct a 'special military operation' in Ukraine to seek its 'demilitarization and denazification'. On the same day, Russian troops crossed various border points into Ukraine, including through Belarus, and launched attacks by land, air and sea"(Citation: Report of the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine (A/HRC/52/62) 2023). The UN Commission investigated the events of February-March 2022 in Kyiv, Chernihiv, Kharkiv and Sumy Provinces(Citation: Report of the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine (A/HRC/52/62) 2023).

On 7 November 1991 the RSFSR president Yeltsin signed decree No. 178, point 1: "To introduce, from 05:00 on 9 November 1991 until 05:00 on 9 December 1991, a state of emergency on the whole territory of the Chechen-Ingush Republic". By the same decree he imposed a curfew, banned rallies and strikes, ordered "the temporary seizure of firearms and cold weapons from citizens, enterprises and organisations", searches of vehicles and dwellings, and "the expulsion of violators of public order who are not residents of the given locality to their place of permanent residence or beyond the territory of the Chechen-Ingush Republic at their own expense", and instructed the minister of internal affairs and the chairman of the KGB (predecessor of today's FSB) of the RSFSR to submit "proposals on bringing in additional forces"(Citation: Указ Президента РСФСР № 178 О введении чрезвычайного положения в Чечено-Ингушской Республике 1991). On 8 November the parliament of the Chechen Republic, chaired by Khusein Akhmadov, demanded that Yeltsin "within 24 hours withdraw all armed formations from the territory of the sovereign Chechen Republic" and resolved "to inform the parliaments and peoples of the world of the armed interference of the leadership of Russia in the internal affairs of the sovereign Chechen Republic"(Citation: Постановление Парламента Чеченской Республики № 25 О незаконности Указа Президента РСФСР о введении чрезвычайного положения на территории Чеченской Республики 1991). The journalist Tsyganok, in the article "Ten Days That Cancelled the Peace", quotes the summary of the RSFSR ministry of internal affairs for the morning of 10 November: "To ensure the regime of the state of emergency, units of the MVD [ministry of internal affairs] of the RSFSR with a total strength of about 1.2 thousand men have been sent to the North Caucasus region"(Citation: Десять дней которые отменили мир 2021). According to the chronicle of events, on 8-9 November "two military transport aircraft with special-forces detachments on board, but without weapons, landed at the Khankala military airfield near Grozny… the airfield is blockaded by Dzh. Dudaev's guardsmen, leaving the aircraft is impossible, so on the morning of 9 November the aircraft fly away"(Citation: Чечня 1990-1991: хроника и документы 2007). The National Guard of Chechnya and unarmed townspeople surrounded the building of the ministry of internal affairs in Grozny; on 9 November the first deputy minister of internal affairs of the RSFSR Komissarov reported to Moscow: "We are blockaded in the building of the MVD [ministry of internal affairs] of the ChIR [Chechen-Ingush Republic]. We are surrounded by a crowd of about 4,000 people, fuel tankers are standing opposite"(Citation: Десять дней которые отменили мир 2021). On 9 November the Moscow leadership recorded that "the heads of the executive bodies (Barannikov [minister of internal affairs of the USSR], Bakatin [chairman of the KGB of the USSR], Komissarov [first deputy minister of internal affairs of the RSFSR]) in a difficult critical situation failed to carry out their direct official duties"(Citation: Постановление Президиума ВС РСФСР от 09.11.1991 Об Указе Президента РСФСР от 7 ноября 1991 г. О введении чрезвычайного положения в Чечено-Ингушской Республике 1991). The nominal head of the USSR, Gorbachev, refused the RSFSR the use of union troops, and on 10 November at 10:45 the internal troops (predecessors of today's Rosgvardiya) began their withdrawal from Grozny(Citation: Десять дней которые отменили мир 2021). On 11 November the deputies in Moscow resolved "to recognise the approval of the Decree as impossible", established "a special regime of entry into and exit from the Chechen-Ingush Republic, excluding the import and export of weapons" and ordered "a parliamentary and an internal (through the MVD of the RSFSR and the KGB of the RSFSR) investigation to establish the persons responsible for taking insufficiently prepared political and military-technical decisions on the introduction of the state of emergency"(Citation: Постановление ВС РСФСР № 1855-I 1991).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers captured the towns and villages of Ichkeria.

On 26 November 1994 the defenders of Grozny, the capital of Ichkeria, routed the Russian tank crews who were storming the city under the banner of the puppet opposition (see: "Staging a Coup")(Citation: Грозный после штурма города 26 ноября 1994 года 1994). By 29 November the Russian army had gathered about 140 combat aircraft for the attack on Ichkeria. On 29 November Russian pilots in six Su-27 aircraft and four helicopters attacked the presidential palace in Grozny(Citation: Chechnya/ Russia - Air Attack On Grozny 1994). On 1 December the crews of Russian Su-25 attack aircraft destroyed all of Ichkeria's aircraft on its airfields(Citation: Лётчикам не дали развернуться 1999). On 9 December Russian President Yeltsin, by Decree No. 2166, ordered the government to use all means of the Russian state, including the army, against the Armed Forces of Ichkeria(Citation: Указ Президента Российской Федерации № 2166 О мерах по пресечению деятельности незаконных вооруженных формирований на территории Чеченской Республики и в зоне осетино-ингушского конфликта 1994).

A day before the talks between Russia and Ichkeria scheduled for 12 December, the Russian army and the Internal Troops of the MVD (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) began an offensive in three columns from the neighboring Russian-controlled republics (see: "Negotiations as Cover for an Attack")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Sources differ: some put the strength of these columns at 14,972 men, others at almost 24,000(Citation: Войны с Чечней 2001)(Citation: Первая чеченская война: хроника конфликта 2024). The Russian Ministry of Defense estimated the Armed Forces of Ichkeria at 11,000-12,000 fighters, the Russian MVD at up to 15,000, and both ministries counted another 30,000-40,000 Chechen volunteers(Citation: Первая чеченская кампания 1994-1996 годов 2014). The northern column advanced from Mozdok, and the western column from Vladikavkaz through Ingushetia. The eastern column set out from Kizlyar, a town in Dagestan(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Постановление Правительства Российской Федерации № 1360 Об обеспечении государственной безопасности и территориальной целостности Российской Федерации, законности, прав и свобод граждан, разоружения незаконных вооруженных формирований на территории Чеченской Республики 1994). On 11 December unarmed Chechens of the Khasavyurt district of Dagestan surrounded the armored personnel carriers of the eastern column and did not let the occupation troops through(Citation: За спинами мирных жителей. Захват заложников и использование гражданского населения в качестве «живого щита» федеральными войсками России в ходе вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1996)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 12 December near the village of Novy Sharoy in the west of Ichkeria, thousands of Chechens stood on the road in front of the western column and held it up for a week at the border with Ingushetia(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Хроника первой российской войны в Чечне 2026). On that day the army of Ichkeria stopped the northern column near the settlement of Dolinsky, about ten kilometers northwest of Grozny(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

Before a storming, Russian troops surrounded towns and villages and shelled them with artillery, while Russian aircraft bombed them (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). The occupiers demanded that the Chechens in the surrounded villages expel the defenders and hand over their weapons (see: "Collective Punishment")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). In the captured towns Russian troops set up commandant's offices and garrisons. In Grozny Russia installed the Russian-controlled "Government of National Revival" (see: "Puppet Government")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999).

From 18 December 1994 Russian aircraft bombed the residential districts of Grozny. On 19 December units of the Russian airborne division from Pskov under the command of General Babichev reached the western outskirts of the city(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 31 December the Russian army stormed Grozny from four sides. The defenders of the city routed the occupiers' columns and took more than a hundred Russian servicemen prisoner. The human rights defenders of Memorial write about the troops of General Pulikovsky, who were advancing from the northwest: "The 131st (Maikop) Separate Motorized Rifle Brigade and the 81st (Samara) Motorized Rifle Regiment were almost completely routed"(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 7-9 January 1995 the occupiers stormed Grozny again, from the north and west. Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, the vice president of Ichkeria, who together with Aslan Maskhadov led the defense of the presidential palace, wrote in his memoirs about the evening of 18 January: "We were deciding one question: to stay and die, which was tantamount to the destruction of the Main Staff, or to leave the Presidential Palace and set up a new headquarters on the other side of the Sunzha [the river in the center of Grozny]"(Citation: Чечения - битва за свободу 1996). On the night of 19 January Russian pilots dropped concrete-piercing bombs on the palace, and the defenders were forced to leave. On 19 January Russian soldiers captured the ruins of the palace. The occupiers stormed the remaining districts of Grozny for another month and a half. By early February 1995 Russia had brought the number of its troops in Ichkeria up to 70,000 men(Citation: Первая чеченская кампания 1994-1996 годов 2014). The defenders fought longest in Chernorechye in the south of the city, and on 6 March 1995 the Internal Troops of the Russian MVD captured this district(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 23 March 1995 the occupiers captured Argun, a town to the east of Grozny(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 24 March Russian troops broke into Achkhoy-Martan, a district center in the west of Ichkeria, but fighters of the army of Ichkeria liberated the village with a counterattack(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). On 28 and 29 March the Russian army surrounded Gudermes, the second-largest town of Ichkeria, and Shali, a town to the southeast of Grozny. Russian commanders demanded that the townspeople persuade the defenders to leave, and on 30-31 March, when the fighters of the army of Ichkeria were forced to leave both towns, the occupiers captured them without a fight(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 12 May the Russian army began an offensive into the mountains in the south of Ichkeria. On 3 June the occupiers captured Vedeno, a district center to the southeast of Grozny, and on 12 June Shatoy to the south of the capital and Nozhai-Yurt in the southeast(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 18 June 1995 Chernomyrdin, the chairman of the Russian government, agreed on a cessation of fighting with Shamil Basayev, the commander of the fighters of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria who had taken hostages in Budyonnovsk, a Russian-controlled town to the northwest of the republic. That evening the occupation troops halted their offensive (see: "Sham Treaties")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). At the end of July, Grozny, Argun, Gudermes, Shali and the mountain district centers were under occupation by the Russian army, while in most villages there were no Russian troops(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). On 14 December 1995 the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Gudermes to disrupt the "vote" for the head of the puppet government. On 19-20 December, after six days of shelling and bombing of residential districts, the occupiers captured the town again(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Caught in the Crossfire: Civilians in Gudermes and Pervomayskoye 1996).

On 17-20 February 1996 the Russian army shelled and captured by storm Novogroznensky, a settlement to the east of Gudermes(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 3 March Russian troops broke into Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria, on the day their commanders had set for signing a peace with the leaders of the village, and the defenders drove the attackers out. By 9 March, after six days of shelling, the defenders of Sernovodsk were forced to leave, and the occupiers captured the village(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 6 March the Armed Forces of Ichkeria under the command of Ruslan Gelayev attacked the occupiers in Grozny and liberated most of the city. The army of Ichkeria did not try to hold the city and left it on 8 March(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). On the night of 14 March Russian troops surrounded Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, and on 15 March began a storming with tanks, artillery, helicopters and aircraft. On 19 March the fighters of the army of Ichkeria under the command of Khizir Khachukayev ran out of ammunition and were forced to leave(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 4 April, after six days of bombing, Russian soldiers broke into Goyskoye, a village to the southwest of Grozny, but the defenders under the command of Akhmed Zakayev repelled the storming. On 7 May the occupiers under the command of General Shamanov captured Goyskoye(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 24 May, after three months of stormings, shelling and bombing, the Russian army captured Bamut, a village in the west of Ichkeria at the border with Russian-controlled Ingushetia, while the defenders under the command of Ruslan Khaikhoroyev broke out of the encirclement(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 9 July 1996, six days after the Russian presidential election, the occupiers violated the ceasefire agreement signed with Ichkeria on 27 May and launched a new offensive (see: "Sham Ceasefire")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On that day Russian units under the command of General Tikhomirov, the commander of the occupation troops, surrounded and shelled Gekhi, a village to the southwest of Grozny, where a unit of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria was stationed. By 12 July the occupiers had killed the unit's commander Doku Makhayev and destroyed more than a third of the village(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-139) 1996). On 15 July the occupiers captured Makhkety, a mountain village of the Vedeno district in the southeast of Ichkeria, which they had surrounded five days earlier(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999).

The Russian human rights defenders of Memorial write that the Russian army with aircraft, heavy artillery and tanks fought against Ichkeria, although the president and government of Russia passed the war off as a police disarmament(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 19 January 1995 the European Parliament in a resolution condemned Russia's use of the army against Ichkeria(Citation: Resolution on the situation in Chechnya (European Parliament, 19 January 1995) 1995). The Parliamentary Assembly of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe in a declaration of 8 July 1995 condemned Russia's war in Ichkeria as a gross violation of international law(Citation: Ottawa Declaration of the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly and Resolutions Adopted by the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly at the Fourth Annual Session, Ottawa, 8 July 1995 1995).

In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers. In three days of fighting the army of Ichkeria retook the center and about 80 percent of the city(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). The defenders forced Russia to the negotiating table. On 22 August 1996 in the village of Novye Atagi in the south of the republic, Russia and Ichkeria signed an agreement on the withdrawal of Russian troops from Grozny and joint control over certain districts of the city(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-164) 1996). On 31 August 1996 General Lebed, the secretary of the Russian Security Council, and Aslan Maskhadov, the chief of the Main Staff of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria, signed a joint statement in Khasavyurt, a town in Russian-controlled Dagestan. In it Russia acknowledged that resolving disputed issues by force or the threat of force was inadmissible (see: "Sham Treaties")(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996).

By 31 August 1996 the occupation troops had left Grozny for their main bases in Khankala on the eastern outskirts of the city and at the Severny airport to the north of it. Russian police officers and soldiers of the Internal Troops of the MVD remained in the city. Russia withdrew its troops from Vedeno, Shatoy, Nozhai-Yurt and Kurchaloy, villages in the south and east of Ichkeria. Russian units still stood in Shali, near Bamut and in the Naur and Shelkovskaya districts in the north of Ichkeria(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). In these two districts beyond the Terek river there was no fighting during the whole war. On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

An attempt to physically eliminate the leader of the democratic opposition V. Yushchenko at the height of the election campaign by dioxin poisoning: in late December 2004 "a patient presented with TCDD poisoning; the levels in his blood serum (108000 pg/g lipid weight) were more than 50 000-fold greater than those in the general population"(Citation: TCDD poisoning in Victor Yushchenko 2009). The poisoning led to severe disfigurement of the candidate's face.

The physical elimination of legitimate representatives of local government who resisted the occupation: "the mutilated body of Volodomyr Rybak, a member of the 'Batkivshchyna' party and deputy of the Municipal Council of Horlivka (Donetsk region), was found near the village of Raihorodok," and "Rybak was abducted on April 17 by pro-Russians, following a pro-Ukrainian gathering in Horlivka. He was then tortured and murdered"(Citation: Ukraine: The Forgotten Victims 2014).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Russia killed the leaders of Ichkeria, put them on wanted lists and arrested the republic's representatives in Moscow.

Russian President Yeltsin, by Decree No. 1226 of 14 June 1994, allowed anyone suspected of ties to criminal groups to be held without charge for up to 30 days(Citation: Russia: Amnesty calls on Russian authorities to release or charge Chechen detainees 1995). Under this decree, the FSB and the Russian police detained representatives of Ichkeria in Moscow(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-95-119) 1995)(Citation: Постановление Правительства Российской Федерации № 1360 Об обеспечении государственной безопасности и территориальной целостности Российской Федерации, законности, прав и свобод граждан, разоружения незаконных вооруженных формирований на территории Чеченской Республики 1994).

On 1 February 1995, the Prosecutor General's Office of Russia put Dzhokhar Dudayev, the elected president of Ichkeria, on the wanted list in order to arrest and try him (see: "Manufacturing Criminals")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 17 June 1995, officers of the FSB and the Moscow police arrested Khamad Kurbanov, the representative of the president of Ichkeria in Russia, and two days later Ramzan Muzaev, secretary of the Chechen news agency Chechen-Press(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-95-119) 1995). The FSB and police officers held both without charge, released the agency's secretary by 26 July, and the president's representative a month after his arrest(Citation: Russia: Amnesty calls on Russian authorities to release or charge Chechen detainees 1995)(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-95-144) 1995)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). On 8 October 1995, during the "ceasefire", Russian pilots bombed Roshni-Chu, a village southwest of Grozny, and killed 28 people, among them Magomed Khachuev, head of security of the delegation of Ichkeria at the talks. Human rights defenders of Memorial write that the target of the strike was Dzhokhar Dudayev, the president of Ichkeria, who at times lived in the village and was unharmed(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 21 April 1996, Dzhokhar Dudayev, with his wife Alla Dudayeva, his associates and his guards, drove out of Gekhi-Chu, a village southwest of Grozny, to a clearing in the mountains. The president put a satellite phone on the hood of the car and called Konstantin Borovoy, a deputy of the Russian parliament and a mediator in the peace talks. Russian servicemen struck the clearing with missiles(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-080) 1996). The occupiers killed the president of Ichkeria, Prosecutor General Magomet Zhaniev and Khamad Kurbanov, the republic's former representative in Moscow. Alla Dudayeva was standing twenty meters from the car. In her memoirs, the president's wife wrote: "Suddenly, from the left, came the sharp whistle of an incoming missile. In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers looted Chechen homes and carried the belongings away in military vehicles(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

Officers of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs and soldiers of the Russian Internal Troops (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia), during "zachistkas" ("sweeps", as the Russians called house searches and detentions of Chechens) in Grozny, went from house to house with weapons. The occupiers took money, gold and valuables from the owners. Chechen families filed the most complaints of looting against them(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

From December 1994, Russian police officers and fighters of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs looted Chechen families in the stanitsa of Assinovskaya in the west of Ichkeria(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). In mid-January 1995, the elders let Russian troops into the stanitsa after they promised to do no harm (see: "False Guarantees of Safety"), and the occupiers looted the homes of Chechens(Citation: Russia: Three Months of War in Chechnya 1995). On 28 and 29 January, the Russian military surrounded a block in the settlement of Butenko on the outskirts of Grozny with armored personnel carriers, went from yard to yard with weapons, took a thousand dollars from Leila Bapayeva, and from her neighbor, a mother of eleven children, her "Mother Heroine" medal(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). In late January, the occupiers loaded appliances from abandoned houses of Grozny into armored personnel carriers, and a Russian captain drove a covered truck full of furniture through the city(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). In February, because of the looting in Assinovskaya, the head of the Achkhoy-Martan district in the west of Ichkeria and a representative of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria refused to let the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs into the villages of the district(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995).

In the winter of 1995, after the seizure of Grozny, the Russian military carried the belongings of Chechens on army vehicles through Ingushetia to North Ossetia, Russian-controlled republics to the west of Ichkeria. Russian traffic police recorded many such cases at their posts in Ingushetia(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In February 1995, Russian Justice Minister Kovalyov and General Babichev, who commanded one of the occupiers' groupings, declared on air that soldiers who take food from abandoned houses, or whatever is lying around unguarded, commit no crime(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 1 March 1995, Sobolev, deputy director of the FSK (predecessor of today's FSB), admitted on the Vremya program of the ORT television channel that the Russian military in Ichkeria had looted. Russian soldiers who on 30 March 1995 seized Gudermes, the second-largest town of Ichkeria, took whatever they wanted at the market and did not pay(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Caught in the Crossfire: Civilians in Gudermes and Pervomayskoye 1996). On 7-8 April 1995, the Internal Troops and police special forces of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs stormed Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, and killed 103 peaceful Chechens (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians"). Чечня. Апрель 1995. Дневник правозащитника 1995). In April 1995, Albast Madayev from Samashki wrote to Govorukhin, chairman of the Russian parliament's commission investigating the causes of the war in Ichkeria: "They burned my house with a shot from a flamethrower, killed 3 cows and 12 sheep. In April 1995, an officer of the Russian FSB confirmed in Ichkeria to Viktor Kurochkin and Viktor Sheinis, deputies of the Russian parliament, that soldiers of the occupation troops were looting the seized villages on a mass scale. On the night of 7 July 1995, the Russian soldiers Korovin, Shulin and Petrov came from their unit to the settlement of Rodina to demand money and gold from Chechens, killed two of them and wounded three. On 15 September 1991 the deputies of the Supreme Soviet of Chechen-Ingushetia, at their last session, chaired in person by Khasbulatov, a Chechen from the Moscow leadership, then acting head of parliament, dissolved themselves and chose from their own ranks a Provisional Supreme Council of 32 members headed by Khusein Akhmadov to hold new elections(Citation: Russia Confronts Chechnya: Roots of a Separatist Conflict 1998). Filatov, in 1991 secretary of the parliament's leadership in Moscow, recalled: "with the energetic participation of Khasbulatov the Supreme Soviet of the republic was dispersed — what remained was the so-called Small Council, some artificial formation that was to work until new elections were held"(Citation: Совершенно несекретно 1999). Khusein Akhmadov took the side of Dzhokhar Dudaev's congress and on 4 October signed a resolution on the KGB (predecessor of today's FSB): "to terminate the activity of the KGB of the ChIR [Chechen-Ingush Republic] and of all its structures on the territory of the Chechen Republic"(Citation: Постановление Временного Совета Чеченской Республики О прекращении деятельности Комитета Государственной безопасности Чечено-Ингушской Республики 1991). Then Moscow began to build its own power out of this council. On 25 September five of its members headed by the council's deputy chairman Chernyi, Khasbulatov's man, came out against Dzhokhar Dudaev's congress; on 26 September Khasbulatov himself threatened by telegram not to recognise the elections; on 5 October thirteen of the council's thirty-two members, backed by the local KGB, tried to remove Khusein Akhmadov(Citation: Russia Confronts Chechnya: Roots of a Separatist Conflict 1998). On 8 October the Moscow leadership, over Khasbulatov's signature, having heard vice-president Rutskoi back from Grozny, declared lawful in the republic only the council "under the chairmanship of comrade B. D. Bakhmadov" - a procurator whom they themselves had installed - and instructed it "to take all necessary measures to stabilise the situation"(Citation: Постановление Президиума ВС РСФСР № 1723-I О политической ситуации в Чечено-Ингушской Республике 1991). General Sokolov, head of the occupation army's training centre in Grozny, reported to his command: "the chairman V. D. Bakhmadov was appointed by the Chairman of the Supreme Soviet of the RSFSR R. I. Khasbulatov", and the council itself "has no practical power"(Citation: Чечня 1990-1991: хроника и документы 2007). On 9 October the leadership of the National Congress of the Chechen People, Dzhokhar Dudaev's congress, called Bakhmadov's council "unlawful, puppet" and demanded that it "dissociate itself from the attempt to resurrect" the Supreme Soviet "dissolved by the people"(Citation: Постановление Президиума Исполкома ОКЧН от 09.10.1991 1991). After the elections of 27 October Bakhmadov's council addressed the residents of the republic: the elections "are unconstitutional and have no lawful force, not a single decree of the so-called president D. Dudaev, not a single resolution of the parliament of the so-called Chechen Republic has legal force or is subject to execution"(Citation: Обращение Временного Высшего Совета Чечено-Ингушской Республики к народам, партиям, движениям, трудовым коллективам 1991). On 7 November the RSFSR president Yeltsin, by decree No. 178, resolved: "To introduce... on the territory of the Chechen-Ingush Republic, as a special form of administration, a Provisional Administration of the Chechen-Ingush Republic"; as its head he appointed his own representative in the republic, Arsanov, as deputy the republic's minister of internal affairs Ibragimov, and instructed them "to form the Provisional Administration of the Chechen-Ingush Republic within 3 days"(Citation: Указ Президента РСФСР № 178 О введении чрезвычайного положения в Чечено-Ингушской Республике 1991). On 8 November the parliament of the Chechen Republic, chaired by Khusein Akhmadov, replied: "The leadership of Russia, following the lead of the overthrown totalitarian forces and proceeding from imperial interests, has introduced it [the state of emergency] on the territory of a republic whose sovereignty was proclaimed as far back as November 1990" - and declared the decree "unlawful and having no legal force"(Citation: Постановление Парламента Чеченской Республики № 25 О незаконности Указа Президента РСФСР о введении чрезвычайного положения на территории Чеченской Республики 1991). Neither Bakhmadov's council nor Arsanov's Provisional Administration ever got to work in Chechnya: on 11 November the deputies in Moscow refused to approve Yeltsin's decree(Citation: Постановление ВС РСФСР № 1855-I 1991).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Russia installed governments under its control in Ichkeria.

On 23 November 1994 the Provisional Council, a puppet opposition, announced the creation of a "Government of National Revival" headed by Khadzhiyev(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). The Russian army handed the Provisional Council armored vehicles and helicopters with crews for the storming of Grozny, the capital of Ichkeria, but on 26 November the Armed Forces of Ichkeria routed the attackers' troops (see: "Staging a Coup")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 17 December 1994, six days after the open invasion, Russian President Yeltsin, by Decree No. 2200, created an occupation administration in Ichkeria headed by Yegorov, the Russian minister for nationalities (see: "Installation of a New System of Governance")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Указ Президента Российской Федерации № 2200 О восстановлении федеральных территориальных органов исполнительной власти на территории Чеченской Республики 1994). On 26 December the puppet opposition announced Khadzhiyev's "government" for the second time. The "government" declared that it was ready for talks with Russia and did not demand the withdrawal of Russian troops(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 24 October 1995, two weeks after Moscow halted the talks with the leadership of Ichkeria, Russia replaced Khadzhiyev as head of the puppet government with Zavgayev, the last leader of the Soviet regime in Chechen-Ingushetia. On 14-17 December Russia held a "vote" under occupation and declared its protégé the "elected" head of the republic (see: "Sham Expression of Popular Will")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

At the end of January 1996 Chernomyrdin, the chairman of the Russian government, wrote to the deputies of the Russian parliament that the results of the "vote" showed support for Zavgayev in the republic, and proposed to resolve the war as a dispute among Chechens themselves(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 27 May 1996 Russian President Yeltsin received in the Kremlin a delegation of Ichkeria headed by Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, the acting president. Russia included Zavgayev in its delegation. The Chechen negotiators demanded that Moscow's protégé leave the table, but the Russian side refused. Russia insisted that the head of the puppet government sign the ceasefire agreement, and the delegation of Ichkeria objected again. All members of the Russian delegation, including Zavgayev, signed the document, as did the representatives of Ichkeria. A report by the NTV correspondents Cherkasov, Rebrov and Melikhov for the program "Itogi" says that the Russian protégé did not want to sign any agreements with Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev: "However, the center [Moscow] gave the order and the region [the puppet government] answered 'yes, sir'"(Citation: Итоги: переговоры Ельцина и Яндарбиева в Кремле 1996).

On 14 July 1996 Russian President Yeltsin, by the decree "On Measures to Stabilize the Activities of the Bodies of State Power of the Chechen Republic", declared that the puppet Committee of National Accord and the "Government of National Revival" were no longer needed(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-136) 1996)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). In their place Moscow recognized the "elected" Zavgayev, his government, the puppet parliament and the heads of districts as the leadership of the republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-136) 1996).

The human rights defenders of Memorial write that the Russian occupation administration in fact controlled the puppet government(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). They write about Decree No. 435, by which Russian President Yeltsin on 31 March 1996 promised to halt the offensive, begin talks with Ichkeria and declare an amnesty: "all these measures were regarded as auxiliary in the process of legitimizing [recognizing as lawful] the puppet regime"(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Tim Guldimann, the head of the mission of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe in Grozny from January 1996, wrote in 1998 that Moscow pushed the Armed Forces of Ichkeria southward with its troops and used Zavgayev's government to strengthen Russia's influence in the Chechen Republic(Citation: Supporting the Doves against the Hawks: Experiences of the OSCE Assistance Group to Chechnya 1998).

On 31 July 1996, at a meeting with Chechens living in Moscow, Zavgayev, the head of the puppet government, said that the Armed Forces of Ichkeria did not control most of the districts of the republic(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-148) 1996). On 6 August the army of Ichkeria attacked the occupiers in Grozny(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 7 August Zavgayev fled to the base of the occupation troops in Khankala, on the eastern outskirts of the city(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999), and then left the Chechen Republic(Citation: Доку Завгаев видит в Чечне только хорошее 2001). At the end of August the police officers of the puppet government moved from their buildings to the Russian military at the Severny airport to the north of the capital(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). The defenders liberated Grozny from the occupiers and forced Russia to the negotiating table. On 31 August 1996 Moscow signed peace agreements with the leadership of Ichkeria in Khasavyurt, a town in Russian-controlled Dagestan (see: "Sham Treaties")(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996). Until November 1996 the colonizer called the departed Zavgayev the "head of the republic"(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Премьер в загоне 1999). On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left Ichkeria. On 27 January 1997 the Chechens elected Aslan Maskhadov president of Ichkeria(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).
