On 10 September 1991 the RSFSR president Yeltsin sent to Chechen-Ingushetia a delegation headed by state secretary Burbulis and instructed it "to explain the policy of the Russian Federation and of the President of the RSFSR at the present stage"(Citation: Распоряжение Президента РСФСР № 38-рп О направлении делегации РСФСР в Чечено-Ингушскую Республику 1991); the delegation came back with nothing(Citation: Чечня 1990-1991: хроника и документы 2007). On 8 October the Moscow leadership, over Khasbulatov's signature, resolved "until the election of a new composition of the Supreme Soviet of the Chechen-Ingush Republic, to regard the Provisional Supreme Council of the Republic as the only lawful body of state power on the territory of the Chechen-Ingush Republic" and ordered "the illegal armed formations [this is what the coloniser called the fighters for independence from Russia] to surrender their weapons to the bodies of internal affairs by 24:00 on 10 October 1991"(Citation: Постановление Президиума ВС РСФСР № 1723-I О политической ситуации в Чечено-Ингушской Республике 1991). The Chechens did not surrender their weapons: on 9 October the leadership of the National Congress of the Chechen People replied that the resolution had been adopted "with the sole aim of preserving colonial domination over the Chechen people, over the peoples of the Caucasus and their natural riches", announced the mobilisation of men from 15 to 55 and put the National Guard on combat alert(Citation: Постановление Президиума Исполкома ОКЧН от 09.10.1991 1991). On 10 October Moscow instructed vice-president Rutskoi and the RSFSR government "to ensure the necessary conditions for the restoration of legality and law and order in the Chechen-Ingush Republic"(Citation: Постановление ВС РСФСР № 1733-I О положении в Чечено-Ингушской Республике 1991). On 15 October the chairman of the KGB of the RSFSR (predecessor of today's FSB) Ivanenko suspended the work of the KGB of Chechen-Ingushetia "until 27 October 1991" and by his own order appointed an acting chairman for it(Citation: Чечня 1990-1991: хроника и документы 2007). On 19 October Yeltsin addressed the leadership of the congress with an ultimatum: "I demand from the leaders of the Executive Committee of the National Congress of the Chechen People and the groupings supporting them the cessation of unlawful actions and unconditional submission to the law… all measures provided for by the laws of the RSFSR will be taken"(Citation: Обращение Президента РСФСР к лидерам исполкома Общенационального конгресса чеченского народа 1991). On 24 October Moscow resolved that the elections set for 27 October "have no legal basis and their results cannot be recognised as lawful", and entrusted the preparation of different elections to the Provisional Supreme Council and to the RSFSR deputies from the republic(Citation: Постановление ВС РСФСР № 1804-I О проведении выборов в высшие органы государственной власти Чечено-Ингушской Республики 1991). The Chechens voted anyway: on 27 October, according to the electoral commission of the Chechen Republic, 72 % of voters turned out, and 90.1 % voted for Dzhokhar Dudaev(Citation: Чечня 1990-1991: хроника и документы 2007). On 1 November Dzhokhar Dudaev signed a decree: "Guided by the Declaration on the state sovereignty of the republic and by the will of the citizens of the Chechen Republic expressed in direct and universal elections, to proclaim the state sovereignty of the Chechen Republic from 1 November 1991"(Citation: Указ Президента Чеченской Республики О государственном суверенитете Чеченской Республики 1991). On 2 November Moscow answered with a resolution: "To recognise the elections to the supreme body of state power (the Supreme Soviet) and of the President of the republic held in the Chechen-Ingush Republic on 27 October 1991 as unlawful, and the acts adopted by them as not subject to execution"(Citation: Постановление СНД РСФСР № 1847-I О признании незаконными выборов, проведенных 27 октября 1991 года в Чечено-Ингушской Республике 1991). On 7 November Yeltsin, in decree No. 178, named as the reason for the state of emergency an aggravation "caused by the unlawful actions of the executive committee of the National Congress of the Chechen People and its leaders, who seek, by organising mass disorders, with the use of violence, to remove the lawfully acting state bodies from power", and in point 6 banned any elections: "elections of bodies of state power and of local self-government shall not be held during the whole period of the state of emergency"(Citation: Указ Президента РСФСР № 178 О введении чрезвычайного положения в Чечено-Ингушской Республике 1991). None of these bans worked: the elections took place, the president and the parliament of Chechnya were at work, and on 11 November the deputies in Moscow refused to approve the decree itself(Citation: Постановление ВС РСФСР № 1855-I 1991).

The publication of the manifesto "On the Historical Unity of Russians and Ukrainians" (July 2021), constructing a pseudo-historical myth: "Russians and Ukrainians are one people, a single whole," while modern borders are declared the result of the fact that "the Bolsheviks' actions in severing from Russia its historical territories are not considered a criminal act"(Citation: Статья Владимира Путина «Об историческом единстве русских и украинцев» 2021). The same article describes how Lenin personally "persuaded" the leaders of the Donetsk-Kryvyi Rih republic "to act within Soviet Ukraine," and how the Central Committee resolved "to create at the congress 'one government for all of Ukraine'"(Citation: Статья Владимира Путина «Об историческом единстве русских и украинцев» 2021). On the eve of the invasion the thesis was taken to its limit: in his address of February 21, 2022 Putin declared that "modern Ukraine was entirely and wholly created by Russia, or, to be more precise, by Bolshevik, communist Russia," and called the country "Ukraine named after Vladimir Ilyich Lenin" - "He is its author and architect"(Citation: Обращение Президента Российской Федерации 21 февраля 2022 года 2022).

The manufacturing of an appearance of mass pro-Russian mobilization on the peninsula: behind the "self-defense forces," in whose name the operation was conducted, stood Russian troops, as Putin admitted on 17 April 2014: "behind the backs of Crimea's self-defense forces, our servicemen, of course, stood"(Citation: Territorial integrity of Ukraine (A/RES/68/262) 2014). Rally and "volunteer" crowds supplied the picture of a popular impulse whose legal significance the UN rejected(Citation: Прямая линия с Владимиром Путиным 2014).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Russia twice held "elections" on the seized land of Ichkeria to pass off the puppet government as chosen by the people(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

By the autumn of 1995, the Russian army had seized Grozny, the capital of Ichkeria, and the plain in the north of the republic. On 24 October 1995, Russia put Zavgayev at the head of the puppet government in Grozny (see: "Puppet Government")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 1 November 1995, the puppet parliament, assembled from deputies of the Soviet era, introduced the post of head of the republic. On 5 November, the deputies scheduled the election for this post for 16 December, the day of the elections to the Russian parliament. On 12 May 1996, the puppet deputies scheduled the election of a new parliament for 16 June, the day of the Russian presidential election(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

From 16 November 1995 until voting day, Russian servicemen at checkpoints let only people registered there into the stanitsa of Assinovskaya and the village of Sernovodsk in the west of Ichkeria, and did not let candidates and campaigners through (see: "Transport Blockade"). From 11 to 20 December, Shkirko, commander of the occupation troops, forbade entry into Grozny without a special pass. The occupiers at checkpoints did not let accredited journalists into the city(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 12 December 1995, the puppet parliament allowed voting at any polling station with any document(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). The Russian-controlled election commissions of the republic and of Grozny gave numbers of the city's voters that differed twofold: 120 and 250 thousand(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-95-242) 1995). Both commissions refused to show the voter lists(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

The staff of the Assistance Group, the mission of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), left Ichkeria for the voting days in December 1995. There were no international observers at the elections. On 9 June 1996, a week before the new elections, the puppet government declared the Assistance Group undesirable (see: "Expulsion of Foreign Missions")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 6 December 1995, Russian soldiers at checkpoints did not let delegates from the south of Ichkeria into Grozny, and the congress of supporters of Khasbulatov, the former head of the parliament in Moscow, did not take place. On 9 December, Khasbulatov, Zavgayev's main rival, withdrew from the election(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

From 14 to 17 December 1995, the occupiers held the vote for head of the republic. Russian troops did not control the Shali district southeast of Grozny or the mountain districts in the south, and there was no voting there. Hundreds of thousands of citizens of Ichkeria had fled the war out of the republic and could not vote(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 18 December, the Russian-controlled election commission in Grozny announced that more than 60% of the population had voted and about 90% of them had chosen Zavgayev(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 21 April 1996, Ruslan Akhtakhanov, adviser to Dzhokhar Dudayev, the president of Ichkeria, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Moscow about the voting in Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria: "The residents of Samashki said that there had been no elections in their village. <...> a week after the scheduled elections Mr. Zavgayev, sitting in a television studio, thanked the population of the republic that had supported him so vigorously. And he said that the strongest support — 70-80 percent of the population — came from the village of Samashki." According to Ruslan Akhtakhanov, before the elections members of the Russian-controlled village administration went around the village and copied the Chechens' passports and signatures into lists. Ninety-nine percent of those who voted on 17 December, he said, were from these lists(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

On 14 December 1995, the Russian-controlled administration of Gudermes, the second-largest town of the republic, broadcast by radio that the elections would be held anyway and that no one would shoot at people, while the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated the town from the occupiers that day. On 17 December at nine in the evening, as soon as the polling stations closed, Russian pilots began bombing Gudermes (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")(Citation: Caught in the Crossfire: Civilians in Gudermes and Pervomayskoye 1996).

On 10 June 1996, in Nazran, a town in Russian-controlled Ingushetia, the delegations of Russia and Ichkeria recorded in the ceasefire protocol that elections would be held after the withdrawal of Russian troops and the disarmament of the army of Ichkeria(Citation: Протокол заседания Комиссий по переговорам о прекращении огня, военных действий и мерах по урегулированию вооруженного конфликта на территории Чеченской Республики 1996). After the signing of the protocol, Lobov, the representative of the president of Russia in Ichkeria, said on Grozny television: "I see no serious reasons for their [the elections'] cancellation or postponement, as the separatists demand" (that is what the Russians called the government and the Armed Forces of Ichkeria)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 14-16 June, the colonizer held the election of a new parliament of the republic and of the president of Russia, although its army remained in Ichkeria. Irina Dementyeva, correspondent of the Moscow newspaper Izvestia, wrote on 20 June: "As early as the morning of the sixteenth… the head of the republic [Zavgayev] named the percentage of those who had voted — 50. An hour and a half later the chairman of the republican izbirkom [election commission]… told the same journalists: as of 12 noon, 23 percent of the voters had voted". The Russian-controlled election commission in Grozny announced that more than 60% of the voters had voted and that Russian president Yeltsin had received more than half the votes in the Chechen Republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 17 and 18 June, the OSCE stated that the elections had not been free and fair and that the decision to hold them had violated the protocols of 10 June on the withdrawal of troops(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: RFE/RL Newsline, 19 June 1996 1996)(Citation: OSCE dismisses Chechnya election 1996).

On 16 June 1996, Gudermes and the villages of Bachi-Yurt, Alleroy and Tsentoroy in the east of Ichkeria did not vote. The stanitsa of Shelkovskaya in the north of the republic, the town of Shali and the villages of Kurchaloy and Vedeno southeast of Grozny did not vote(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). After 16 June, officials and public figures of the republic confirmed in writing that there had been no elections in Gudermes, or in 64 villages, stanitsas and settlements of six districts of Ichkeria, including places where, according to official data, Russian troops were stationed. Heads of administrations subordinate to Russia signed some of these papers and certified them with seals bearing the coat of arms of Russia, and one paper was signed by the chairman and secretary of the election commission of the Gudermes district(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 3 July, in the second round of the election, there was no voting in Shali, Novye Atagi, Gekhi and Gekhi-Chu south of Grozny. The election commission closed the polling station in Urus-Martan, a town southwest of Grozny, at four in the afternoon, announcing that 98% of the voters there had already voted. According to the commissions' protocols, in the second round 74% of the voters in the Chechen Republic voted and 73% of them chose Yeltsin, and the Central Election Commission of Russia reported that it had received no information about violations(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

Human rights defenders of Memorial write that both times the elections were not genuine and the voters could not freely express their will(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996). On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic. On 27 January 1997, the citizens of Ichkeria elected the president and parliament of the republic. Aslan Maskhadov became president(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Russia signed agreements with Ichkeria and its villages under which the defenders handed over their weapons while Russian troops stayed in the republic, and violated these agreements.

Russian delegations wrote into the agreements that Russian units would leave the republic as the Armed Forces of Ichkeria handed over their weapons(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). While the talks were going on, Russian president Yeltsin kept troops in the republic on a permanent basis by decree(Citation: Указ Президента Российской Федерации от 3 июля 1995 г. № 663 «О дислокации органов военного управления, соединений, воинских частей, учреждений и организаций Вооруженных Сил Российской Федерации на территории Чеченской Республики» 1995)(Citation: Указ Президента Российской Федерации от 25 июня 1996 г. № 985 о выводе сил и средств, входящих в состав Временных объединенных сил, с территории Чеченской Республики 1996).

On 14 June 1995, fighters of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria took hostages in Budyonnovsk, a Russian-controlled town northwest of the republic, and demanded an end to the war. On 19 June, Russia began talks with Ichkeria in Grozny(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 20 and 21 June, the delegations signed protocols under which Russian troops would leave the republic district by district(Citation: Protocol of the Meeting of Delegations on the Issue of Peaceful Resolution of the Crisis in the Chechen Republic with OSCE Support 1995)(Citation: Conflicting parties agree to cease hostilities during talks on Chechnya (press release, 22 June 1995) 1995). On 3 July, Russian president Yeltsin signed decree No. 663: "To permit the stationing [placing] on a permanent basis on the territory of the Chechen Republic… of military units… of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation"(Citation: Указ Президента Российской Федерации от 3 июля 1995 г. № 663 «О дислокации органов военного управления, соединений, воинских частей, учреждений и организаций Вооруженных Сил Российской Федерации на территории Чеченской Республики» 1995). On 27 July, the head of the Russian delegation, Minister for Nationalities Mikhailov, stated at the talks in Grozny that Russia "no longer links the signing of the agreement on military questions to a political agreement and the status of Chechnya"(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 30 July, the delegations signed an agreement on the cessation of hostilities. In it, the army of Ichkeria was called "illegal armed formations", and it was written that first the army would hand over its weapons, then the Chechens who guarded their villages with arms, then everyone else(Citation: Чечня (Нохчичьо) - взгляд изнутри 1995)(Citation: Agreement on the peaceful regulation of the situation in the Chechen Republic (on a set of military issues) 1995). Under the agreement, Russian troops would leave "simultaneously with disarmament", while a brigade of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) and a brigade of the Russian army would stay in the republic. The Russian delegation added a note to the text that the legislation of Russia does not recognize Ichkeria (see: "Deprivation of Agency")(Citation: Чечня (Нохчичьо) - взгляд изнутри 1995)(Citation: Agreement on the peaceful regulation of the situation in the Chechen Republic (on a set of military issues) 1995).

After the agreement, fighters of the army of Ichkeria began handing over their weapons and returned to their villages, while the Russian units did not leave the republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). On 9 October 1995, ten weeks after the agreement, Russia blamed supporters of Dzhokhar Dudayev, the president of Ichkeria, for an attempt on the life of Romanov, the commander of the occupation troops, suspended the talks and ordered the troops to resume the offensive (see: "Aggressor Claiming Victim Status")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In the spring of 1996, the command of the occupation troops and the puppet government in Grozny signed "Protocols on Peace and Accord" with the villages of Ichkeria, under which a village undertook not to let fighters of the army of Ichkeria in, and Russia promised to spare it from fighting(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Supporting the Doves against the Hawks: Experiences of the OSCE Assistance Group to Chechnya 1998). By 28 March 1996, according to the French news agency AFP, more than 120 villages had signed such protocols(Citation: RFE/RL Newsline, 28 March 1996 1996). Before the signing, Russian troops surrounded the village and shelled it (see: "Collective Punishment")(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). Russian pilots bombed villages that had signed the protocols (see: "False Guarantees of Safety")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 27 May 1996, Chernomyrdin, the chairman of the Russian government, and Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, the acting president of Ichkeria, signed a ceasefire agreement in Moscow(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 10 June, in Nazran, a town in Russian-controlled Ingushetia, the delegations of Russia and Ichkeria supplemented it with a protocol in which Russia undertook to withdraw its troops from the republic by the end of August 1996(Citation: Протокол заседания Комиссий по переговорам о прекращении огня, военных действий и мерах по урегулированию вооруженного конфликта на территории Чеченской Республики 1996). On 25 June, Russian president Yeltsin, by decree No. 985, ordered that only the units of four military districts be withdrawn by 1 September, while the formations stationed in the republic permanently were to be provided with facilities(Citation: Указ Президента Российской Федерации от 25 июня 1996 г. № 985 о выводе сил и средств, входящих в состав Временных объединенных сил, с территории Чеченской Республики 1996). On 9 July, six days after Yeltsin won the Russian presidential election, the occupiers began a new offensive (see: "Sham Ceasefire")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 22 August, when the Armed Forces of Ichkeria had surrounded the occupiers in Grozny, General Lebed, the secretary of the Russian Security Council, and Aslan Maskhadov, the chief of the Main Staff of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria, signed a ceasefire agreement in Novye Atagi, a village south of Grozny. In it, Russia undertook to withdraw its troops from Grozny by 26 August and from the whole republic by the end of August, but began leaving the city on 28 August(Citation: «За три года после Хасавюрта мы проиграли мир» 2023)(Citation: Agreement «On Urgent Measures to Stop Fire and Combat Operations in the City of Grozny and on the Territory of Chechnya» 1996)(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999).

The human rights defenders of "Memorial" write that Russia did not take the talks with Ichkeria seriously(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 31 August 1996, after the Armed Forces of Ichkeria had liberated Grozny from the occupiers(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999), General Lebed and Aslan Maskhadov signed the peace agreements in Khasavyurt, a town in Russian-controlled Dagestan. In them, Russia and Ichkeria wrote down the renunciation of force and the threat of force in resolving disputed questions. The sides agreed to conclude an agreement on the foundations of their relations by 31 December 2001(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996). The last Russian troops left the republic on 31 December 1996, four months after the deadline in the agreement of Novye Atagi(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Three years after the agreements in Khasavyurt, Russia attacked Ichkeria again. On 21 September 1999, Russian pilots began bombing Grozny, and on 29 September the Russian army invaded the republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

The instigation of armed clashes in Odesa on May 2, 2014: the UN records the violence committed "in Odesa on 2 May 2014 during clashes between supporters of unity and supporters of the federalization of Ukraine, as a result of which 48 people died, mostly supporters of the country's federalization," and notes that "no one has yet been held to account"(Citation: Доклад Верховного комиссара ООН по правам человека о положении в области прав человека в Украине (A/HRC/27/75) 2014). The culmination was the fire in the Trade Union Building where activists had taken refuge: the UN monitoring mission listed among the key uninvestigated questions "what caused the fire in the Trade Union building" and "who are the perpetrators of the killings"(Citation: Report on the human rights situation in Ukraine, 15 June 2014 2014).

An attempted armed seizure of power in the spring of 2014 by storming regional administrations: the UN recorded that already "in mid-April 2014" "groups of armed men unlawfully carried out a well-organized and coordinated seizure of public buildings and police and security service offices in towns and villages of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions," and "in order to retain control of the seized areas these groups set up barricades and checkpoints"(Citation: Доклад Верховного комиссара ООН по правам человека о положении в области прав человека в Украине (A/HRC/27/75) 2014). In Kharkiv the coup was quickly suppressed.

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Russian special services and the army gave the puppet opposition money, weapons, instructors, tank crewmen and pilots in order to overthrow Dzhokhar Dudayev, the elected president of the Chechen Republic.

In the summer of 1994, Russia's Ministry for Nationalities Affairs and the FSK (a predecessor of today's FSB) helped the puppet opposition recruit armed fighters in Znamenskoye, a village in the northwest of Ichkeria, and in Urus-Martan, a town southwest of Grozny(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Russia allocated more than 150 billion rubles to the Provisional Council, the leadership of the puppet opposition, which it had confirmed at a congress on 3 June. In an analytical memorandum, the FSK named the head of the Provisional Council the most suitable candidate for support(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 3 September 1994, the Russian government, in an address to the Chechen people, proposed that Dzhokhar Dudayev resign(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 5 September 1994, the General Staff of the Russian army ordered that 10 armored personnel carriers and 6 combat helicopters with crews be handed over to the Provisional Council(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). From these helicopters, Russian pilots fired rockets at residential houses in Ichkeria (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks"). In November, the Russian army handed tanks over to the council(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Оппозиция копит силы для последнего штурма 1994).

In September and October 1994, Russian officers trained more than a hundred fighters of the Provisional Council to drive T-62 tanks and fire army mortars at the "Prudboy" training ground near Volgograd, a city in the south of Russia(Citation: Чеченцы тренируются в Волгограде 1994)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In October 1994, Savostyanov, the head of the Moscow directorate of the FSK, ordered that Russian soldiers and officers who knew how to maintain armored vehicles and fight in them be found for the Provisional Council. The military counterintelligence of the FSK selected the candidates(Citation: «Парад планет». Ноябрьский штурм Грозного: подготовка и осуществление 2004). From 3 to 9 November, FSK officers travelled around military units near Moscow and signed contracts with tank crewmen(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: «Парад планет». Ноябрьский штурм Грозного: подготовка и осуществление 2004).

In November 1994, Kolesnikov, the Chief of the General Staff of the Russian army, authorized sending the recruits to the Caucasus. Kotenkov, Russia's deputy minister for nationalities affairs, directed the dispatch, and by 16 November the recruits had been brought to Mozdok, a town in Russian-controlled North Ossetia near the border of the Chechen Republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Russia denied that it was sending its servicemen to fight for the Provisional Council (see: "Lies about Its Own Actions").

In the autumn of 1994, FSK officers fought on the side of the puppet opposition(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

From September 1994 until the assault on Grozny on 26 November, fighters of the Provisional Council and Russian crews attacked Ichkeria. On 2 September, fighters of the council and a column of twelve tanks with Russian crews attacked Grozny. The Armed Forces of Ichkeria stopped them at the settlement of Dolinsky, northwest of Grozny, knocked out a tank and took eight men prisoner, among them, according to initial reports, Russian servicemen(Citation: Оппозиция перешла в наступление 1994)(Citation: Программа «Новости» от 2 сентября 1994 года: бой у посёлка Долинское 1994)(Citation: Хроника первой российской войны в Чечне 2026)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Russia Confronts Chechnya: Roots of a Separatist Conflict 1998)(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-94-172) 1994). On 30 September, Russian pilots in four helicopters of the Provisional Council fired rockets at the "Severny" airport in Grozny and destroyed five civilian aircraft and two aircraft of the army of Ichkeria, and fighters of the puppet opposition blocked the entrances to the city(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Оппозиция предложила Дудаеву сдаться 1994)(Citation: Chechen capital on war alert after raid 1994). Dzhokhar Dudayev rejected the Provisional Council's ultimatum to surrender within six hours, and the council's fighters dispersed without attacking Grozny(Citation: Оппозиция предложила Дудаеву сдаться 1994)(Citation: Наступление было непродолжительным 1994). On 15 October, fighters of the Provisional Council stormed Grozny from the south and from the north, and the Armed Forces of Ichkeria repelled the assault. The defenders took several dozen attackers prisoner, among them, according to various reports, 12 to 15 Russian officers(Citation: Наступление было непродолжительным 1994), and on 16 October the council's fighters retreated to their bases in Znamenskoye and in Gekhi, a village southwest of Grozny(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 17 November 1994, nine days before the assault on Grozny, a group of Russian officers headed by Kolesnikov, the Chief of the General Staff, flew from Moscow to Mozdok(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Valery Yakov, special correspondent of the Moscow newspaper Izvestia, wrote about the preparation of the assault in November 1996: "There, in Mozdok, at the 'Arsenal' base, the contract soldiers [recruited Russian servicemen]… trained the Chechen crews [of the Provisional Council]… In all, the contract soldiers received 40 brand-new tanks, 16 of which had 'Russian' crews"(Citation: Победившая нас война. Часть 2 2025)(Citation: «Парад планет». Ноябрьский штурм Грозного: подготовка и осуществление 2004). On 26 November, fighters of the Provisional Council and Russian tank crewmen under the command of Zhukov, the deputy commander of a Russian army corps from Volgograd, stormed Grozny(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: «Парад планет». Ноябрьский штурм Грозного: подготовка и осуществление 2004). Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, the vice president of the Chechen Republic, wrote in his memoirs that in the morning he saw the start of the assault from the window of his office in the presidential palace: "on the northeastern outskirts of the city, from the direction of Tolstoy-Yurt [a village north of Grozny where the fighters of the Provisional Council were stationed], tank and artillery fire began to thunder"(Citation: Чечения - битва за свободу 1996). The tanks reached the center of Grozny, where fighters of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria shot them up with grenade launchers(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). The defenders routed the attackers and, according to the government of the Chechen Republic, took 68 Russian servicemen prisoner(Citation: Chechnya - Dudayev's Men Take Opposition Soldiers 1994). Among the prisoners were soldiers and officers of the Russian Kantemirovskaya Tank Division from near Moscow(Citation: Преданные. Как начиналась «первая чеченская» 2004).

Human rights defenders of Memorial write that without Russia's military help the puppet opposition could not have overthrown Dzhokhar Dudayev(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

After the defeat of 26 November, the Provisional Council withdrew its fighters to its bases(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Fifteen days later, on 11 December 1994, the Russian army openly invaded the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria (see: "Military Intervention")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

The instigation of the threat of splitting the country in response to the protests: at the congress in Sievierodonetsk on November 28, 2004, Regions faction leader R. Bohatyriova gave a direct promise of a separatist referendum - "we will not go to it with you, we will hold a referendum on the creation of a South-Eastern state (ovation, applause)"(Citation: Стенограмма Северодонецкого съезда 2004). The presence of Russian officials lent this Moscow's sanction: the mayor of Moscow Yu. Luzhkov reminded the hall from the rostrum that "our President of Russia Vladimir Vladimirovich Putin was the first to congratulate Viktor Fedorovych Yanukovych on his victory"(Citation: Стенограмма Северодонецкого съезда 2004).

From April 2022 the Russian occupation administrations marked the seized territories with imperial signs - in stone and on paper. In Kherson oblast more than 110 Lenin monuments had been dismantled before the invasion, with practically none left; after the occupation the invaders put up ten new ones: the first in Henichesk in April 2022 - the first Lenin monument on Ukrainian territory since 2014 - and at the end of that same month a monument was returned to its pedestal by the city council in Nova Kakhovka(Citation: Ідеологія в бронзі: навіщо Росія «засіває» окуповану Херсонщину своїми монументами 2026). In Mariupol on 5 May 2022 a monument to a woman with a red flag was unveiled, and the ceremony was published in his Telegram channel by Andrei Turchak, secretary of the general council of "United Russia"; the Square of the Warrior-Liberators, named in honor of those who freed the city from the Nazis, was given back its Soviet name of "Lenin Komsomol Square" by the occupiers(Citation: У Маріуполі окупанти встановили пам'ятник «бабці з червоною ганчіркою» 2022). In parallel the occupation administration papered the territory with banners: in Kherson and Nova Kakhovka hung Russian-language billboards reading "Russia is here forever!," "Kherson - forever with Russia," "Kherson is a Russian city," and for them they bought, for twenty cents on a stock-photo site, a picture by the Ukrainian photographer Anna Pasichnyk - her son Yaroslav with a friend in vyshyvankas in a rapeseed field near Kyiv - painting a Russian flag in behind the children's backs(Citation: Украинка обнаружила свою фотографию с детьми в вышиванках на билборде в поддержку аннексии Херсона 2022). In Balakliia in Kharkiv oblast the occupiers pasted over a city banner: first they hung "Ukraine and Russia are 'one'" on top of it, then a poster with a tricolor reading "We are one people with Russia!". On 10 September 2022 Ukrainian soldiers tore the tricolor down - and beneath it emerged the lines of Shevchenko that had stood there through the entire occupation: "Fight - and you shall prevail! God is helping you! Truth is with you, glory is with you, and holy freedom!"(Citation: «Борітеся - поборете»: історія плаката з рядками Шевченка, який росіяни заклеїли під час окупації Балаклії 2023). The signs held only until de-occupation: on 11 November 2022, a "Russia is here forever" poster in liberated Bilozerka in the Kherson region was torn down by local residents - the video was published by the Telegram channel "Nikolaevsky Vanek"(Citation: В освобожденной Белозерке Херсонской области срывают плакаты «Россия здесь навсегда» 2022).

Engagement in combat operations of Russian neo-Nazi groups (such as the "Rusich" sabotage and reconnaissance group under the command of A. Milchakov), whose ringleaders openly called for unmotivated sadistic violence against civilians ("Slaughter the homeless, the puppies, and the children!")(Citation: Рашизм: Звір з безодні 2023).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. Russian servicemen looted museums and the homes of Chechens in Grozny, and specialists of the Russian ministry of culture took the most valuable of the surviving paintings from the ruins to Moscow.

From 1 to 4 January 1995, the occupiers shelled the building that housed the Chechen National Museum and the Museum of Fine Arts, and burned both museums almost completely (see: "Destruction of Historical Memory")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

Until the spring of 1995, Russian servicemen let none of the Chechens into the ruins of the museums and plundered what had survived. The occupiers took exhibits as trophies, according to rank and position(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

Russian soldiers loaded exhibits of the National Museum onto armored personnel carriers(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). Commanders of the occupation troops, with the help of soldiers, took more than one truckload of ancient books from the museum's manuscript department toward Mozdok, a town in North Ossetia, and Ingushetia, both under Russian control(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

In February 1995, officers of the FSK (a predecessor of today's FSB) packed paintings and other works of art from the ruins into a 20-ton railway container(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). At the end of March, the Russian ministry for emergency situations brought five specialists from the Russian ministry of culture and Moscow museums to Grozny. The group catalogued the works from the container(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996). Khotin, deputy director of the ministry of culture's museum center and one of the five, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Moscow in February 1996: "We tried to carry out of the ruins everything that could be carried out. At the same time, the state of preservation of the works was practically zero. … We conserved, made presentable and took away about 60 works of fine art"(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996). Isa Adayev, director of the National Museum, told this tribunal in Prague in May 1996: "The art experts who came from Moscow helped to steal things, picking out what they wanted by degree of significance. These experts left behind what they called 'useless junk'"(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

In 1995, during the capture of Grozny, Russian soldiers twice looted the home library of the Chechen journalist Aslan Dukaev in the city, and his sister saved only a few books(Citation: Chechnya's Literary Pyre 2004). In 1995, after the capture of Grozny, servicemen of unit 3111 of the Dzerzhinsky Division of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) searched the house of a Chechen on the outskirts of the city and took away a collection of ancient manuscripts, books and icons that Mikhail Patalov, a former deputy director of the Grozny Philharmonic, kept there. His complaint passed through eleven levels of the prosecutor's office, the prosecutors opened a case, but it went nowhere(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In July 1995, the delegation of Ichkeria at the talks with Russia in Grozny demanded the return of the National Museum's exhibits. The Russian delegation verbally promised to look into it(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). Seven months later, in February 1996, the removed paintings lay in the storerooms of the Russian ministry of culture awaiting restoration(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996). In July 2002, 43 works from the Grozny Museum of Fine Arts hung in Moscow at an exhibition of the Tretyakov Gallery(Citation: Grozny's war-torn treasures 2002).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers destroyed the towns and villages of Ichkeria together with their housing, hospitals and schools(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

Russian pilots and artillerymen destroyed residential neighborhoods with bombing and shelling (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). In captured villages and towns, Russian soldiers and police officers looted houses (see: "Pillage") and then set them on fire with gasoline, hay or flamethrowers(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995)(Citation: Russia: Partisan War in Chechnya on the Eve of the World War II Commemoration 1995)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). After the war of 1994-1996, 60,000 families of Grozny were left without housing(Citation: Кавказский ренессанс 2002).

The occupiers destroyed substations, tore down power lines and blew up gas pipelines(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

In December 1994, Russian aviation bombed Grozny, the capital of Ichkeria. On 9 January 1995, Irina from the Third Microdistrict on the outskirts of Grozny told Human Rights Watch in Russian-controlled Ingushetia: "Our region was the first to suffer… either December 17th or 18th, three nine-story apartment buildings of the institute 'Promavtomatika' were bombed out. People all become homeless"(Citation: Russia. War in Chechnya. New Report From the Field 1995). On the night of 20 December, Russian pilots dropped two bombs on a block of one-story houses at the intersection of Moskovskaya Street and Noya Buachidze Street and completely or partially destroyed 18 houses(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Russian aviation bombed a substation, and Grozny was left without electricity(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996). On 31 December 1994, the occupiers began the assault on the city. After 20 February 1995, Russian special forces set fire to and blew up houses in Grozny and destroyed pipes and power lines(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). More than two months after the start of the assault, by 6 March 1995, Russian troops had captured Grozny. On 1 May 1995, the Russian journalist Yevgenia Albats, who had been in the city in January, said at a hearing of a commission of the US Congress: "There is no such city any more. There isn't a single house in Grozny that hasn't been destroyed one way or another by the war"(Citation: Hearing on Chechnya (CSCE 104-1-6) 1995).

On 3 February 1995, soldiers of the Russian OMON (police special forces) and of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) searched houses in Petropavlovskaya, a stanitsa northeast of Grozny, and burned 14 houses. In all, the occupiers destroyed 86 houses in the stanitsa(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). In February 1995, Russian pilots bombed two schools, a sports school, a hospital and a kindergarten in Argun, a town east of Grozny(Citation: Russia: Three Months of War in Chechnya 1995). At the end of March 1995, Russian troops captured Gudermes, the second-largest city of Ichkeria, without a fight, and on 29 and 30 March soldiers burned houses in it with flamethrowers; on Parkhomenko Street two houses were left intact(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Russia: Partisan War in Chechnya on the Eve of the World War II Commemoration 1995). In April 1995, Russian troops shelled for a month Alleroy, a village in the east of Ichkeria with 4,500-5,000 inhabitants. The occupiers completely destroyed a fifth of the houses of Alleroy with rockets(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 7 April 1995, the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs and the OMON stormed Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria. Chechens in Samashki told observers of the Russian human rights organization "Memorial" that the soldiers and OMON men burned houses on 8 April, when they were searching the village. Russian servicemen spent the night in the school on Kooperativnaya Street, and in the morning set it on fire, and the school burned out from the inside(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). On 10 April, a Chechen woman named Karnukayeva from Rabochaya Street told the Observer Mission of Russian human rights organizations: "The houses are burned. I have nowhere to go now. I am left on the street hungry and cold with 4 children"(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). Viktor Lozinsky of "Memorial" examined the burned houses of Samashki from 18 April to 1 May 1995. In February 1996, he told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation: "The village was being burned out systematically. The houses were set on fire like this: a window was broken with a rifle butt, and wiping cloth [rags] soaked in some diesel fuel was simply put on the windowsill and set alight"(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996). The Observer Mission published a list drawn up by the administration of Samashki of 198 yards where the occupiers had completely destroyed at least one house, and in 155 of them almost all the houses had burned down(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). The human rights defenders of "Memorial" write that the Russian military and officers of the Ministry of Internal Affairs burned most of the houses in the village deliberately(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

From 30 September 1995 to March 1996, Russian Internal Troops and police kept Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria, encircled, tore down the power lines near the village and blew up the gas pipeline several times (see: "Transport Blockade")(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). In December 1995, after the Armed Forces of Ichkeria had liberated Gudermes, Russian troops shelled and bombed the city. According to refugees and journalists' estimates, the occupiers destroyed or damaged about 40 percent of the buildings of Gudermes(Citation: Caught in the Crossfire: Civilians in Gudermes and Pervomayskoye 1996).

From 3 to 9 March 1996, Russian troops stormed Sernovodsk, burned or destroyed 30 percent of the houses of the village, and Russian soldiers set fire to the apartments of refugees on the northern outskirts of the village with hand-held flamethrowers(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). On 15 March 1996, 11 months after the first assault, Russian troops stormed Samashki again and razed to the ground the House of Culture and the school, which the Chechens had rebuilt. Journalists who came after the assault saw only three surviving houses in the whole village(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). On 3 and 4 April 1996, Russian pilots bombed Shalazhi, a village in the southwest of Ichkeria, and destroyed dozens of houses, the whole upper part of the village(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). On 6 April 1996, Russian troops captured Zhani-Vedeno, a mountain village of 38 yards in the southeast of Ichkeria, from which the Chechens had fled the shelling, and for a month let no one near it. When the Russian servicemen left, one intact house remained in the village, and in place of most of the houses an observer of "Memorial" found ashes with no traces of shells or bombs(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). From 9 to 11 July 1996, Russian artillery shelled and aviation bombed Gekhi, a village southwest of Grozny. A correspondent of the Moscow newspaper Izvestia wrote that the occupiers had destroyed more than a third of the village(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-139) 1996). On the night of 11 July, Russian artillerymen shelled Makhkety, a mountain village in the southeast of Ichkeria, with the Grad and Uragan multiple rocket launchers, which cannot fire with precision, and destroyed 150 houses(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-139) 1996). From 6 to 22 August 1996, Russian troops shelled Grozny with heavy artillery and bombed it, and on 21 August Russian pilots dropped incendiary bombs on the blocks of five-story buildings on Saikhanov and Ulyanov Streets, from which the buildings burned out from the inside(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). The bulletin of the International Committee of the Red Cross of 2 September 1996 says that after the August strikes all 80,000 people in Grozny were left without electricity and medical care: all the hospitals of the city were destroyed or badly damaged(Citation: Russian Federation/Northen Caucasus: Drinking water scarce in Grozny 1996).

On 26 July 1995, the UN Human Rights Committee, in its comments on Russia, expressed regret that the Russian armed forces had destroyed schools, hospitals and other civilian buildings(Citation: Comments of the Human Rights Committee: Russian Federation (CCPR/C/79/Add.54) 1995).

In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996). On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers surrounded the villages of Ichkeria with a ring of checkpoints and did not let people or vehicles through.

On 9 December 1994, two days before the open invasion, Chernomyrdin, the chairman of the Russian government, by resolution No. 1360 ordered the Ministry of Internal Affairs to close the borders of the Chechen Republic and the Ministry of Defense to ban flights over it for the time being(Citation: Постановление Правительства Российской Федерации № 1360 Об обеспечении государственной безопасности и территориальной целостности Российской Федерации, законности, прав и свобод граждан, разоружения незаконных вооруженных формирований на территории Чеченской Республики 1994). On 1 February 1995, the occupiers blocked the border of Ichkeria with Russian-controlled Ingushetia with checkpoints(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

From the end of February 1995, units of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs set up checkpoints on the roads between villages in the west of Ichkeria(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). By the end of March 1996, there were checkpoints on these roads almost every kilometer(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

Russian servicemen at the checkpoints let into villages and towns only those who were registered as residents there(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-95-241) 1995). At the posts, Russian soldiers unlawfully detained Chechen men who were leaving the surrounded villages and took them to the filtration camps in Grozny and in Mozdok, Pyatigorsk and Stavropol, Russian-controlled cities northwest of Ichkeria (see: "Filtration Camp System")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In February 1995, Russian servicemen at the checkpoints near Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, fired at dusk on any vehicles, including ambulances(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). In the second half of February, the soldiers at checkpoint No. 13 near the village stopped letting trucks in(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). From 13 March 1995, Russian servicemen blocked all the roads into Samashki and for 25 days, until the assault on 7 April, kept the village under blockade(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). On 7 April, the day of the assault on Samashki, the occupiers stopped 12 vehicles with Chechens who were leaving the village at a checkpoint of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and before the shelling began they let about a hundred people through. Some of the men among them Russian servicemen took by helicopter to the filtration camp in Mozdok, while those who had not managed to leave stayed in the village under shelling(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). On 8 April, 800-1,000 people gathered at the Russian checkpoint at the crossroads of the roads from Samashki and Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria near the border with Ingushetia. On the orders of Kulikov, the commander of the occupation troops, the commanders of the post did not let observers or Chechens from the village into Samashki. On 11 April, the Russian guards of checkpoint No. 13 did not let into Samashki Chechen women who were marching there against the war(Citation: Трагедия села Самашки. Чечня. Апрель 1995. Дневник правозащитника 1995).

On 30 September 1995, the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) and Russian police special forces surrounded Sernovodsk. The occupiers demanded that the Chechens of the village disarm the fighters of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria and open the road to Russian military vehicles (see: "Collective Punishment")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). According to "Memorial", there were more than 10,000 people in the village, according to the UN 20,000, and another more than 3,000 refugees lived in the buildings of the resort on the outskirts(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: The situation of human rights in the Republic of Chechnya of the Russian Federation. Report of the Secretary-General (E/CN.4/1996/13) 1996). On 26 October, Russian troops blocked the last road into Sernovodsk and stopped letting any vehicles into the village, including those with food (see: "Medical and Humanitarian Blockade")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Patricia Krokol, a representative of a British Christian community of opponents of the war, got into the village that day across a field, and on 20 April 1996 in Moscow she told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation: "At 11 in the morning we got into Sernovodsk, and 40 minutes later they blocked that road too, putting up 14 tanks"(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). In November, Russian servicemen began letting a bus with people and an ambulance into the village four times a day(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: CHECHEN REPUBLIC - RUSSIAN FEDERATION: Civilians in Sernovodsk (EXTRA 34/96, EUR 46/13/96) 1996)(Citation: Russian Federation: Human rights violations in the Chechen Republic (EUR 46/20/96) 1996).

Russian troops surrounded Sernovodsk for more than five months, until the assault on 3 March 1996. On 4 March, the occupiers opened the way out of the village, but Russian soldiers and officers of the Ministry of Internal Affairs at the posts did not let people leave in their own cars. On that day, about 10,000 people left Sernovodsk. On 5 March, the occupiers again closed the entry and exit, and about 7,000 Chechen civilians remained in the village (see: "Sham Corridor"). With shelling, Russian troops killed and wounded hundreds of them (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks"). On 9 March, after the capture of Sernovodsk, Russian servicemen opened the entry into the village and the exit from it, and only then did the Chechens take out the wounded(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: CHECHEN REPUBLIC - RUSSIAN FEDERATION: Civilians in Sernovodsk (EXTRA 34/96, EUR 46/13/96) 1996)(Citation: Russian Federation: Human rights violations in the Chechen Republic (EUR 46/20/96) 1996).

On 10-11 December 1995, the Russian army surrounded Gudermes, the second-largest city of Ichkeria, east of Grozny, and let no one out of it. On 14 December, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated the city, and on 19-20 December Russian troops captured it (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")(Citation: Caught in the Crossfire: Civilians in Gudermes and Pervomayskoye 1996). From 11 to 20 December 1995, before the "elections" that Russia had scheduled in Ichkeria, Shkirko, the commander of the occupation troops, banned vehicles without passes from entering Grozny (see: "Sham Expression of Popular Will")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 14 March 1996, units of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs and of the Russian 58th Army surrounded Samashki and let no one through the checkpoint on the southern road to the village of Novy Sharoy(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). On 19 March, the occupiers let the Chechens out of the encirclement(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). In early April 1996, Russian pilots bombed every 15-20 minutes during the day the only road from Shali, a town southeast of Grozny, to Vedeno, a district center in the mountains in the southeast of Ichkeria (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks"). Chechens from Vedeno and the neighboring village of Dyshne-Vedeno left along this road for the plain at night(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). In the spring of 1996, Russian servicemen at the checkpoint near Shalazhi, a village southwest of Grozny, did not let Madina Magomadova from Grozny through to her parents, because she was registered as a resident of the city(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).

The human rights defenders of "Memorial" write that throughout the war Russian troops surrounded the villages and towns of Ichkeria again and again, restricted or completely closed entry and exit, and soldiers at checkpoints often blocked traffic on the roads(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 10 June 1996, Russia and Ichkeria signed a protocol to the ceasefire agreement of 27 May. The Russian delegation undertook to remove the checkpoints at the exits from villages and towns by 7 July(Citation: Протокол заседания Комиссий по переговорам о прекращении огня, военных действий и мерах по урегулированию вооруженного конфликта на территории Чеченской Республики 1996). On 7 July, the command of the occupation troops refused to remove all the posts, citing the fact that the situation had not normalized (see: "Sham Ceasefire")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 8 September 1996, Russian units began leaving their checkpoints and Ichkeria(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999)(Citation: Хроника високосного года: октябрь 1996 1996).

In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996). On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers shielded themselves with peaceful Chechens from the fire of the Armed Forces of Ichkeria.

Russian soldiers led Chechens out of the basements where they were hiding from shelling, took men from their homes and seized doctors and patients in a hospital. The occupiers put them on armored vehicles or placed them in front of themselves so that the soldiers of the army of Ichkeria would not shoot(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Russia/Chechnya: A Legacy of Abuse 1997). Russian servicemen threatened to burn or shoot the captured Chechens if the defenders fired or did not hand over captives(Citation: За спинами мирных жителей. Захват заложников и использование гражданского населения в качестве «живого щита» федеральными войсками России в ходе вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1996). Russian soldiers released some Chechens from the human shield after a few hours and took others to their bases. There the occupiers put them in pits and beat them (see: "Torture and Abuse")(Citation: За спинами мирных жителей. Захват заложников и использование гражданского населения в качестве «живого щита» федеральными войсками России в ходе вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1996).

On 6-8 March 1996, when the army of Ichkeria encircled Russian checkpoint No. 6 in Grozny, an officer of the Russian commandant's office of the city advised the soldiers at the checkpoint over the radio to seize a couple of Chechen families and shield themselves with them. The soldiers at the post did not do so(Citation: Чечня - радиоперехват Грозный 96 1996)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Взгляд 06.09.1996 1996).

From 15 March 1996, the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) and the Russian 58th Army stormed Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria (see: "Military Intervention")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 17 March, Russian soldiers drove Chechens out of the basement of a house on Rabochaya Street, where they were hiding from shelling. A major, the commander of a Russian unit, forced three women and the three Kireyev boys - aged five, eleven and twelve - to climb onto an armored vehicle(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: За спинами мирных жителей. Захват заложников и использование гражданского населения в качестве «живого щита» федеральными войсками России в ходе вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1996). Leila Gaerbekova, one of the three women on the vehicle, told the human rights defender Andrei Mironov on 4 May 1996: "At gunpoint they put us on a tank [an armored vehicle] on Rabochaya Street. Three children, their mother Koka, me and my sister Anya Gaerbekova. <...> They placed us in front of the tank and said: 'If a single bullet comes from over there, we will burn you'. And there were no bullets from over there, nothing". The soldiers placed almost everyone who had been hiding in the basement in front of the vehicle and led them at gunpoint for about 300 meters, to the canal in the middle of the village. Between 12 and 2 p.m., the major told the Chechens to disperse. Khizir Khachukayev, the commander of the unit of the army of Ichkeria in Samashki, told the human rights defenders of "Memorial" that his soldiers did not fire at the armored vehicles with people on them and were forced to retreat, and put up their main resistance in the center of the village once the occupiers had let the people out of the human shield(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: За спинами мирных жителей. Захват заложников и использование гражданского населения в качестве «живого щита» федеральными войсками России в ходе вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1996).

On 15 March 1996, in Samashki, Russian soldiers led two elderly Chechens, the owner of a house on Vygonnaya Street and his neighbor, out of the house, put them on top of an armored vehicle and drove them around under bullets for six or seven hours. After nine in the evening, the occupiers' commander let both of them go(Citation: За спинами мирных жителей. Захват заложников и использование гражданского населения в качестве «живого щита» федеральными войсками России в ходе вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1996).

On 10 August 1996, when the Armed Forces of Ichkeria were liberating Grozny, soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs searched City Hospital No. 9 in Grozny. For two days, the occupiers held about 500 patients, their relatives, doctors and nurses hostage (see: "Hostage-Taking"). Movsar Tembulatov, the deputy chief physician, told the human rights defenders of "Memorial" and Human Rights Watch in the hospital on 13 October 1996 how Russian soldiers went down into the basement: "they put me or one of the other doctors in front as some kind of cover, with a submachine gunner behind"(Citation: За спинами мирных жителей. Захват заложников и использование гражданского населения в качестве «живого щита» федеральными войсками России в ходе вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1996)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 12 August 1996, soldiers of the army of Ichkeria repelled an attack by Russian troops trying to break through to the occupiers encircled in the hospital. The commander of the Russian servicemen in the hospital agreed to lead his soldiers out in exchange for captives and demanded 100 doctors, nurses, walking patients and their relatives as a human shield for himself. Khadis Malsagov, one of the hostages, told the human rights defenders of "Memorial" on 24 August 1996: "As soon as everyone had moved away from the hospital, they [the Russian soldiers] line the women up and say they will shoot them if the captives are not handed over to them immediately". The soldiers of Khizir Khachukayev handed over all the captives. At the gates of their base, the occupiers released the people from the human shield. When the people were returning to the hospital, Russian troops fired several dozen mortar shells at it, killed the nurse Toita Kutukhanova and wounded two nurses, two doctors and a woman patient (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks"). On the evening of 12 August and the morning of 13 August, the patients and medics left the hospital for the building of the International Committee of the Red Cross nearby(Citation: За спинами мирных жителей. Захват заложников и использование гражданского населения в качестве «живого щита» федеральными войсками России в ходе вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1996)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

On 12 August 1996, soldiers of the 101st Brigade of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs took men from the blocks of Grozny around the "15th Gorodok", their base on Lenin Street, and shielded themselves with them on the way there (see: "Hostage-Taking")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Two of them, a father and son, the occupiers tied with wire to an armored personnel carrier, drove under fire to Khankala, the main base of the occupation troops on the eastern outskirts of the city, and released on 16 August(Citation: За спинами мирных жителей. Захват заложников и использование гражданского населения в качестве «живого щита» федеральными войсками России в ходе вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1996).

The 1996 report of "Memorial" says that Russian servicemen and officers of Russian agencies in Ichkeria systematically took hostages and shielded themselves with human shields. According to the report, the occupiers shielded themselves with Chechens during the last six months of the war, from March to August 1996, most often the soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs(Citation: За спинами мирных жителей. Захват заложников и использование гражданского населения в качестве «живого щита» федеральными войсками России в ходе вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1996).

The prosecutors of the Russian army did not investigate how Russian troops shielded themselves with Chechens during assaults and held no one accountable for it (see: "Impunity of Perpetrators")(Citation: Russia/Chechnya: A Legacy of Abuse 1997)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996). On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).
